artists.name: Adjoa Kessiri
artists.tagline: A garden of desire, sung in multiplying voices
artists.bio: Adjoa Kessiri is an Accra-born singer, songwriter and producer whose art pop turns botanical processes into accounts of appetite, attachment and self-invention. Raised in a household where seed packets were saved alongside household receipts, she developed an early fascination with the practical language of cultivation. Her 2018 debut EP, Germination Instructions, translated that language into plucked nylon-string guitar, homemade percussion and multiplying vocal rounds. Recorded largely in a borrowed sewing workspace after business hours, its five songs established her characteristic tension between intimate confession and intricate arrangement.

artists.name: Aino Kuurasto
artists.tagline: The body's lost victories, held in kantele and strings
artists.bio: Aino Kuurasto is a Tampere songwriter whose chamber folk locates drama in the interval between physical effort and recollection. Debuting in 2023 with small performances built around voice and prepared kantele, she developed her repertoire through conversations with retired competitors, volunteer coaches and people returning to exercise after injury. Her songs rarely recount a decisive contest. Instead, they linger on a wrist taped by habit, the smell of a vinyl equipment cupboard, or the walk home when training no longer structures the day.

artists.name: The Alder Parliament
artists.tagline: Coastal folk suites with cathedral-sized harmonies
artists.bio: Formed in Aberystwyth in 1971, The Alder Parliament brought the scale of choral music to songs rooted in boarding houses, tidal crossings and the working coastline of west Wales. Singer and guitarist Iestyn Vale began trading arrangements with violist Ruth Fenwick and guitarist Tomos Reed at informal university-room sessions; bassist Marian Bell and drummer Gareth Pike completed a group whose five-part singing became its defining instrument. Their debut, The Estuary Keeps Its Counsel, balanced rough-edged acoustic playing with unusually patient suites, while the concert recording Five Voices Under Timber established the force of those arrangements before an audience.

artists.name: Alderwake
artists.tagline: Canal-side histories in long-form acoustic suites
artists.bio: Formed in Leeds in 1969, Alderwake built progressive folk around the working histories of the waterways: toll disputes, boat families, maintenance gangs and streets erased by redevelopment. Singer and guitarist Martin Vale met fiddler Ruth Ainsley while collecting local accounts for an adult-education history project. Guitarist Peter Hesk, bassist and harmonium player Colin Wray, and percussionist and flautist Stephen Marr completed the quintet. Their debut, The Lockkeeper’s Measure, paired hand-drawn survey-map imagery with acoustic suites in which independent vocal lines carried different witnesses through the same event. A regional breakthrough, it established a devoted audience without securing the touring income needed to sustain them; the group suspended regular work in 1974.

artists.name: Amalia Zorzán
artists.tagline: Earthbound love songs from an old observatory
artists.bio: Amalia Zorzán emerged in Córdoba, Argentina, in 2016, carrying a nylon-string guitar into a songwriting residency at an old hillside observatory. Raised between the city and her grandparents’ home in the Sierras, she absorbed family zambas alongside the formal discipline of youth chamber ensembles. Her early performances paired quietly articulated Spanish lyrics with viola and cello, treating the observatory’s creaking floorboards and long plaster reverberation as part of the arrangement. The six-song debut Perigeo established her central subject: human attachment measured against distances too large to comprehend.

artists.name: Ansel Bellweather
artists.tagline: Small household rituals scored for a quiet ensemble
artists.bio: Ansel Bellweather emerged from Portland’s small-room folk circuit in 2008 with Thumb Against String, a five-song EP recorded in a rented duplex between shifts repairing instruments at a neighborhood music shop. Raised in a household where singing accompanied chores rather than performances, he developed a repertoire around the sounds and negotiations of ordinary upkeep. His nylon-string guitar and closely doubled, murmured vocals initially carried almost everything; cellist Mara Venn and harmonium player Ellis Rook soon became his principal recording collaborators, lending the songs a chamber ensemble’s responsiveness without formalizing the project as a band.

artists.name: Aperture Republic
artists.tagline: Broken planetariums become rooms for collective hope
artists.bio: Formed in Johannesburg in 2014, Aperture Republic began when projection technician and guitarist Kabelo Radebe invited singer-pianist Naledi Maseko to score a community screening beneath a damaged portable planetarium dome. Cellist and arranger Amara Naidoo, bassist Sizwe Khumalo and drummer Pieter Venter completed the group that year. Their earliest performances paired amber star-map projections with string ostinatos, amplifier distortion and recordings of people describing shuttered public buildings. The witnesses were named, paid and given approval over their contributions—a practice that became central to the band's working method.

artists.name: The Astrolabe Union
artists.tagline: Stargazers’ ballads in intricate, sunlit movements
artists.bio: Formed in Canterbury in 1972, The Astrolabe Union began when singer-guitarist Martin Vale and viola player Elin Fenwick assembled a concert around translations of medieval astronomical instructions. Pianist Peter Hesketh, bassist Ruth Dacre, and drummer Simon Pell turned the project into a working band, rehearsing above a bookbinder’s shop and carrying a harmonium to village halls in a borrowed delivery van. Their debut, Sunward Pilgrims, caught five musicians discovering how intricate arrangements could retain the generosity of a shared song. Equinox brought their breakthrough in 1975: connected acoustic movements, buoyant electric passages, and stacked harmonies that made scholarly subject matter feel unexpectedly sunlit.

artists.name: Atlante Obliquo
artists.tagline: Obsolete observatories become orchestral guitar epics
artists.bio: Atlante Obliquo formed in Bologna in 2007 around six guitarists rehearsing in a former technical-school annex. Singer-guitarist Elia Vannini and violinist Viola Neri established the ensemble’s governing idea: orchestral scale built from small, plainly articulated melodies. With viola, cello and Ruggero Bassi’s percussion completing the ten-person lineup, their early performances paired patient instrumental writing with projections adapted from obsolete observatory plans. The images were manually advanced, sometimes leaving a single adjustment mechanism suspended above the musicians for an entire piece.

artists.name: Aurelian Voltage
artists.tagline: Private doubts turned into floodlit victory hymns
artists.bio: Formed in Birmingham in 1976, Aurelian Voltage brought the scale of a civic celebration to songs first rehearsed above a musical-instrument repair shop. Singer-pianist Julian Vane, guitarist Kit Arden, bassist Martin Rook and drummer Celia March built their early following through Midlands ballroom bookings, arriving with homemade chrome collars, satin trousers and a piano whose battered casing concealed an unusually fierce attack. Brassbound introduced their combination of intimate lyrical doubt and massed vocal release; Lionhearted supplied the breakthrough with “Stand Beside Me, Darling,” a love song whose unaltered male pronouns became central to their audience’s identification with the band.

artists.name: Avelune
artists.tagline: Tender domestic dramas in impossible costumes
artists.bio: Avelune is the recording and performance project of Montreal singer, composer and costume-maker Maëlle Desrosiers, who debuted in 2016 after presenting short song cycles in artist-run spaces. Raised in a francophone household and writing principally in English, Desrosiers developed her earliest material while helping care for her mother during a prolonged recovery. Those experiences supplied neither confession nor consolation so much as dramatic particulars: a badly peeled orange, an argument conducted in whispers, the indignity of needing help. Prepared piano and translucent, ribbed costumes became complementary signatures, making ordinary gestures sound and look newly precarious.

artists.name: Benedict Spindle
artists.tagline: A retired magician’s dazzling songs of disbelief
artists.bio: Benedict Spindle emerged from Melbourne's small-theatre circuit in 1975, a retired stage magician who exchanged paid astonishment for songs about the need to believe. Born in 1950, he had spent his early twenties performing close-up tricks and supporting suburban variety bills. His debut, Professional Doubter, brought that patter to fingerpicked guitar, upright piano and unexpectedly muscular electric passages. Pianist and arranger Miriam Vale became his enduring musical counterpart; guitarist Clive Ransome, bassist Ada Pell and drummer Martin Quill supplied an ensemble capable of making elaborate arrangements feel physically played rather than merely assembled.

artists.name: Borrowed Viaduct
artists.tagline: Songs of rebuilding, carried by a ragged choir
artists.bio: Borrowed Viaduct formed in Christchurch in late 2011, when singer-guitarists Mara Bell and Eli Sutherland began rehearsing with double bassist Tessa Rook and drummer Finn Mercer in a fluorescent-lit unit behind a joinery workshop. All four had been playing informal benefits and borrowed-room shows during the city’s earthquake recovery. Their name came from Bell’s description of friendship as infrastructure nobody owned. The 2012 EP Propwork established their signature: Bell’s grainy alto crossing Sutherland’s tensile tenor, a bow worrying the bass strings beneath acoustic strumming and electric-guitar abrasion.

artists.name: Bracken Dial
artists.tagline: Acoustic labyrinths for gamblers and guilty consciences
artists.bio: Formed in Edinburgh in 1969, Bracken Dial brought the disputatious intimacy of a late-night folk session into contact with early-music counterpoint. Guitarist and singer Euan Riddell, fiddler Mairi Keddie and reed player Alastair Veitch first worked together in borrowed university rehearsal rooms; bassist Niall Strachan and percussionist Isobel Drennan completed the quintet before its debut, Nine Knots. Riddell's dry, conversational baritone anchored arrangements in which alternate-tuned guitar, crumhorn and bowed strings seemed to pursue different routes through the same difficult question.

artists.name: Breakwater Atlas
artists.tagline: Shipyard elegies rising into choral storms
artists.bio: Formed in Glasgow in 2008, Breakwater Atlas grew out of informal rehearsals between singer-guitarist Eilidh Kerr, violist Mairi Sutherland and drummer Fraser Baird. Cellist and keyboard player Callum Reid and bassist Niall Mercer completed a quintet whose early performances paired fingerpicked songs with monochrome maritime films projected onto borrowed sheets. Their debut EP, Basalt Psalms, established the essential contrast: Kerr’s low, close voice against bowed strings, patient percussion and crescendos that seemed to gather from the building itself.

artists.name: Calder Rusk
artists.tagline: Dry-country confessionals with a gathering roar
artists.bio: Calder Rusk emerged from Saskatoon in 2024 with songs that treated prairie drought not as scenery but as a pressure exerted on families, work and speech. A solo songwriter supported by a small recording ensemble, Rusk built his earliest arrangements around baritone guitar and an inexpensive banjo played with a cello bow. Before his debut, he worked seasonal maintenance jobs outside the city and tested songs at small listening rooms, where his habit of beginning almost below conversation level made the eventual eruptions feel startlingly close.

artists.name: Carmine Rookery
artists.tagline: Tabloid monarchs in velvet-clad rock pageants
artists.bio: Carmine Rookery formed in Birmingham in 1973 around singer-pianist Julian Vane and guitarist Ellis Marrick, former school friends who rehearsed above a theatrical costumier’s workshop. Bassist and arranger Ruth Calder and drummer Martin Quill completed a quartet whose scarlet capes and portable chessboard stage belied a practical apprenticeship in working men’s clubs. Their debut, Velvet Pretenders, paired twelve-string intimacy with massed vocal arguments, establishing the band’s enduring subject: ordinary people seduced, employed or discarded by counterfeit greatness.

artists.name: Cassian Mothusi
artists.tagline: Backyard astronomer, earthbound guitar romantic
artists.bio: Cassian Mothusi is a Pretoria singer-songwriter whose alternate-tuned guitars and close three-part harmonies turn private longing into expansive folk-rock. He began performing under his own name in 2011, bringing songs from backyard observing sessions to small acoustic bills around Hatfield. An amateur astronomer with a secondhand reflector telescope, he drew star charts by hand and rehearsed beneath the red lamp he used to preserve his night vision. Bassist and singer Lerato Kwele and drummer, guitarist and singer Pieter Venter became his recurring studio and touring partners, giving his solitary writing a recognisable ensemble sound.

artists.name: Clube dos Cometas
artists.tagline: First loves and losing teams, buoyed by woodwinds
artists.bio: Clube dos Cometas formed in Lisbon in 2020 around songs Tomás Seabra wrote after evening sessions with an amateur athletics group. Seabra, a guitarist and pianist, recruited violinist Inês Valente and clarinetist Duarte Falcão through shared rehearsal spaces; bassist Leonor Matos and drummer Vasco Pires completed the quintet. Their earliest performances paired the modest bustle of local sports-club gatherings with arrangements unusually attentive to small sounds: a bow lifting from a string, a clarinet taking breath, trainers squeaking beyond the rehearsal-room door. Hand-painted team pennants became a recurring stage detail, linking their chamber pop to the affectionate, unglamorous world it described.

artists.name: The Copper Census
artists.tagline: Orchard-town harmonies, gathering electric weather
artists.bio: The Copper Census formed in Wenatchee, Washington, in 2008 around siblings Jonah and Mara Voss, whose interlocking harmonies grew out of singing together during long drives between packinghouse shifts. Joined by organist Ellis Rook, bassist Tessa Vale, and drummer Ben Calder, they rehearsed in a former refrigeration-service shop. Their name came from a coffee tin used to count rehearsal contributions: a modest accounting ritual that suited songs about wages, distance, and the people a town could not afford to lose.

artists.name: Crown of Satellites
artists.tagline: Stage-fright ballads in sequins and six-part harmony
artists.bio: Formed in Birmingham in 1973, Crown of Satellites turned backstage terror into arena-scale theatre. Choir-trained singer and pianist Adrian Venn met guitarist Martin Rook while accompanying amateur dramatics; bassist Celia Brand, drummer Hugh Mercer and keyboardist Philip Sayer completed the quintet. All five sang, building six-part studio harmonies by double-casting Venn’s upper line. Their early shows paired twelve-string ballads with brass-like guitar fanfares and homemade astronomical costumes, sequins shedding across pub stages. Beneath the pageantry lay songs about wages, family expectations and the peculiar shame of wanting applause.

artists.name: Céleste Vaudrel
artists.tagline: Small family histories, scored for an enormous heart
artists.bio: Céleste Vaudrel is a Montréal songwriter whose chamber folk gives family anecdotes the scale of orchestral scenes without sanding away their awkwardness. Raised in a francophone household in the city’s east end, she learned guitar from an aunt and began arranging songs around the bass clarinet after hearing its low register through a rehearsal-room wall. Her 2018 debut EP, Dimanche chez Lucie, grew from performances in apartments and small listening rooms. Its nylon-string guitar, close-miked mezzo-soprano and spare woodwind parts established a method she would retain: begin with something somebody actually said, then compose around what they avoided saying.

artists.name: The Damask Engine
artists.tagline: Clockwork pop epics with sawdust on their boots
artists.bio: Formed in Bristol in 1972, The Damask Engine grew from folk-club acquaintances and a rehearsal arrangement above a joinery workshop. Singer and twelve-string guitarist Gabriel Venn brought sharply observed character songs; pianist Ruth Calder supplied the harmonic machinery that could turn a modest refrain into an album-side drama. With guitarist Martin Pike, bassist and cellist Celia Rook, and drummer Owen Brice, they developed a progressive pop whose grand designs still smelled of hot dust and cut wood. Their debut, Copper Apron, established the combination of acoustic bustle, Mellotron haze and meticulously overdubbed vocal fanfares.

artists.name: Daria Zorvelli
artists.tagline: Scandal-sheet ballads with a velvet orchestral sting
artists.bio: Daria Zorvelli emerged from Trieste in 1995 with songs that treated the newspaper column as both miniature theater and unreliable evidence. Raised by a municipal archivist and a dressmaker, she studied piano, arranged music for a student theater company and supported her earliest recordings by proofreading overnight copy. Her debut, Errata, paired harpsichord and plucked strings with a low, confidential vocal; its narrators sounded less interested in clearing their names than in choosing which details survived. Zorvelli remained the project’s sole songwriter and central performer, working with a recurring circle of chamber players rather than a fixed backing band.

artists.name: Eira Solhavn
artists.tagline: Polar-night confessions blooming into weightless choirs
artists.bio: Eira Solhavn is a Tromsø singer, songwriter and producer whose ambient pop turns the small acoustics of domestic life into enveloping choral spaces. She began releasing music in 2018, assembling the five-track EP Lydspor around a felt-muted upright piano, a borrowed recorder and layers of her own voice. Recorded between evening shifts at a community arts venue, its songs retained radiator clicks and the scrape of piano pedals. Solhavn’s restrained delivery, alternating Norwegian verses with brief English refrains, established a persona less remote than her surroundings suggested: observant, dryly tender and attentive to the practical rituals that carry people through darkness.

artists.name: elayra.exe
artists.tagline: Acoustic ghosts inside wide-screen pop release
artists.bio: elayra.exe is the recording alias of Singaporean producer, songwriter and singer Elian Teo, who debuted in 2017 with the five-track EP Peachbuffer. Raised in the northeast of Singapore, Teo learned guitar through school performances before becoming absorbed in the tiny sounds surrounding a take: a thumbnail catching a string, a chair shifting, an unfinished breath. His earliest productions rearranged those scraps into buoyant electropop, with close-recorded tenor vocals multiplied into luminous falsetto stacks. The executable suffix signaled a working method rather than a virtual character: songs treated as systems that could be opened, altered and run again.

artists.name: Elspeth Rooke
artists.tagline: Family letters scored for woodwinds and wonder
artists.bio: Elspeth Rooke is a Wellington songwriter whose chamber pop draws its emotional detail from family correspondence: affectionate instructions, crossed-out admissions, and news once considered too ordinary to preserve. She debuted in 2018 with Sepal, a five-song EP developed from letters exchanged by her grandmother and great-aunt. Recorded with a small circle of local instrumentalists, it established her characteristic proportions: close, conversational singing; nylon-string guitar; and woodwinds that seem to think alongside the words. Pressed flowers, initially used in her handmade release packaging, became a recurring visual signature.

artists.name: Euan Tern
artists.tagline: Crooked guitar patterns carried by submerged beats
artists.bio: Euan Tern is a Bristol singer, guitarist and producer whose work joins intricate alternate tunings to percussion assembled from field recordings. He began performing under his own name in 2010, bringing a steel-string guitar, a small sampler and recordings gathered along reservoir margins to seated shows in upstairs venues. His debut EP, Bracken Index, established the essential contrast: close, fallible singing against rhythms that seemed to rise from beneath the floor. Tern remained the sole permanent artist, working with a changing circle of instrumentalists rather than a fixed band.

artists.name: Faro de Cobre
artists.tagline: Harbor-born rock with operatic, ocean-wide lift
artists.bio: Formed in Valparaíso in 1986, Faro de Cobre built their sound from the city’s steep domestic streets and working waterfront. Singer and twelve-string guitarist Tomás Araya, keyboardist and alto vocalist Inés Mella, guitarist Gabriel Leiva, bassist Mauricio Cisternas and drummer Paula Rojas rehearsed above a marine-electrical workshop, where their first recordings caught as much stairwell echo as amplifier sound. The EP Turno de noche and debut album La mesa de todos paired maritime labor narratives with bright acoustic attack, melodic bass and harmonies conceived for several people singing at once.

artists.name: Foxglove Abacus
artists.tagline: Elaborate folk fables from an unreliable herbarium
artists.bio: Formed in Canterbury in 1971, Foxglove Abacus turned the English folk group into a committee of unreliable natural historians. Singer-guitarist Martin Pell and guitarist Elspeth Vane met while mounting a small exhibition of invented medicinal plants; bassoonist Judith Rook, bassist Owen Cresswell and percussionist Nicholas Wren completed the ensemble. Their early performances paired interlocking acoustic guitars with modal vocal rounds and solemn readings from a hand-engraved imaginary herbarium. Mandrake Witness caught the intimacy of those evenings: chair noise, breath through reeds and Pell’s uncannily persuasive accounts of impossible specimens.

artists.name: Gorse Arithmetic
artists.tagline: Empty-town stories rising into open-road choruses
artists.bio: Gorse Arithmetic formed in Dunedin in 2008 around siblings Ewan and Mereana Bell, whose low guitar figures and interlocking voices gave the quartet its distinctive scale: intimate enough to catch a breath, broad enough to suggest an entire district beyond the window. Bassist Ruth Calder and drummer Tom Ransome completed the group after meeting the Bells through local benefit shows. Their debut EP, Census of Porches, recorded in a borrowed community hall, introduced songs drawn from shrinking school rolls, shuttered businesses and the complicated loyalties of people who leave rural towns.

artists.name: Hushframe
artists.tagline: Voice-note intimacy blooming into neon choruses
artists.bio: Hushframe formed in Seoul in 2023 around the small noises usually edited out of pop records: a swallowed breath, a chair shifting, the pause before someone decides what to say. Singer and songwriter Han Iseul had been recording acoustic sketches into her phone when producer and keyboardist Park Doyun began arranging them in a spare room near Mangwon Market. Their name described the space they wanted to build around those recordings—a quiet enclosure capable of holding a very large chorus. Iseul’s unforced mezzo-soprano remained close enough to reveal the grain of each consonant, even as Doyun surrounded it with plucked synthesizers, elastic bass, and stacked vocoder harmonies.

artists.name: Hushmere
artists.tagline: Bedside lullabies opening onto an endless horizon
artists.bio: Hushmere is the recording name of Wellington songwriter and home-recordist Eli Mercer, who began the project in 2023 during a period of overnight care for a family member. Working between a small rented room in Newtown and a borrowed practice space, Mercer recorded fingerpicked guitar, secondhand harmonium, and a tenor pitched barely above conversation. The earliest sessions were shaped by necessity: headphones instead of monitors, short takes between household tasks, and microphones placed close enough to catch breath without requiring volume. The name Hushmere joined the quiet of those rooms to the imagined breadth beyond them.

artists.name: hushrelay
artists.tagline: Apartment whispers dissolving into neon weather
artists.bio: hushrelay is the Taipei ambient-pop duo of vocalist and songwriter Lin Yu-ning and producer Chen Yi-an, formed in 2022 after exchanging recordings made in neighboring rented apartments in Zhongshan District. Lin brought nylon-string guitar figures and melodies sung quietly enough not to disturb the corridor; Chen supplied cassette transfers, synthesizer drones, and contact-microphone recordings of domestic machinery. Their name describes the process: one person’s near-silence passed to another, then returned with an altered atmosphere. Early performances paired a seated vocal setup with a folding table of tape players, allowing songs to drift between recognizable choruses and stretches of fluttering sound.

artists.name: Inés Talavera
artists.tagline: Songs of water and inheritance, carried by strings
artists.bio: Inés Talavera emerged from Valparaíso in 2021 with songs that treated water as both a physical necessity and a contested inheritance. Raised between the port’s steep neighborhoods and relatives’ smallholding in the Aconcagua Valley, she learned charango from an uncle and later studied arrangement while working as a music copyist. Her early performances paired a solitary, dark alto with wiry plucked figures; handwritten ochre maps laid beside her instruments became an enduring visual signature. Talavera performs under her own name, with cellist Lucía Arancibia and woodwind player Tomás Leiva forming the core of a changing chamber ensemble.

artists.name: Inês Valdouro
artists.tagline: Fingerpicked migration songs with a string horizon
artists.bio: Inês Valdouro emerged in Coimbra in 2013 with songs that made a fingerpicked guitar sound capable of carrying an orchestra. Raised between the city and her maternal grandparents’ village near Arganil, she learned sewing alongside guitar, later making embroidered stagewear whose branching stitches became a recognizable counterpart to her arrangements. Her debut EP, Linho Elétrico, paired close-recorded Portuguese vocals with a string sextet, tracing the experiences of young people moving from inland villages into rented urban lives. Its modest first pressing circulated through independent bookshops and university concerts before finding a wider audience on national cultural radio.

artists.name: Isotherm Chapel
artists.tagline: Wordless winter hymns rising into orchestral thunder
artists.bio: Isotherm Chapel formed in Sapporo in 2022 around pianist and alto vocalist Mio Takase, guitarist Ren Shidara, and cellist Aya Fushimi. Bassist Sōta Naruse and drummer Kei Mizuno completed a lineup whose earliest rehearsals paired chamber arrangements with the patient amplification of ambient rock. Their name described an imagined place of equal temperature: a shelter in which individual sounds could coexist without losing their edges. Takase sang entirely without words, letting breath and vowel carry melodies that began with the directness of folk song before opening into long, glacial crescendos.

artists.name: Isóbara
artists.tagline: Fingerpicked fault lines opening into vast sound
artists.bio: Formed in Valparaíso in 2012, Isóbara began with songwriter and guitarist Amalia Véliz and electronics builder Celia Neira trading recordings of stairwell reverberation and guitar harmonics. Guitarist Tomás Arancibia and percussionist Darío Leiva completed the quartet before its first release, the five-track EP Cizalla. Recorded above a working upholstery shop, it established their distinctive scale: fingertips rasping across bronze strings in the foreground, slow electronic movement extending far behind them. Their name, borrowed from the lines joining points of equal atmospheric pressure, suited music whose apparently calm surfaces concealed intricate rhythmic forces.

artists.name: Ivara Sorel
artists.tagline: Baroque pop theatre for the selves we invent
artists.bio: Ivara Sorel emerged from Antwerp’s small-theatre circuit in 2014, bringing a pianist’s attention to touch and a costume-maker’s sense of transformation to orchestral pop. The solo project’s early performances used portable mirrored flats, cobalt tailoring and a prepared upright piano; trumpeter Mila Declerck and percussionist Bram Vercauteren became recurring collaborators rather than a fixed backing band. Sorel’s debut EP, Cobalt Alias, established her dark alto and characteristic dramatic scale: a whispered social exchange could suddenly expand into bright brass harmony, then collapse to the sound of a pedal lifting. Its five songs introduced the museum after closing as both a physical setting and a place where identities could be tried on without witnesses.

artists.name: Iver Ruskedal
artists.tagline: Fingerpicked songs dissolving into glacial circuitry
artists.bio: Iver Ruskedal is a Bergen singer, guitarist, and electronic producer whose fingerpicked songs seem to change state as they unfold. Debuting in 2012 with Moraine Teeth, he established a method of recording acoustic guitar at close range, then breaking its resonance into grains that could drift around the original performance. His early sessions took place in a rented rehearsal cellar, where rain entering a ventilation shaft became an accidental percussion source. Ruskedal remained the project’s sole permanent member, treating outdoor recording trips and solitary editing sessions as equally important parts of composition.

artists.name: The Juniper Detention
artists.tagline: Schoolyard secrets, six voices, widescreen guitars
artists.bio: Formed in Athens, Georgia, in 2008, The Juniper Detention joined two sibling households into a six-voice folk-rock band. Mara, Eli and Owen Bellamy had sung together since childhood; Lena, Caleb and Tess Voss brought mandolin, bass and a drummer’s instinct for turning a singalong into a charge. Their name came from the nickname for a supervised lunch period beside a school’s juniper hedge. Early rehearsals took place in the Bellamys’ converted carport, where acoustic instruments competed with borrowed amplifiers and the voices learned to cut through both.

artists.name: Karstové Divadlo
artists.tagline: Cavernous guitar suites with a beating human pulse
artists.bio: Formed in Brno in 2008, Karstové Divadlo began when guitarist Matěj Křenek and hammered-dulcimer player and singer Tereza Vránová started rehearsing in a former scenery workshop. Cellist Lenka Ševčíková, bassist Ondřej Král and drummer Pavel Hradil completed the group that year. Their name, meaning “Karst Theatre,” reflected an early fascination with the nearby Moravian Karst: not merely its grandeur, but the peculiar intimacy of hearing a footstep travel farther than a voice. Their debut album, Vápenné ticho, established the essential contrast between patient guitar loops, struck strings and Vránová’s unforced Czech alto.

artists.name: kasane/84
artists.tagline: Forgotten cinemas flicker inside weightless songs
artists.bio: Formed in Kyoto in 2016, kasane/84 is the partnership of singer and guitarist Emi Kuroda and sound artist Sota Nishimura. They met while helping catalogue equipment from a closed neighborhood cinema, where Nishimura recorded the ventilation system and Kuroda tested songs in the empty auditorium. Their name joins the Japanese word for layering to the eighty-four-second cassette loop used in their first performance. Forgotten cinemas became more than a visual signature: the duo treated their pockets of silence, worn upholstery and mechanical hum as acoustic materials.

artists.name: kitenge/64
artists.tagline: Pirate-radio folk with thumb-piano loops and lift
artists.bio: Formed in Nairobi in 2013, kitenge/64 began as a collaboration between singer and nylon-string guitarist Nyambura Kibe, thumb-piano player and vocalist Musa Kaviti, and producer Wanja Mugo. Their first recordings were made after hours in a borrowed rehearsal room in Ngara, with a laptop balanced on an equipment case and traffic entering through the window. The name paired a patterned kitenge cloth used to wrap their cables with the 64-step sequencer underlying their earliest arrangements. Their debut EP, Request Line, established a distinctive vocabulary: plucked strings, chipped electronic beats and dedications delivered with the closeness of an unlicensed late-night broadcast.

artists.name: kitevault
artists.tagline: Poolside memories cresting into floodlit synth release
artists.bio: kitevault is the recording alias of Bristol songwriter and producer Ellis Mercer, who debuted in 2014 after abandoning a competitive swimming routine that had structured most of his adolescence. Early recordings were assembled in a rented room from secondhand synthesizers, acoustic guitar and a borrowed hammered dulcimer. Mercer recorded the instrument close enough to capture the clatter of its dampers, then cut those sounds into bright, uneven loops. The six-track EP Splitlane introduced his defining contrast: a vulnerable tenor surrounded by machinery built for collective release.

artists.name: Kito Mwangala
artists.tagline: Night-bus stories in thumb piano and fractured light
artists.bio: Kito Mwangala emerged in Nairobi in 2012 with Diesel Arithmetic, a five-track EP assembled between paid recording jobs and late journeys home. Raised in Eastlands, he learned guitar through neighborhood rehearsals and began treating a secondhand thumb piano as both melodic instrument and recording clock. His earliest tracks preserved the small mechanical sounds surrounding a performance: chair joints, jacket fasteners and the click of a recorder being handled. Mwangala remained the sole songwriter and principal performer, bringing collaborators into sessions rather than maintaining a fixed band.

artists.name: Käigukuma
artists.tagline: Precision pop for prodigies learning how to lose
artists.bio: Käigukuma formed in Tallinn in 2020, bringing together singer and pianist Liise Vaher, electronic producer Rasmus Keld and string player Marta Lees. Vaher had spent her school years on Estonia's junior chess circuit; Keld was recording small acoustic ensembles, and Lees moved between chamber recitals and experimental performance spaces. Their first sessions took place in a borrowed rehearsal room, where pizzicato viola and the click of a piano pedal became material for tightly gridded pop arrangements. Their name suggests the lingering glow of a move: an action completed, its consequences still unfolding.

artists.name: The Lacquer Picnic
artists.tagline: Polite family feuds that bloom into orchestral rapture
artists.bio: The Lacquer Picnic formed in Wellington in 1998 around singer and guitarist Felix Ransome and pianist-arranger Imogen Vale, who met while accompanying a community theatre production in Newtown. With woodwind player Mereana Bell, violist Tessa Quill, bassist Owen Prentice and drummer Daniel Hume, they developed a chamber-pop language of fingerpicked guitar, mobile inner harmonies and family disagreements conducted at exemplary volume. Their debut EP, Good China, was recorded after hours in a borrowed rehearsal room; its close harmonies and dry, almost tactile sound established the ensemble’s preference for intimacy before spectacle.

artists.name: Ladderwake
artists.tagline: After-hours folk songs built for a roomful of voices
artists.bio: Ladderwake formed in Leeds in 2021 around friendships sustained between late shifts rather than a pre-existing music scene. Singer and acoustic guitarist Daniel Rusk met electric guitarist Priya Sen while working for an event-installation contractor; bassist Beth Armitage and drummer Owen Kellett joined through a shared rehearsal arrangement in a former upholstery workshop in Holbeck. Their name came from the pale ladder-shaped marks left on a warehouse floor after equipment was cleared away. Early sets paired interlocking guitar figures with harmonies learned around a single microphone, lending songs about ordinary obligations an unexpectedly expansive reach.

artists.name: Las Falsas Magnolias
artists.tagline: Baroque pop tricks with no promise of a happy ending
artists.bio: Formed in Buenos Aires in 2010, Las Falsas Magnolias began when singer and songwriter Inés Valdés brought a folder of Spanish-language songs to keyboardist Tomás Lezama, then accompanying rehearsals in a small Almagro theatre. Cellist and arranger Lucía Berón and drummer Mateo Soria completed the quartet. Their debut EP, Pronósticos desiertos, was recorded between rehearsals, its nylon-string guitar, clipped cello figures and overlapping voices suggesting elaborate stage machinery assembled in a rented apartment. Early performances paired borrowed harpsichords with mirrored costume panels and posters advertising wonders the band conspicuously declined to deliver.

artists.name: Lenka Vratilová
artists.tagline: Gold-leaf ballads about what museums cannot keep
artists.bio: Lenka Vratilová is a Brno songwriter whose chamber folk examines the uneasy passage from possession to care. She began performing under her own name in 2023, bringing nylon-string guitar songs to small listening spaces and artist-run exhibitions. Trained in photographic documentation for conservation work, she developed a lyrical vocabulary from condition reports, disputed provenance, and the tiny interventions through which damaged objects become presentable. Her songs resist the reassuring idea that preservation settles ownership: a polished surface can conceal a journey nobody consented to.

artists.name: Les Escaliers de Poche
artists.tagline: Small-room stories dressed in woodwinds and wonder
artists.bio: Les Escaliers de Poche formed in Montréal in 2015 around siblings Anaïs and Rémi Venne, whose first arrangements were devised at an upright piano in their rented Villeray apartment. Anaïs wrote closely observed French-language songs about shared kitchens, difficult telephone calls and the small negotiations of living together; Rémi supplied guitar and sibling harmonies. Clarinetist Maude Bélisle and cellist Étienne Sirois completed a quartet whose woodwind miniatures and lightly bowed counterlines could make a domestic exchange feel almost theatrical. Their name came from Rémi’s folded-paper staircase models, originally used to work out how four musicians might fit onto cramped café stages.

artists.name: León de Alambre
artists.tagline: Masked rivalries played out in colossal guitar choruses
artists.bio: León de Alambre formed in Monterrey in 2012, bringing the intimacy of acoustic song circles into the city's hard-edged rock circuit. Singer and nylon-string guitarist Mateo Sada joined electric guitarist Inés Treviño, bassist Julián Leal and drummer Alma Cantú after a benefit concert in a converted upholstery workshop. Their early sets began almost unamplified, with scraped strings and heel taps, before erupting into braided guitar lines and choruses sung by all four members. Violet followspots and commissioned lucha masks turned those transitions into miniature confrontations.

artists.name: Liisi Orvek
artists.tagline: Family letters unfolded into strings and snow
artists.bio: Liisi Orvek emerged from Tallinn’s chamber-folk circuit in 2018 with Vowel Atlas, a five-song EP that placed her close-miked alto among nylon-string guitar, viola and softly argumentative woodwinds. Raised in a household where singing and sewing occupied the same evening, she began writing after sorting correspondence exchanged by her mother and grandmother during successive Baltic winters. Rather than setting complete letters to music, Orvek extracted salutations, practical details and unfinished thoughts, building songs around the emotional pressure of ordinary language. Her embroidered stagewear developed alongside the arrangements: restrained silhouettes marked with branching stitches copied from family textiles.

artists.name: Lucía Bermejal
artists.tagline: An estranged pupil's songs, blooming into orchestral grace
artists.bio: Lucía Bermejal is a Córdoba-born singer, composer and charango player whose orchestral folk turns private correspondence into patient, large-scale song. Before her recording debut in 2020, she moved between neighborhood peñas and informal chamber rehearsals, learning to hear Argentine dance rhythms as material for ensemble writing rather than decorative accompaniment. Her early compositions grew from unsent letters to the arranger who had taught her orchestration. Their estrangement, which Bermejal has declined to explain publicly, became a recurring subject without becoming a publicly staged dispute.

artists.name: Lumen Relay
artists.tagline: Whispered verses, acoustic ghosts, euphoric release
artists.bio: Formed in Melbourne in 2016, Lumen Relay brought the close grain of acoustic songwriting into the expansive architecture of electronic pop. Singer and guitarist Mara Venn met producer and pianist Theo Sayer while sharing rehearsal space in North Melbourne; percussionist Felix Orr joined after supplying a borrowed drum kit for their first show. Their debut EP, Borrowed Hours, made a vocabulary from small sounds: guitar-string squeaks, felted piano, brushed timber and Venn's husky, near-spoken alto. Those details survived even when the songs opened into broad, buoyant refrains.

artists.name: Luvo Nqolase
artists.tagline: Spiraling guitar patterns beneath a sky of voices
artists.bio: Luvo Nqolase emerged from Makhanda’s small acoustic circuit in 2011 with Seven Against Nine, a self-financed EP whose fingerpicked guitar figures seemed to rotate at different speeds. Singing in isiXhosa and English, he paired a clear, woody tenor with lyrics about family plots, seasonal work and the distances used to measure the sky. Early performances relied on a battered acoustic guitar, occasional concertina and vocal phrases repeated until a solitary singer suggested a gathering.

artists.name: Madoriel
artists.tagline: Private piano dreams unfolding into choral art pop
artists.bio: Madoriel is the recording and performance identity of Osaka composer, pianist and singer Rika Minase, who debuted in 2023. Raised in a household where an upright piano shared space with sewing equipment, Minase developed an ear for incidental percussion: pedal knocks, scissors closing, the dry chatter of a bobbin. After studying composition and working as an audio editor, she began presenting short piano-and-electronics sets in small galleries around Osaka. Her earliest performances placed the audience close enough to hear the objects laid across the strings, with translucent, articulated costumes catching the movement of her shoulders as she played.

artists.name: Malena Urdavia
artists.tagline: Songs of chance, scored for strings and strange rhythms
artists.bio: Malena Urdavia emerged from Buenos Aires in 2019 with Spanish-language songs that treated superstition as both family inheritance and compositional method. Raised in Villa Crespo, she learned nylon-string guitar at home and later arranged music for small independent theatre productions. Her earliest performances paired unamplified guitar with bass clarinet, leaving room for the scrape of a thumbnail or a sharply inhaled breath. Although billed under her own name, Urdavia developed a recurring ensemble around clarinetist Inés Cárdenas and string arranger Tomás Varela.

artists.name: Mireille Dorsenne
artists.tagline: A vanished magician's tricks, sung without illusion
artists.bio: Mireille Dorsenne emerged from Montréal’s small-theatre circuit in 2021, singing French-language chamber songs whose elegance never concealed their workings. Raised in Rosemont, she studied harpsichord while earning money as a rehearsal accompanist and theatre dresser. Her early performances placed the instrument beside a bare work light, with pulley ropes and microphone cables left in view. Dorsenne developed a recurring narrative persona: the daughter of a vanished stage magician, less interested in solving his disappearance than in describing the weight of his props. Violist and singer Anaïs Viger, bassist and singer Lucien Bérard, and drummer Émile Sauriol became her regular recording collaborators.

artists.name: morrow// FM
artists.tagline: Bedroom confessions built for the last festival set
artists.bio: Formed in Melbourne in 2014, morrow// FM began as the exchange of unfinished recordings between singer-guitarist Eli Venn and electronic producer Mara Keane. Venn recorded after hospitality shifts in a Brunswick rental; Keane rebuilt his fingerpicked demos into loops on headphones, keeping the squeak of strings and the click of the room’s ceiling fan. Their name joined Venn’s habit of postponing difficult conversations until tomorrow with Keane’s fascination with the intimate, disembodied company of late-night radio. The debut EP Soft Reset introduced their defining contrast: a voice apparently inches from the listener, surrounded by a horizon of synthetic sound.

artists.name: Municipal Swans
artists.tagline: Small-town ceremonies, lavishly sung and quietly sad
artists.bio: Municipal Swans formed in Ghent in 1997 around siblings Pieter and Lotte Vervaet, whose close harmonies had developed singing at family gatherings and amateur theatrical productions. With cellist Anke De Smet, reed player Bram Declerck and drummer Jonas Verhelst, they rehearsed in a former parish meeting hall, building elaborate songs from acoustic guitar, upright piano and instruments borrowed from local ensembles. Their debut, Velvet Procession, treated provincial ceremonies as intimate dramas: a ribbon-cutting witnessed from the refreshment table, a retiring official trying to finish his speech. Pieter’s unhurried baritone and Lotte’s bright, delayed entrances became their defining signature.

artists.name: Myrglass
artists.tagline: Fingerpicked weather systems and fractured beats
artists.bio: Myrglass formed in Bergen in 2017 around singer and guitarist Eirik Velde, sound artist Signe Røed and percussionist Maja Helle. Velde and Røed began exchanging recordings after meeting at a listening session in a converted print workshop; Helle joined when their first live arrangements proved too elastic for a fixed drum machine. Early performances paired fingerpicked guitar with the close, brittle sounds of ice, gravel and meltwater, recorded on trips into western Norway’s glacial valleys. Their name came from Velde’s notebook description of peatland pools that appeared opaque until the light changed.

artists.name: Nacreline
artists.tagline: Featherlight verses, enormous choruses, no easy resolutions
artists.bio: Nacreline formed in Seoul in 2022 around singer and lyricist Han Seorin and producer and multi-instrumentalist Kang Ijun. They met while recording incidental music for a student dance production, discovering that Seorin’s softly articulated melodies could remain legible inside Ijun’s densely edited acoustic fragments. Their earliest sets in small rooms around Mullae paired a single microphone and steel-string guitar with a laptop, placing domestic sounds against electronic arrangements large enough to suggest an outdoor stage.

artists.name: Nacreloop
artists.tagline: Voice-note intimacy carried on luminous pop pulses
artists.bio: Nacreloop is a Seoul electropop duo formed in 2023 by singer and guitarist Han Iseul and producer Seo Dabin. They met while editing sound for a small contemporary-dance production in Mullae, where Han's fingerpicked rehearsal recordings became material for Seo's sampler. Their name joins nacre—the reflective lining of a shell—to the repeating audio fragments that became their working method. Early sessions took place in Seo's compact apartment studio, with a linen curtain hung behind the microphone and buses audible beneath quieter takes.

artists.name: Nandi Veyalo
artists.tagline: Hushed songs of care, unfolding in brass and strings
artists.bio: Nandi Veyalo is a Cape Town singer-songwriter whose chamber folk makes an expansive sound from quiet domestic acts. Debuting in 2024, she first performed seated with a nylon-string guitar, shaping songs around the pauses and interruptions of helping care for an older relative. Her writing resisted both confession as spectacle and the easy dignity often assigned to caregiving: tenderness shared space with boredom, resentment and an unexpectedly funny remark over a cooling meal. Her low, textured voice and patient guitar figures became the center of a small ensemble with cellist Mira Davids and flugelhorn player Tebo Maseko.

artists.name: Neem Circuit
artists.tagline: Garden songs taking root inside restless beats
artists.bio: Neem Circuit formed in Bengaluru in 2012, when singer and guitarist Kavya Rao began recording conversations at a neighbourhood vegetable-growing cooperative where she volunteered. Producer Nikhil Soman, then editing location sound for short films, turned the hiss of irrigation hoses and the click of pruning shears into percussion. Bassist and keyboard player Leela Dev joined before their debut EP, Dripline, appeared that November. Its combination of close, unvarnished singing and guitar splintered into luminous digital grains established their guiding tension: songs rooted in particular patches of earth, pulled forward by an impatient city.

artists.name: Nell Harrowby
artists.tagline: Small household stories, quietly immense arrangements
artists.bio: Wellington songwriter Nell Harrowby debuted in 2021 with A Cup Left Cooling, a chamber-folk record in which household routines carried the weight usually reserved for grand declarations. Raised in the city’s southern suburbs, she learned guitar on an instrument with a lifting bridge and began writing during a period of shared family caregiving. Her songs kept the practical details: a rearranged appointment, the wrong brand of soup, the embarrassment of needing someone to stay. Singing in a warm, grain-edged alto, Harrowby treated these incidents as relationships in motion rather than lessons to be delivered.

artists.name: The Ninth Velodrome
artists.tagline: Faded sporting dreams swell into orchestral thunder
artists.bio: The Ninth Velodrome formed in Brno in 2004 around guitarist and harmonium player Matěj Vávra and cellist Eliška Konečná, whose early rehearsals brought conservatory players together with musicians from the city's basement concert circuit. Joined by Ondřej Bartoš, Tereza Malá, Viktor Šimek and choir director Zuzana Havelková, the six-person collective developed an instrumental language of bowed guitars, orchestral percussion and wordless massed harmonies. Their name referred not to a particular arena but to an imagined extra circuit beyond the official race: effort continuing after the result had ceased to matter.

artists.name: The Ochre Switch
artists.tagline: Coal-country confessionals with open-road choruses
artists.bio: Formed in Newcastle in 2008, The Ochre Switch built their first songs around the distance between a family kitchen and the highway out of town. Siblings Eli Venn, on lead vocals and baritone guitar, and Mara Venn, on acoustic guitar and harmony vocals, began performing together at small Hunter venues before bassist Tom Calder and drummer Nina Bell completed the group. Their debut EP, Borrowed Driveway, caught the scrape of picks, close sibling harmonies and a rhythm section already leaning toward bigger rooms. Its songs treated departure as a negotiation with the people left holding spare keys.

artists.name: Odile Marchand-Lowe
artists.tagline: Tender art pop from an imaginary operating theatre
artists.bio: Odile Marchand-Lowe is a Montreal songwriter, arranger, and producer whose art pop makes the language of surgery unexpectedly tender. Debuting in 2018, she emerged from small acoustic performances and self-recorded experiments in which nylon-string guitar shared space with bass clarinet, bowed strings, and modular synthesizer. Her songs initially circulated through local listening nights rather than conventional band bills. Raised in a French- and English-speaking household, she writes primarily in English, favoring exact physical details over grand declarations: adhesive against skin, the taste of an anesthetic, a sleeve rolled carefully past a bruise.

artists.name: Oisín Keld
artists.tagline: Restless guitar patterns, rivers of gathering voices
artists.bio: Oisín Keld emerged from Galway’s small listening rooms in 2021 with songs that seemed to change their footing while remaining unmistakably singable. A solo songwriter working with a recurring chamber ensemble, he developed his low acoustic tunings while accompanying informal singing sessions and volunteering on river-restoration days in County Galway. The practical vocabulary of that work—fencing, planting, surveying, waiting—entered his writing without becoming a programme. His early performances paired restless fingerpicked patterns with unamplified passages in which the audience could hear the strings ringing against his sleeves.

artists.name: Orin Pell
artists.tagline: Hushed rooms, patient strings, enormous feeling
artists.bio: Orin Pell emerged from Dunedin’s small-room music circuit in 2009, bringing the measured pace of his work as a home-support worker into chamber folk. A solo artist with a recurring ensemble, Pell built his early recordings around thumb-picked guitar, a felt-prepared upright piano and a baritone that seemed to arrive from just across the kitchen. Violist Mara Venn and cellist Eli Fenwick became central collaborators, their low, closely spaced lines giving even his sparsest songs an unusual physical presence.

artists.name: Oskar Bellwether
artists.tagline: Apartment-life dramas scored for a tiny orchestra
artists.bio: Oskar Bellwether emerged from Vienna’s small listening bars and artist-run performance spaces in 2014, singing meticulous domestic dramas over nylon-string guitar. Raised in Ottakring, he studied piano before taking work preparing rehearsal scores, an apprenticeship audible in arrangements that give every instrumental entrance a dramatic purpose. Bellwether is a solo songwriter with a recurring chamber ensemble, appearing in monochrome formalwear that suggests both an underpaid master of ceremonies and a guest who has misunderstood the invitation. His first album, Satin Arithmetic (2015), established his miniature scale: whispered financial negotiations, disastrous flirtations and private humiliations framed by viola, cello and bass clarinet.

artists.name: Palacio Fulgor
artists.tagline: Acoustic beginnings, operatic endings, open arms
artists.bio: Palacio Fulgor formed in Buenos Aires in 1986, when singer and twelve-string guitarist Julián Varela and pianist Malena Costa began rehearsing after hours in a dance academy near Once. Electric guitarist Ramiro Soria, bassist Inés Duarte, and drummer Tomás Leiva completed a lineup whose acoustic introductions routinely became operatic finales. Their debut EP, Bravura, captured that transformation with borrowed microphones and a chorus assembled from friends in the city's underground performance circuit.

artists.name: Parlor Cartography
artists.tagline: Apartment-window dramas in strings and Technicolor
artists.bio: Parlor Cartography formed in Prague in 2012, when singer and pianist Tomáš Vorel began arranging his apartment-life songs with violist and orchestrator Klára Havelková. Their first performances took place in a borrowed rehearsal flat in Vršovice, where listeners sat between music stands and a folding paper proscenium. Violinists Eliška Beranová and David Kotek, cellist Marta Jelínková and percussionist Pavel Šimek completed a sextet whose chamber discipline gave Vorel’s theatrical instincts a practical counterweight. Their 2013 debut, Tenants Wearing Gold, turned overheard arguments, laundry disputes and borrowed formalwear into tightly furnished pop songs, with audible piano pedals beneath luminous strings.

artists.name: petalcodec
artists.tagline: Distant friendships tuned through mountain static
artists.bio: petalcodec formed in Taipei in 2021 around singer and guitarist Lin Yu-ning, keyboardist and recording engineer Chen Yi-heng, and percussionist Hsu Pei-jun. The three began exchanging musical postcards while Chen was helping maintain a relative’s tea plot near Pinglin: guitar phrases, sung messages and late-night radio scans passed between the hills and the city. Their name joined the delicacy of a petal to the practical business of encoding sound. Early performances paired Lin’s close, unforced singing with cassette machines, brushed percussion and harmonies that seemed to hover just beyond the loudspeakers.

artists.name: Podium Static
artists.tagline: Big hooks for the beautiful losers on the podium
artists.bio: Podium Static formed in Melbourne in 2014, when singer and hammered dulcimer player Lena Voss met producer Arun Mehta while helping stage an independent dance performance in a suburban recreation centre. Drummer and sampler operator Kit Mercer joined after recording the squeak of trainers and the metallic clatter of a dismantled basketball stand for their early demos. Those sessions established the trio’s vocabulary: struck strings, pumping synthesizers and enormous choruses about the small humiliations of trying hard. Their name came from a malfunctioning public-address system at a local athletics presentation.

artists.name: The Porcelain Astronauts
artists.tagline: Seaside space operas with a human heart
artists.bio: Formed in Brighton in 1972, The Porcelain Astronauts turned the resort town's off-season melancholy into progressive pop of unusual tenderness. Singer and pianist Adrian Vale, harpsichordist Celia Rook, guitarist Kit Fenwick, bassist Martin Sayer and drummer Nell Cresswell first rehearsed above a theatrical scenery workshop, whose discarded flats became their earliest airbrushed planetary landscapes. Their debut, Saltwater Rocketry, placed elaborate vocal arrangements around songs about ordinary people imagining extraordinary departures; the scrape of piano pedals remained audible beneath the celestial machinery.

artists.name: Pumice Choir
artists.tagline: Fault-line folk-rock with harmonies built to withstand storms
artists.bio: Pumice Choir formed in Dunedin in 2008 around siblings Mara and Kit Vale, whose interlocking acoustic guitars and close, friction-rich harmonies became the band's defining instrument. Joined by bassist Rowan Keene and drummer Anika Bell, they rehearsed in a draughty former joinery, developing songs in which a picked figure could persist almost unchanged while the band gradually transformed the ground beneath it. Their 2009 debut, Cinderwake, caught that early economy: audible strings, lightly scuffed vocals and electric endings that seemed to gather beyond the edge of the recording.

artists.name: The Quarry Hours
artists.tagline: Weather-beaten verses with a whole town in the chorus
artists.bio: The Quarry Hours formed in Dunedin in 2009, bringing the scale of a communal singalong to songs that still sounded as though they had been written in cold rented kitchens. Singer-guitarist Ewan Calder and pianist Mara Teviot first performed as a duo at benefit evenings before recruiting string player Nell Sutherland, bassist Toby Rusk and drummer Isaac Fenwick. Their name came from rehearsals scheduled around Fenwick’s early shifts at an aggregate yard. On their 2010 debut, Splitlip, Calder’s scraped baritone and Teviot’s bright, unsentimental answers sat amid rattling percussion, bowed strings and the unpolished noise of five people sharing a room.

artists.name: Relayweather
artists.tagline: Acoustic fragments become last-train euphoria
artists.bio: Formed in Melbourne in 2014, Relayweather built their first songs from sounds usually edited out of acoustic recordings: fingertips sliding across strings, a piano pedal releasing, the hollow knock of a guitar body. Singer and guitarist Elliot Vale met producer and keyboardist Mara Sethi while sharing a rehearsal building in Brunswick; percussionist and multi-instrumentalist Tom Arlen joined during the sessions for their debut EP, "Pocket Current." Recorded largely after shifts at their day jobs, its small-room performances and amber-lit electronics established the trio's enduring subject: the distance between being surrounded by people and feeling accompanied.

artists.name: Rona Skevick
artists.tagline: Retired champions hear the crowd in chamber-pop songs
artists.bio: Rona Skevick is a Glasgow songwriter, violist and producer whose chamber-pop songs follow retired competitors beyond the presentation photograph. Debuting in 2024 with Personal Best, she established a language of close-miked strings, prepared acoustic guitar and sampled crowds, setting small, almost spoken verses against choruses of massed voices. Raised in Glasgow, Skevick played viola in youth ensembles and later worked casual shifts at municipal sports facilities. The contrast between ceremonial achievement and everyday upkeep became central to her writing: silver trophies beneath fluorescent tubes, a knee strapped before a supermarket shift, a former champion still counting lengths in sleep.

artists.name: Sabine Desrochers
artists.tagline: Small-room confessions with a chamber ensemble
artists.bio: Sabine Desrochers is a Montreal singer-songwriter whose chamber folk makes domestic space audible: nylon strings scrape softly under the fingers, bass clarinet gathers beneath a sentence, and the refrigerator sometimes continues through the silence. She began releasing music in 2021 while helping care for an older relative, recording around household routines in her apartment. Her debut EP, The Chair Beside the Bed, introduced an unusually unsentimental vocabulary of care, finding affection in pill organisers, badly timed jokes and the negotiations surrounding an open window. Desrochers sings primarily in English, with occasional French phrases carried over from the conversations behind the songs.

artists.name: Saltbréf
artists.tagline: Harbour songs opening into brass-lit northern skies
artists.bio: Saltbréf formed in Akureyri in 2020 around singer and guitarist Elín Rós Magnúsdóttir and violist-arranger Hrafn Einarsson. Their first rehearsals took place in a borrowed teaching room, where Elín’s Icelandic-language songs acquired string countermelodies before anyone thought to add a rhythm section. Horn player Sólveig Arnadóttir and bassist-percussionist Kári Jónsson completed the quartet. The name, roughly “salt letter,” suited songs assembled from small communications: a swimming-pool rendezvous, a late shift, the sound of someone arriving home.

artists.name: Sayo Nerihata
artists.tagline: Poolside reveries where breath becomes a choir
artists.bio: Sayo Nerihata is a Kyoto singer, songwriter and home-recordist whose ambient pop begins with the physical sound of breathing. She debuted in 2019 with self-recorded performances circulated through local listening events, accompanying her close, unhurried voice on nylon-string guitar and a small reed organ. Her early recording practice developed around the acoustics of municipal swimming facilities: ventilation hum, water striking tile and the peculiar clarity of a voice heard across an otherwise empty pool. These spaces supplied an acoustic vocabulary rather than a continuous wash of field recordings.

artists.name: Semaphore Custard
artists.tagline: Supermarket fables with impossible choruses
artists.bio: Semaphore Custard formed in Dunedin in 1986 around songwriter Mara Venn, whose piano-led miniatures acquired startling dimensions through guitarist Ivo Pell, keyboardist and sampler operator Celia Rusk, bassist Tomas Bell and drummer Ned Cask. Rehearsing after hours in a community hall, the quintet built primary-colour cardboard scenery for performances in which checkout operators became prophets and promotional announcements became unreliable narrators. Their debut EP, Trolley Oracle, introduced the essential contradiction: songs as intimate as kitchen conversation, arranged with trapdoors, sudden changes of gear and choruses that seemed impossible until everyone was singing them.

artists.name: Serein Index
artists.tagline: Long-distance devotion suspended in vocal clouds
artists.bio: Serein Index are a Seoul ambient-pop duo formed in 2024 by vocalist and guitarist Yun Hae-in and producer Seo I-gyeom. Their early recordings began as exchanges between Hae-in’s apartment in Mangwon and I-gyeom’s overnight editing desk across the city: guitar sketches, whispered melodies and messages recorded when speaking live was impossible. The name joins the idea of rain falling from a clear sky to the cataloguing language of digital life. Their music makes a similar connection, giving private, sometimes awkward declarations the scale of a luminous electronic landscape.

artists.name: silt//signal
artists.tagline: Fingerpicked songs dissolving into digital weather
artists.bio: Formed in Bergen in 2016, silt//signal is the partnership of singer-guitarist Signe Velde and producer-percussionist Erlend Røed. They met while working evening shifts at a small performance venue, where Velde tested fingerpicked songs through the house system after closing and Røed recorded the spill from the empty auditorium. Their early performances paired a single steel-string guitar with a sampler, a floor tom and images of human figures rendered in thermal-camera colour. The name describes their central process: letting the grain and residue of a physical performance accumulate inside an electronic signal.

artists.name: sluice/09
artists.tagline: Canal-side folk songs wired for the small hours
artists.bio: sluice/09 formed in Bristol in 2010 around singer-guitarist Ellis Vale, sound recordist and electronic musician Mara Dyer, and fiddle player Tom Rook. Vale and Dyer met while helping catalogue recordings for a community oral-history project; Rook joined after lending them a harmonium for an early session. Their name came from a handwritten folder label in Dyer’s recording archive, not a location. Working from a rented rehearsal space in St Philip’s, the trio developed canal-side narratives around fingerpicked guitar, clipped environmental sounds and harmonies that seemed to arrive from different ends of a passageway.

artists.name: spoke/27
artists.tagline: Courier ballads turning bicycle clicks into rhythm
artists.bio: spoke/27 formed in Kyoto in 2018, when singer-guitarist Nao Mibu and sound editor Emi Naruse began recording after Mibu’s evening bicycle deliveries. Their first shared workspace was a cramped room above a cycle repair shop, where a dismantled rear hub became a percussion instrument and reflective tape marked microphone positions on the floor. The name combined the bicycle’s most modest structural part with the number of a delivery route Mibu regularly covered. From the outset, their songs followed people usually encountered only in passing: a cleaner waiting for the first bus, a kitchen porter cooling his hands outside, another rider eating beside a locked entrance.

artists.name: Svalevev
artists.tagline: Restless fingerpicking beneath migrating harmonies
artists.bio: Svalevev formed in Bergen in 2012 around singer and guitarist Ingrid Velde, guitarist and harmonium player Eirik Tveit, and percussionist Mari Helle. Their earliest rehearsals took place in a borrowed sail loft, where Velde’s low-tuned fingerpicking met Tveit’s bowed guitar and Helle’s dry, off-centre drum patterns. The name joins the Norwegian words for swallow and weave, an apt description of music whose independent lines continually cross without settling into symmetry. Their debut EP, Forked Bearings, introduced songs concerned with departure, inherited routes and the small domestic sounds that persist beneath them.

artists.name: Switchyard Orchard
artists.tagline: Small-town departures, widescreen guitar choruses
artists.bio: Switchyard Orchard formed in Dunedin in 2008 around singer and guitarist Tom Riddell and fiddler Mara Keane, whose early songs traced the routes between rented rooms, railway settlements and jobs taken for a season. Bassist Hemi Calder, drummer Elsie Ward and multi-instrumentalist June Bell completed the quintet before its debut EP, Last Road to the Yards, appeared that winter. Recorded with borrowed microphones, it established their defining contrast: Riddell's grainy, conversational baritone set against communal harmonies and electric guitars that seemed to push beyond the walls of the room.

artists.name: Sólveig Kambdal
artists.tagline: Tidal field recordings meet fractured acoustic confession
artists.bio: Sólveig Kambdal is a Tórshavn songwriter and producer whose folktronica treats the Faroese shoreline as both subject and recording instrument. Debuting in 2016 with the EP Basalt Receiver, she paired close-miked, open-tuned guitar with hydrophone recordings made beneath landing stages and along rock shelves outside the town. Cable knocks, submerged engine pulses and the brittle chatter of moving pebbles became a rhythm section around her low, grain-edged voice. Working under her own name rather than a band identity, Kambdal established a practice of solitary recording followed by small, carefully credited ensemble sessions.

artists.name: Tamsin Quillory
artists.tagline: Botanical grief rituals with a radiant pop pulse
artists.bio: Tamsin Quillory emerged from Melbourne’s small-room performance circuit in 2017, presenting songs for prepared piano, laptop and a contralto that could turn a plain instruction into an invocation. Raised in the city’s northern suburbs, she learned piano before beginning experiments with contact microphones and home-built percussion. Work propagating plants at a community nursery supplied both a practical vocabulary and the central concern of her writing: how living things are tended after a death. Quillory performs under her own name, with a changing ensemble rather than a fixed band.

artists.name: Teatro das Marés
artists.tagline: Songs for vanished cinemas, scored in strings and light
artists.bio: Teatro das Marés formed in Porto in 2022, when singer and guitarist Duarte Seabra began setting accounts of the city's vanished cinemas to music. His source material included newspaper listings, licensing notices and conversations with former projectionists, but the songs followed the people behind those records: a cleaner taking the tram before sunrise, an usher recognizing regulars by their footsteps. Celesta player and arranger Inês Valadares helped turn those sketches into a repertoire for voice, guitar and string quartet. Violinists Leonor Sá and Tomás Vilar, violist Beatriz Couto and cellist Miguel Serpa completed the six-piece ensemble.

artists.name: Tomasz Zawrel
artists.tagline: Songs of recovery rooted in a medicinal garden
artists.bio: Tomasz Zawrel emerged from Kraków’s small acoustic listening rooms in 2019 with songs built around nylon-string guitar, viola da gamba and a baritone recorded close enough to catch the breath between clauses. Before his debut, he worked part-time maintaining the teaching beds of a medicinal-plant garden while recovering from a prolonged illness. The work supplied both a vocabulary and a compositional discipline: short tasks, repeated gestures, progress too slight to notice until several days had passed. His lyrics retained that practical scale, finding emotional weight in washing a cup or asking someone else to carry a watering can.

artists.name: Tomoe Kisaragi
artists.tagline: Late-blooming love beneath a paper-cut proscenium
artists.bio: Tomoe Kisaragi is an Osaka singer, composer and instrument maker who made her recording debut in 2024, aged sixty-four, after retiring from nearly four decades arranging music for a small touring puppet-theatre company. Working behind a shallow proscenium, she learned to make six musicians suggest a crowded street, a jealous household or an approaching storm. Her later songs preserve that economy: a bassoon can become an unanswered question, while a scraped wooden block marks the hesitation before a name is spoken.

artists.name: Tomás Nespereira
artists.tagline: Fairground lives unfold in guitar, bassoon and strings
artists.bio: Tomás Nespereira emerged in Porto in 2011 with Bilhete Picotado, a five-song collection that treated travelling fairground workers as neighbours rather than picturesque outsiders. Raised in a household where upholstery work and amateur music overlapped, he began writing after helping a portrait painter transport panels between northern Portuguese fairs. His steel-string guitar and low, softly grainy Portuguese delivery found a defining counterpart in bassoonist Inês Valadares, whose answering phrases gave even the earliest recordings an unusual sense of human conversation.

artists.name: The Trestle Kin
artists.tagline: River-town harmonies that break into electric weather
artists.bio: Formed in Duluth in 2008, The Trestle Kin built their earliest songs around the overlapping voices of siblings Mara and Eli Venn, who had sung together long before they began performing in public. Mara's low, husky lead and Eli's wirier upper harmony found a durable frame in bassist June Salonen and drummer Calvin Rusk. Rehearsing near the St. Louis River, the quartet absorbed the cadence of shift changes, freight crossings, and conversations conducted over machinery. Their debut EP, Room Above the Yard, documented a mostly acoustic band already letting electric guitar hum through the floorboards.

artists.name: Twillphase
artists.tagline: Mill-town memories woven into loops and communal song
artists.bio: Twillphase formed in Manchester in 2011 around singer and nylon-string guitarist Ellis Rook, sampler and sound recordist Mara Kershaw, and percussionist Tom Armitage. Rook and Kershaw met while helping catalogue locally donated recordings of textile workers; Armitage joined after lending them contact microphones for a workshop session. Their earliest performances paired fingerpicked songs with the clack of shuttle mechanisms, winding-frame chatter and interlocking vocal loops. Rather than treating industrial sound as menace or nostalgia, they used it as a measure of human effort: something to sing with, and occasionally against.

artists.name: Ultravellum
artists.tagline: Sleepless desert songs with a sun-bleached halo
artists.bio: Ultravellum is the Adelaide studio project of singer, guitarist and producer Mara Venn, who began recording under the name in 2022. Developed during a period of irregular overnight work and persistent insomnia, her music places close-miked alto and nylon-string guitar beneath sustained synthesizers and fraying tape loops. Early sessions took place in a spare bedroom, where the hum of a portable fan often remained on the recordings. Venn treated those incidental sounds as part of the arrangement, building an ambient pop language in which a plainly sung melody can feel both within reach and impossibly far away.

artists.name: Ultravoam
artists.tagline: Motel insomnia melting into sun-struck melody
artists.bio: Ultravoam formed in Adelaide in 2023 around singer and guitarist Mara Venn, electroacoustic producer Ellis Rook and percussionist Tessa Quill. Venn and Rook began exchanging recordings after working adjacent shifts at a suburban audio-repair workshop; Quill joined when a rehearsal revealed that her barely struck drums gave their drifting guitar loops a human sense of distance. Their name came from a misread handwritten label on a box of packing foam. Early performances paired fingerpicked songs with amplified fan motors, ceramic taps and vocal rounds that seemed to arrive from opposite ends of the venue.

artists.name: Velvet Meridian
artists.tagline: Opera-house ambition with factory-floor heart
artists.bio: Formed in Birmingham in 1976, Velvet Meridian made theatrical rock out of the city's overlapping worlds of engineering shops, municipal stages and Saturday-night finery. Singer Nathaniel Vane, formerly a theatre scenery painter, joined guitarist Elias Rook and pianist Miriam Calder after meeting them at a benefit concert; bassist Martin Sayer and drummer Colin Dace completed the enduring five-piece. Their debut, The Gilded Shift, introduced stacked guitar harmonies, abrupt piano-led detours and choruses that sounded designed for an entire balcony. Last Bus to the Palace brought their breakthrough in 1978, turning the journey between work, performance and home into expansive, sharply observed popular drama.

artists.name: Vesper Cavalcade
artists.tagline: Private reckonings turned into glorious communal release
artists.bio: Formed in Toronto in 1984, Vesper Cavalcade made arena-scale rock from the intimate materials of rented apartments, estranged families and queer nightlife. Singer and pianist Julian Vale met twelve-string guitarist Mara Kessler while both worked at a theatrical costume warehouse; bassist Dev Sethi and drummer Celia March completed the quartet that autumn. Their debut EP, Chrome Confessional, paired audible tape hiss with choruses assembled from scores of vocal takes. Onstage, crimson tailoring, chrome microphone stands and Kessler’s chiming guitar made modest clubs feel extravagantly larger than their dimensions.

artists.name: Vitrajune
artists.tagline: Puppet-stage superstitions with a widescreen human pulse
artists.bio: Vitrajune is the performing name of Ljubljana composer, singer and puppet-theatre performer Neža Vidmar, whose intimate songs unfold into outsized communal finales. She began presenting music under the name in 2018, combining felt-piano pieces with short performances involving folded animal masks and visibly operated puppets. Having worked as a rehearsal pianist and theatre workshop assistant, Vidmar treated the noises usually hidden behind a production—breathing, hinges, feet finding their marks—as part of the score. Her early Ljubljana appearances took place in small rooms where listeners could hear the organ bellows between phrases.

artists.name: YEO:RAE
artists.tagline: Voice-note intimacy opening into widescreen euphoria
artists.bio: YEO:RAE is the recording name of Seoul singer, songwriter, and producer Yeo Rae-in, who debuted in 2023 with performances that let audiences hear acoustic songs turn into electronic arrangements in real time. Raised on fingerpicked guitar and informal home recordings, she began developing her production language while exchanging long-distance voice notes with friends who had moved abroad. The pauses, compressed room sounds, and abrupt endings of those messages became compositional material rather than imperfections to remove. Her stage name separates and rejoins her given name with a colon, a small visual pause echoed in her departure-board graphics and precisely timed live transitions.

artists.name: Yune Sori
artists.tagline: Tender songs for bodies living inside machines
