artists.bio: Yune Sori is a Seoul singer, songwriter and producer whose art pop treats digital existence as a physical condition: something that changes the breath, interrupts sleep and makes an absent person seem almost touchable. Debuting in 2024, she emerged from small interdisciplinary performances in Euljiro, singing over nylon-string guitar and a sampler among suspended sheets of translucent silicone. Sori is a solo persona rather than a band; chamber players and installation collaborators enter her work as changing participants. Her early sets established its governing contrast: a plainly delivered song surrounded by sounds that seemed to be learning how to inhabit it.

artists.name: Zofia Rdest
artists.tagline: City birdsong carried by strings and quiet resolve
artists.bio: Zofia Rdest is a Warsaw singer, guitarist and arranger whose orchestral folk treats the city as a living acoustic habitat. She began performing under her own name in 2023, bringing nylon-string songs to small cultural centres and informal listening evenings on the eastern bank of the Vistula. Her early repertoire grew from walks through Praga-Północ: jackdaws disputing a chimney, swifts circling apartment blocks, the abrupt hush after a tram departed. Sung in Polish, these observations became portraits of neighbourliness, fatigue and quiet persistence rather than pastoral escape.

artists.name: Éloïse Carreau
artists.tagline: Family histories in fingerpicked orchestral miniature
artists.bio: Montreal songwriter Éloïse Carreau makes chamber folk from the small discrepancies that survive in family records: an address crossed out twice, a photograph dated by two different hands, the altered wording of a remembered story. Debuting in 2019 with the five-song EP La Part des objets, she established a close, tactile sound built from fingerpicked guitar, viola and clarinet. Her French-language writing favoured particular objects over sweeping declarations, while her warm mezzo-soprano let conversational pauses carry as much feeling as the melodies. Early performances placed a changing chamber ensemble around her seated guitar, preserving the scale of a living-room gathering even on larger stages.

albums.title: The Lockkeeper’s Measure
albums.label: Towpath Recordings
albums.notes: Alderwake’s debut makes the canal audible as a place of labour: gates resist, accounts disagree, and every journey belongs to someone’s working day. Wide-set steel strings frame a close, leaky centre of fiddle, wooden flute and bass, while Vale’s measured baritone leaves room for other witnesses to contradict him. “Before the First Boat” supplies the descending figure that quietly binds the record; “The Frost Account” turns maintenance into tense, suspended music. The second-side suite, from “What Bellamy Said” to “Below the Sill,” is its boldest passage, building collective force without sacrificing individual testimony. “Another Hand upon the Beam” carries the opening phrase onward rather than bringing it home.

albums.title: Nine Knots
albums.label: Lintel Records
albums.notes: Released by Lintel Records in 1969, Nine Knots establishes Bracken Dial’s counterpoint-first folk in a room you can almost feel cooling. Guitar thirds remain unsettled, bass lines take their own routes, and Riddell’s dry baritone makes each moral compromise sound unnervingly reasonable. “The Ferryman’s Share” conceals its five-beat gait inside an easy lurch; “A Penny on the Clerk” turns narrative wit sour. The extended title instrumental lets the ensemble argue without words before “The Witness at Leith” introduces the crumhorn’s unwelcome testimony. Finger squeaks, chair noises and rattling percussion fittings survive the light compression. “Leave the Door Unlatched” closes without granting anyone a clean resolution.

albums.title: The Estuary Keeps Its Counsel
albums.label: Breakwater Records
albums.notes: The Alder Parliament’s debut makes progressive folk out of working routines: a ferry timetable, washing brought in late, the obligations packed alongside a departing son’s clothes. Recorded on eight-track in a converted schoolroom, its interlocking guitars and five-part harmonies retain the scrape of chairs and the room’s generous decay. “First Ferry” sets a conversational baritone against an unaccompanied refrain; “The Lime on the Wall” finds a darker centre in bowed bass. The three-part “Across the Long Reach” stretches the ensemble’s metres without losing its footing. By “Leave the Lamp,” that early choral breadth has narrowed to two voices, with nothing comfortably settled.

albums.title: Mandrake Witness
albums.label: Rookery Records
albums.notes: Foxglove Abacus’s 1971 Rookery Records debut turns a disputed botanical survey into intimate, quietly unruly folk theatre. Interlocking open-tuned guitars and argumentative bassoon sit close enough for every squeak and breath to register, while Martin Pell’s dry tenor makes village accusations sound like ordinary table talk. “The Mandrake Witness” offers the welcoming handshake; “Five Pence for a False Root” slips a crooked dance beneath it. At the centre, “Where Hester Left Her Gloves” reveals the loss beneath the paperwork. The ensemble grows more communal without sacrificing its kitchen-table scale, before “It Flowers Only Underground” dissolves into drone and departing voices: an unsettled foundation for the band’s later elaborations.

tracks.title: Five Pence for a False Root
Names Omitted from the Parish Book

albums.title: Widow's Gambit
albums.label: Lintel Records
albums.notes: Bracken Dial's 1971 Lintel breakthrough gives their acoustic counterpoint sharper definition without losing the scrape of chairs or the closeness of a shared room. Crumhorn becomes an argumentative equal to fiddle, while independent bass lines trouble every apparent resolution. Across a widow's profitable silence, the songs ask who bears the cost of cleverness. “A Fact Kept Back” states the case; the nearly bare “The Men Who Carried Him” interrupts it with human weight. The alternating metres of “Sixpence for the Judge” restart the machinery, but “No Witness of Mine” dismantles the narrator's certainty. Even the buoyant closing instrumental cannot quite finish honestly.

albums.title: Saltwater Rocketry
albums.label: Lantern Reel Records
albums.notes: On their 1972 Lantern Reel Records debut, The Porcelain Astronauts turn Brighton’s boardinghouses and amusement sheds into a makeshift space programme. Felted piano, fingerpicked guitar and Celia Rook’s clicking harpsichord sit inside a woody live-room sound, with Adrian Vale’s conversational tenor keeping the elaborate arrangements close to home. “The Pier at First Light” opens the shutters; “Mr. Bell’s Mechanical Moon” gives the town its ingenious, cash-strapped machinery. The suite “A Launching of Small Boats” stretches a waltz into restless ensemble exchanges, while “Leave the Landing Light” finds tenderness beneath the spectacle. “Beyond the Last Bus” brings everything back to human scale, ending with voices alone.

albums.title: Sunward Pilgrims
albums.label: Cathedral Steps Records
albums.notes: Recorded over six days in a converted parish schoolroom, The Astrolabe Union’s debut makes its small room feel like the beginning of a much larger journey. Thumb-led guitar, left-leaning viola and softly breathing harmonium frame songs about imperfect measurements and practical faith. “The Road from St Martin’s” establishes the unhurried intimacy; “Hazel Rod” turns crooked counting into an inviting dance. Longer developments in “A Circle Drawn in Ash” and “The Apprentice’s Nocturnal” reveal the ensemble’s expanding reach. After the full-band lift of “Sunward Pilgrims,” “Enough Light to Go” closes with almost nothing between the listener and the wood, strings and voices.

albums.title: Copper Apron
albums.label: Latch Records
albums.notes: The Damask Engine’s 1972 Latch Records debut finds their grand designs still sharing floor space with instrument cases and creaking chairs. Twelve-string guitar, wandering bass and an imperfect upright piano give these apprentice stories a tangible working surface; the vocal arrangements already suggest ambitions beyond the room. “Come Through the Yard” opens with unguarded invitation, while “A Useful Pair of Hands” asks what proficiency actually buys its owner. The near-solitude of “After the Whistle” makes the Mellotron’s later arrival feel genuinely strange. By the linked closing songs, communal enthusiasm survives—not as certainty, but as something worth carrying home.

albums.title: Doctor Fallow's Disputation
albums.label: Rookery Records
albums.notes: Released by Rookery Records in 1972, Foxglove Abacus’s second album turns the close-grained acoustics of Mandrake Witness into a chamber-sized quarrel. Interlocking guitars, argumentative bassoon and bowed bass surround Martin Pell’s dry tenor, while overlapping harmonies make every conclusion provisional. “Procession to the Glasshouse” and “The Examiner’s Thumb” establish the record’s brisk, sly theatricality; tiny witness songs repeatedly puncture its grander claims. On side two, “Twelve Descriptions of a Single Root” drives its changing metres toward startling unaccompanied testimony. Reversed guitar decays and hard tape cuts unsettle the warm room sound, but “Let Each Keep a Leaf” closes with unexpected generosity.

tracks.title: Twelve Descriptions of a Single Root

albums.title: Five Voices Under Timber
albums.label: Breakwater Records
albums.notes: Recorded over two nights in a Welsh university hall, this 1973 Breakwater release catches The Alder Parliament discovering how much force their acoustic lattice could carry. Pike’s spring-loaded drumming propels “The Quay Before Six,” while five-part suspensions give “Carry Your Own Chair” its argumentative lift. The expanded “The Estuary Keeps Its Counsel” opens into a bass-and-recorder hush that makes the hall audible. Three unrecorded songs bring organ and sustained electric guitar into the palette without obscuring the wood and wire. No replacement vocals tidy the breaths or missed consonants; by the twelve-minute “Under Timber, Under Tide,” the audience has become another imperfect, indispensable voice.

albums.title: Velvet Pretenders
albums.label: Garnet Records
albums.notes: Carmine Rookery’s Garnet Records debut builds its grandeur from audible human effort: scraped twelve-strings, close piano hammers and vocal trios bounced into a crowded, velvety haze. A provincial entertainer’s increasingly costly self-invention links the songs, but the quartet never lets the conceit overwhelm the playing. “Borrowed Entrance” stumbles magnificently from bare piano into full-band ceremony; “Sunday Suit” reveals the frightened man beneath the tailoring. The seven-beat “A Crown for Sixpence” punctures the swagger with crooked wit. Across the closing stretch, familiar melodies return as argumentative choirs, until “Leave the Lights” lets the promised triumph collapse into voice, wood and rattling pedal.

albums.title: Ivory Teeth
albums.label: Rookery Records
albums.notes: On their third album, Bracken Dial give their interlocking acoustic lines a harder floor: electric bass moves with independent purpose, and close percussion makes withheld downbeats feel almost confrontational. “The Heir's Table” builds from bare bass into staggered counterpoint, establishing a record preoccupied with inherited comfort and its concealed costs. The extended title track lets crumhorn and a slowed tape double rub uneasily together, an unsettling physical presence rather than a studio spectacle. Riddell's clipped baritone keeps the arguments plain. After the headlong instrumental “The Cabinet Dance,” “What I Kept” withdraws into treble viol, guitar harmonic and an admission that offers no absolution.

albums.title: Gasp
albums.label: Foundry Bell Records
albums.notes: Released by Foundry Bell Records in 1973, Gasp establishes Crown of Satellites’ acoustic-to-amplified theatre without concealing its construction. Twelve-string joints creak, upright piano hammers chatter, and bounced harmonies bloom into a papery haze. “Room for One More” turns a single intake of breath into a brisk entrance; “The Good Shirt” finds the frightened performer beneath the costume. Between stomping refrains, harmonium miniatures expose the silence beyond the stage. The guitar fanfare and six-part architecture of “A House Full of Witnesses” announce their arena ambitions, but “Enough to Get Home” leaves the bill payer alone with an unresolved interval.

albums.title: Captain Clementine
albums.label: Lantern Reel Records
albums.notes: On their second album for Lantern Reel Records, The Porcelain Astronauts turn a pleasure-pier attendant’s accidental command into twelve self-contained chamber-pop scenes. Harpsichord, bass clarinet and a small string section furnish the scenery; Adrian Vale’s dry, close tenor keeps the human stakes within touching distance. “A Hat Is Not a Captain” makes authority sound deliciously absurd, while “Names Against the Glass” reveals the loneliness beneath the passenger bustle. The fractured instrumental core of “Red Lamps, Black Water” earns its alarm through rhythm rather than volume. By “Keep the Landing Light,” spectacle has fallen away, leaving Celia Rook answering Vale across one piano: an intimate resolution to their newly theatrical ambitions.

tracks.title: A Hat Is Not a Captain

albums.title: Municipal Heaven
albums.label: Latch Records
albums.notes: On their second album, The Damask Engine exchange Copper Apron’s workshop miniatures for a model town whose generous spaces cannot guarantee happiness. Acoustic twelve-string still binds the arrangements, but doubled pianos, cello and Mellotron brass give these connected scenes a larger civic scale. “Keys to the Town” opens with convincing optimism; “Saturday at the Precinct” makes shopping bustle dance across the bar lines. The domestic centrepiece, “Room for Another,” exposes the uncertainty beneath the planning language. On side two, communal voices increasingly disagree, culminating in “Lanterns on the Playing Field” and “Sleep, Small Citizen,” an eleven-minute passage from distant public jubilation to intimate, unresolved care.

albums.title: Aunt Hester's Fern
albums.label: Alder House
albums.notes: On their third album, Foxglove Abacus turn the scholarly mischief of Doctor Fallow's Disputation toward the family table. Two close-recorded guitars, bassoon and lightly handled percussion retain their conversational cross-rhythms, but Martin Pell sounds newly unguarded, with Elspeth Vane's harmonies offering company rather than correction. “The Fern in Her Letter” establishes the record's tender uncertainty; “A Room Kept Ready” deepens it with harmonium and bowed bass. Even the wandering instrumental “Uncertain Locality” feels like a relative searching for the right recollection. The late, drum-led warmth of “All Who Remember Hester” makes the unanswered final song more affecting: inheritance becomes something loved without quite being believed.

albums.title: Painted Applause
albums.label: Foundry Bell Records
albums.notes: Released by Foundry Bell Records in 1974, Painted Applause drags the grandeur of Gasp onto a crowded function-room floor. Louder, leaner guitars, Mercer’s dry snare and Brand’s quick-witted bass give these songs the push of a band earning its audience one table at a time. “Give Them Something to Stamp To” and “Eyes This Way” turn embarrassment into dance-floor fuel, while “The Cloakroom Waltz” finds loneliness behind the festivities. The magnificent silliness of “A Triumph at the Interval” has its tender counterweight in “Your Coat Across Your Knees.” By “Leave a Light in the Hall,” communal singing feels less like spectacle than company.

tracks.title: Give Them Something to Stamp To
Leave a Light in the Hall

albums.title: The Long Water Crossing
albums.label: Lantern Acre
albums.notes: On their 1975 Lantern Acre breakthrough, The Alder Parliament turn acoustic interdependence into a panoramic studio language. Twelve-string guitars, piano and harmonium spread across sixteen-track tape, yet every staggered harmony entrance retains the tension of people listening in a room. “Leave Your Coat by the Door” offers an inviting threshold; “The Stakes at Low Water” introduces the seven-beat figure that unsettles the journey ahead. The title suite makes retreat as consequential as departure, before the dry kitchen reckoning of “That Chair” restores human scale. “What We Leave Afloat” closes without consolation: older obligations suspended in five voices above bowed bass.

tracks.title: Leave Your Coat by the Door

albums.title: Equinox
albums.label: Cathedral Steps Records
albums.notes: Equinox turns The Astrolabe Union’s intimate folk language outward, arranging ten songs into two continuous arcs of argument, courtship, and reconciliation. Doubled acoustics and close piano give the music a bright center; melodic electric bass and widely spread harmonies make its irregular meters feel inviting. “Equal Hours” opens with a generous six-beat sway, while “The Graft and the Stock” sets recorder against viola in quick, teasing counterpoint. At the hinge, “An Empty Measure” strips that abundance away. The second side earns its gathering force, cresting in “Room for the Sun” before “What We Owe the Light” leaves only voices, and a question rather than a verdict.

albums.title: Professional Doubter
albums.label: Red Baize Records
albums.notes: Benedict Spindle’s 1975 Red Baize debut builds its theatre from modest materials: fingerpicked steel strings, close piano and harmonies whose changing microphone distances become part of the drama. The ensemble leaves space for his bright tenor’s precise accusations and small retreats. “Terms of Belief” establishes the intimate scale; “The Man Who Sold Tomorrow” gives it a brisk commercial grin. At the centre, “A Demonstration of Faith” and “Under the Table” expose the splice between persuasive patter and electric menace. Late-arriving strings offer sympathy rather than vindication, before “No Further Questions” returns to the opening figure with its comforting conclusion withheld.

albums.title: The Scarlet Wager
albums.label: Garnet Records
albums.notes: Released by Garnet Records in 1975, Carmine Rookery’s second album turns their handmade grandeur into a contest of wills. Twelve-string guitars scrape beneath electric fanfares; close-miked piano triplets propel proclamations that the answering choirs refuse to endorse. “The Applause You Paid For” makes the argument immediately physical, while “A Crown on Credit” introduces a descending bass figure that haunts the ceremonies ahead. The unguarded “Stay Until the Fire Goes Out” briefly leaves the public gallery behind. By the closing suite, “The Scarlet Wager,” heavier guitars and rival choruses have stretched the band’s theatrical instincts into something both communal and deeply uneasy.

tracks.title: Stay Until the Fire Goes Out

albums.title: Jacks Aflame
albums.label: Rookery Records
albums.notes: On Jacks Aflame, Bracken Dial turn the harder edges of Ivory Teeth into eleven bright, tightly wound entertainments with suspect motives. Dulcimer flashes, fiddle bites and small-kit accents keep the opening songs airborne, while independent bass lines quietly dispute their apparent good humour. “A Bid from the Wall” makes counterpoint sound like auction-room collusion; “Below the Salt” brings the record inward, its harmonium supporting a devastatingly confidential account of household generosity. The arrangements are close, colourful and economical, never allowing a pattern to become innocent through repetition. The title-track finale gathers the ensemble at full tilt, then leaves Riddell alone to name the person their celebration has excluded.

albums.title: The Gilded Shift
albums.label: Latchlight Records
albums.notes: Velvet Meridian’s 1976 Latchlight debut turns a working week into a coronation held just beyond the factory gates. Recorded largely together in a converted rehearsal hall, The Gilded Shift makes its crowded arrangements tangible: piano pedals creak, drums bleed into guitar microphones, and communal choruses fray at the edges. “Clocking In” announces their ascending guitar harmonies over bare boot stamps; “The Borrowed Cuff” finds equal drama in a machinist’s preparations for a dance. The crooked waltz inside “Mayor for a Minute” establishes their taste for unstable grandeur. By “Our Names Above the Door,” amplification yields to ordinary voices—the spectacle’s human foundation.

albums.title: Brassbound
albums.label: Cinder Records
albums.notes: Aurelian Voltage’s 1976 Cinder Records debut makes arena-sized promises with the sound of four people testing their nerve in one room. Piano hammers bite, amplifiers breathe and Celia March’s toms turn hesitation into forward motion. “Strike the Match” sets the pace with a clipped piano figure and a charging shuffle; “Your Coat on My Chair” reveals the tenderness beneath Julian Vane’s declarations. The overdubbed choirs are used sparingly enough to feel like doors opening. From the boot-stomp solidarity of “Stand Your Ground” to the earned, communal release of “Room for Us All,” Brassbound establishes courage as something practised together.

albums.title: Radio Sherbet
albums.label: Kiteglass Records
albums.notes: On their third album, The Porcelain Astronauts turn a faulty spacecraft radio into their sharpest pop instrument. Released by Kiteglass Records in 1976, Radio Sherbet trims Captain Clementine’s chamber-theatre transitions into spring-loaded bass lines, clipped guitars and synthesizer replies. “Good Morning, Elsewhere” and “Pocketful of Sunshine” make the opening rush irresistible; “The Operator’s Window” exposes the tired man maintaining the illusion. At its centre, “Dancing on the Emergency Band” dissolves through interference into the piano-led “Interval for a Blue Planet.” The closing “Stay Tuned” gradually dismantles the broadcast, leaving Adrian Vale’s conversational tenor without its protective sparkle.

albums.title: Pendulum Children
albums.label: Cresset Music
albums.notes: On their third album, The Damask Engine turn the school day into a miniature civic epic. Pendulum Children joins Copper Apron’s tactile acoustic detail to a side-long dramatic logic: music-box piano becomes procession, playground counterpoint becomes discipline, and discipline slowly unravels. “The Inheritance Lesson” is the hinge, its reassuring cadences slipping beneath increasingly unsettled voices. Across the second side, the opening tune passes between adults whose good intentions no longer agree. Wide twelve-strings, close cello and receding banks of five-part voices give the record extraordinary depth; “Home at Walking Pace” finally removes that architecture, leaving only breath, melody and an unanswered promise.

albums.title: Paper Sovereigns
albums.label: Garnet Records
albums.notes: Released on Garnet Records in 1976, Paper Sovereigns brings Carmine Rookery’s pageantry down to street level. Bass and kick push beneath sharply separated guitars, while the piano sounds close enough to hear the hammers. Following The Scarlet Wager, this successor finds its drama among the people paid to maintain somebody else’s magnificence. “Run the Morning Edition” opens at a sprint; “Your Name in Small Print” exposes the loneliness behind the machinery. The twisting “Sixpence for the Ferryman” makes rhythmic instability feel communal, and “Until the Lamps Go Out” crowns the record with a massed refrain before leaving its promises suspended over bare acoustic strings.

albums.title: Parish Impostors
albums.label: Alder House
albums.notes: On their fourth album, Foxglove Abacus turn the herbarium into contested property: specimens become boundary markers, and scholarly courtesy hardens into accusation. Cresswell’s electric bass and Wren’s close, dry drum kit give the acoustic arguments new leverage, while Vane’s wiry electric guitar cuts across the fingerpicked patterns. “The Parish Has No Witness” arrives already fighting; “A Dance for Absent Tenants” makes eviction sound horribly danceable. The second side culminates in the splintered, repeatedly unresolved “Whose Hand Drew the Boundary?” Then “A Correction to the Register” removes the amplification—and exposes the human cost concealed inside a clerical amendment.

albums.title: Hexachord
albums.label: Meridian House
albums.notes: On their 1976 Meridian House breakthrough, Crown of Satellites turn six-part harmony into load-bearing architecture. Piano, guitar and melodic bass trade recurring figures while voices enter from opposite sides of a remarkably spacious mix. “A Better Mannequin” makes an extra half-bar feel like a missed stair; “Please Don’t Say My Name” expands a solitary, audible breath into monumental unease. The clipped exchanges of “Stand Where I Stand” give way to the twelve-string intimacy of “His Good Coat,” clearing space for a three-song climb. “When the Last Door Closes” finally resolves an interval left suspended on Gasp: grandeur earned through confession rather than disguise.

tracks.title: Please Don’t Say My Name
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]
Please don’t say my name.
The room has only just gone still.

[Verse]
I turned my collar at the stair,
The laundry mark was showing through.
My mother stitched a number there;
The gold initials came from you.
I wear them where the light falls blue.

[Pre-Chorus]
The doorman knows which coat to take,
The boys outside know where I stand.
I practise how a hand should shake
With nothing steady in my hand.

[Chorus]
Please don’t say my name,
Not with all the windows wide.
Let the lettering remain;
Let the man go back inside.
You can keep me in the frame—
Please don’t say my name.

[Verse]
My father eats at half past six,
His folded paper by the plate.
He saves the photographs they print
And asks if I am working late.
I say the trains are in a state.

[Chorus]
Please don’t say my name,
Not with all the windows wide.
Let the lettering remain;
Let the man go back inside.
You can keep me in the frame—
Please don’t say my name.

[Bridge]
There’s someone laughing through the wall;
I nearly answer with a laugh.
A porter wheels me down the hall
In six feet of a photograph.
He tips it sideways at the bend.
I hold the door and let him pass.

[Chorus]
Please don’t say my name,
Not with all the windows wide.
Let the lettering remain;
Let the man go back inside.
You can keep me in the frame—
Please don’t say my name.

[Outro]
The cuff is caught upon the chair.
I leave it caught. I leave it there.

albums.title: Cabinet Fever
albums.label: Red Baize Records
albums.notes: On his second album, Benedict Spindle makes professional envy sound like chamber music with its collar too tight. Clavinet, clipped bass and argumentative choruses propel “A Better Class of Miracle”; the acoustic refrains of “Your Name on the Door” and “Flowers for the Committee” grow less reassuring with each return. Compared with Professional Doubter, the parts have greater independence: dry percussion interrupts wiry strings, while close guitars keep the spectacle within touching distance. The extended “The Cabinet Examination” turns competition into counterpoint. After the comic collapse of “Naturally, I Have Friends,” the closing duet offers neither acquittal nor a finished sentence.

tracks.title: Tell It as You Told Me

albums.title: Unfinished Match
albums.label: Rookery Records
albums.notes: Recorded across two Edinburgh concerts, Bracken Dial's 1977 Rookery Records live set treats the stage as a workshop rather than a victory lap. The unaccompanied opening makes every subsequent entrance count; on “Widow's Gambit,” crumhorn inherits the refrain, while “Ivory Teeth” pushes electric bass and clipped accents to their hardest edge. The long, hushed “The Pardon at Leith” resets the second half. Two previously unrecorded pieces—the title track and “A Boundary in Rain”—leave their arguments deliberately unsettled. Retained tuning, chairs and audience sound place these intricate exchanges firmly in the room. “The Borrowed Coat” offers an encore without a triumphant release.

albums.title: Rooms Our Fathers Left
albums.label: Lantern Acre
albums.notes: Released on Lantern Acre in 1978, Rooms Our Fathers Left draws The Alder Parliament's expansive vocal architecture into rooms small enough to hear a sleeve brush a guitar. Nylon-string, upright piano and viola carry the weight once shared by wider arrangements; harmonies enter late, like relatives arriving after a difficult conversation has begun. “His Coat on the Peg” establishes the exposed scale, while “A Share of the House” gives inheritance a dry folk-rock edge. Three concise portraits surround the hymn-fragment instrumental “Four Notes from Sunday.” By “The Keys Are Still Here,” private possessions have become a town's unfinished business, held in a final, unresolved ensemble chord.

albums.title: Last Bus to the Palace
albums.label: Latchlight Records
albums.notes: On their 1978 Latchlight Records breakthrough, Velvet Meridian discover that an arena anthem can carry the weight of a late shift. Rook’s widely spread guitar harmonies leave Calder’s piano room to argue, while melodic bass lines tug the choruses toward home. The charging “Borrowed Jacket” opens the doors; “Last Bus to the Palace” turns waiting into a communal act. At the centre, a three-song conductor’s suite expands from ticket-machine rhythms to the orchestral release of “Everybody Off.” Just as importantly, the band know when to retreat: “The Caretaker’s Light” brings grandeur within speaking distance before “Leave the Door Unlatched” earns its final, enormous resolution.

albums.title: Lionhearted
albums.label: Cinder Records
albums.notes: Released by Cinder Records in 1978, Lionhearted turns Aurelian Voltage’s lean stage attack into a breakthrough language of shared courage. Doubled grand piano supplies the muscle; guitar harmonies flare like brass, while repeatedly bounced vocal overdubs retain their breaths and frayed edges. The opening rush of “Raise the Roof” and “Nobody Kneels Tonight” yields to the expansive devotion of “Stand Beside Me, Darling.” Even the grandest gestures have intimate stakes: a lover beside you, a lamp left burning, a coat given permanent space. The title track crowns side one, but “Until the Morning Finds Us” delivers the lasting revelation—an anthem grows larger because more people join, not because it moves faster.

albums.title: Neptune's Boardinghouse
albums.label: Kiteglass Records
albums.notes: On their fourth album, The Porcelain Astronauts turn chamber-pop hospitality into something quietly threatening. Dark violas, low synthesizer pulses and percussion recorded with the room left audible surround songs about lodgers returning from an expedition nobody remembers alike. Following Radio Sherbet’s brighter surfaces, Neptune’s Boardinghouse lets its instrumental corridors grow longer and its familiar melodies become unreliable. “Breakfast for the Missing” hides accusations inside a jaunty shuffle; “The Expedition According to Mr. Bell” opens into a chilling, slow-moving suite. The acoustic “Your Coat on the Banister” brings the story back to ordinary tenderness before “A Room Facing Earth” gathers the witnesses without settling their accounts.

tracks.title: The Expedition According to Mr. Bell

albums.title: HURRAH MACHINE
albums.label: Cresset Music
albums.notes: On their fourth album, The Damask Engine turn public jubilation into a precision instrument. Recorded for Cresset Music in 1978, HURRAH MACHINE trades Pendulum Children’s orchestral depth for close drums, forward bass and electric-piano figures that keep smiling after the words have stopped. “Everybody Up” and “Approved Weather” make exhilarating pop from obedience; the dragging “Under the Bunting” reveals who clears the square afterward. “A Cup of Ordinary Water” briefly opens a door onto acoustic air. Across the second side, instrumental links feed an increasingly crowded celebration, until “Leave by Different Doors” lets the collective promise fall back into fallible human voices.

tracks.title: The Best Street in the World

albums.title: Gossip Jubilee
albums.label: Garnet Records
albums.notes: On Gossip Jubilee, Carmine Rookery trade ceremonial entrances for the impatient snap of a newsroom: dry drums, clipped guitars and backing voices that heckle rather than herald. Following Paper Sovereigns, their arrangements become leaner without losing their harmonic traps or theatrical nerve. “Everybody Knows Your Name” arrives already waving from the balcony; “An Exclusive Audience” turns self-importance into a breathless sales pitch. Then “The Photograph of You” stops the machinery with twelve-string guitar and an admission nobody can monetize. The lavishly ridiculous “Waltz for the Well-Informed” and full-throttle “Bring Down the Balcony” make the eventual hush of “After the Guests” feel earned—and distinctly uncomfortable.

albums.title: Chalk Pilgrims
albums.label: Alder House
albums.notes: Released by Alder House in 1978, Chalk Pilgrims trades the crowded electricity of Parish Impostors for distance: guitars occupy separate corners, bassoon phrases outlast the footsteps, and room decay becomes part of the counterpoint. Its expedition concerns a flowering plant nobody can verify, but the real subject is what keeps a doubtful company walking. “The Parish Pace” sets the measured tread; “No Specimen Taken” briefly turns disagreement into electric force. The exposed guitar routes of “Two Paths Above the Quarry” prepare the quietly devastating “What We Brought Home,” where failure becomes something less easily classified. Their widest-open record is also among their most companionable.

albums.title: Nobody Claps Backstage
albums.label: Meridian House
albums.notes: After a punishing tour, Crown of Satellites turn away from the architectural overdubs of Hexachord and let the room carry the drama. Released by Meridian House in 1978, Nobody Claps Backstage keeps piano pedals, twelve-string finger noise and the uneasy space around Adrian Venn’s tenor in plain hearing. “Leave the Lights Low” declines the customary entrance fanfare; the harmonies finally open on “A Suit for Sunday.” The asymmetrical pulse of “By the Stage Door” makes waiting feel physical, while “Two Plates” finds sanctuary in an ordinary kitchen. Only “The House Is Yours” reaches arena scale before the title track leaves breath and distance to finish the record.

albums.title: Scarlet Demonstration
albums.label: Proscenium Records
albums.notes: Released by Proscenium Records in 1979, Scarlet Demonstration turns Benedict Spindle’s meticulous progressive pop into public spectacle. The contrapuntal bustle of Cabinet Fever opens into singable refrains, widescreen harmony stacks and strings that trade phrases with massed electric guitars. “A Reason to Applaud” introduces the smiling host; the brisk single “Take My Word” makes his assurances dangerously irresistible. Beneath the polish, descending bass lines keep shifting the emotional ground. Side two’s acoustic confession, “Your Side of the Bed,” leads into the three-part “Scarlet Demonstration” suite, whose electric coronation gives way to “After the Flowers,” a farewell recorded close enough to hear the entertainer stop smiling.

albums.title: Dangerous Splendour
albums.label: Meridian Crown
albums.notes: On their third album, Aurelian Voltage turn the communal grandeur of Lionhearted into sharper, brighter theatre. Close-miked drums, disciplined bass and terse synthesizer hooks give the opening rush—from “Dress for the Fire” to the title track—an unusually concentrated force. Yet visibility comes with a bill: “When the Room Is Empty” strips away the costumes, while the strutting “Look, Don't Touch” insists that attention is not ownership. The darker second side briefly loses language altogether in “Breath Between,” before “Somewhere We Can Stand” rebuilds the spectacle around something sturdier: companionship, shared breath and a patiently ascending piano.

albums.title: Satin Alibis
albums.label: Vesper Sound
albums.notes: On Satin Alibis, Carmine Rookery exchange public pageantry for the negotiations behind the velvet rope. Metallic guitar strokes, glossy electric piano and sharply gated drums give their handmade grandeur a colder finish, while close microphones expose every consonant and hesitation. The welcoming surface of “Your Name at the Door” cracks into the bass-led interrogation of “Who Paid You?” At the centre, “What I Owe You” turns a piano ballad into an unsettled account of affection. Calder’s contrary replies make even the danceable songs feel contested. By “When the Guests Have Gone,” the finery falls away, leaving the band playing beneath a painfully ordinary need to be loved.

albums.title: Apocrypha for Bassoon
albums.label: Reed Court
albums.notes: On their sixth album, Foxglove Abacus move beyond the exposed distances of Chalk Pilgrims into a chamber music of interruptions and disputed authority. Rook’s bassoon sets the grammar: clipped objections, rasping pedal notes and upper-register phrases of surprising warmth. “The Rectory Copy” introduces the argument; “A Hand Unlike My Own” lets unequal vocal entries quietly dismantle it. Clear, unvarnished production makes every crossing guitar line and intake of breath consequential. As earlier melodies return inside increasingly crowded arrangements, the scholarly comedy acquires a human cost. “Leave the Name Unwritten” answers with unusual directness, before “Reed Court” leaves the bassoon alone with the last word.

tracks.title: The Hedge Is Not the Boundary

albums.title: Dress Rehearsal
albums.label: Meridian House
albums.notes: After the exposed wood and room sound of Nobody Claps Backstage, Crown of Satellites return to spectacle with every entrance rehearsed. Recorded for Meridian House, Dress Rehearsal sets bright piano and massed guitar fanfares against tightly controlled drums, letting analogue synthesizers strengthen the architecture without obscuring the players. “Put Your Face On” and “Nothing to Worry About” turn reassurance into exhilarating, suspiciously immaculate choruses. At the centre, “The Cost of Looking Well” opens a door onto household exhaustion. Syncopated bass and clipped harmonies subsequently disturb the polish, until “Leave the House Lights Burning” makes ceremony sound like a fragile request. Adrian Venn’s wavering sustained notes keep the magnificent façade human.

albums.title: The Clockmaker's Weather
albums.label: Lantern Acre
albums.notes: On their fifth album, The Alder Parliament bring electric piano and a discreet synthesizer pulse into their interlocking acoustic language. The Clockmaker's Weather is their most intricate studio construction, but its impossible municipal machine remains grounded in wages, inherited duties and coats left by the door. “Minutes Against the Rain” turns five-part harmony into public argument; “Escapement” lets bass and drums drive the mechanism towards failure. After the stark harmonium setting of “Your Coat Behind the Door,” the record gradually relinquishes control. “Leave the Weather Be” finds its resolution not in perfect time, but in five voices waiting for one another to breathe.

tracks.title: At Six the Vanes Turn
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
At six the vanes turn inland,
Each brass tail wet with rain.
The fitter wipes his thumb clean
And checks the north again.
Below, the bakery shutters
Go rattling up their chain.

[Pre-Chorus]
A wire runs down the stairwell,
A bell beside each door.
My father sets his cup down:
“What are they ringing for?”

[Chorus]
Leave us a little weather,
Leave us an hour unclaimed.
The wind comes over the water
With nothing to be named.
Set every wheel together;
Leave one that turns by hand.

[Verse]
The board allots the rainfall,
The quay receives its share.
Wet coats along the railings
Drip beneath the stair.
They've marked my father's landing
For half an hour of air.

[Chorus]
Leave us a little weather,
Leave us an hour unclaimed.
The wind comes over the water
With nothing to be named.
Set every wheel together;
Leave one that turns by hand.

[Interlude]

[Bridge]
I took the work they offered;
I helped to draw the scale.
My father's hands held steady
While mine drove home the nail.
Now through the kitchen ceiling
We hear the counterweight.
He asks me if it's early.
I tell him it is late.

[Chorus]
Leave us a little weather,
Leave us an hour unclaimed.
The wind comes over the water
With nothing to be named.
Set every wheel together;
Leave one that turns by hand.

[Outro]

tracks.title: A Fair Wind for Every Shift

albums.title: Adrian
albums.label: Kiteglass Records
albums.notes: After the unsettled expanses of Neptune's Boardinghouse, Adrian brings The Porcelain Astronauts home without sending the band away. Released by Kiteglass Records in 1981, it places Vale's conversational tenor among felted piano, fingerpicked guitar, brushed drums and the small sounds of people sharing a room. “Your Side of the Table” makes absence tangible; “The Magnificent Mr. Monday” briefly opens the curtains on their old theatrical sparkle. At the centre, “What You Call Returning” gives Rook room to challenge the narrator's account. The closing “Leave the Landing Light” earns its full-band refrain through patience, making staying sound less like surrender than a difficult new adventure.

albums.title: Mercy Circuit
albums.label: Cresset Music
albums.notes: After the tightened machinery of HURRAH MACHINE, Mercy Circuit brings The Damask Engine close enough to hear piano felt, fingers changing chords and the breath before a line. Written after Gabriel Venn’s prolonged vocal exhaustion, these nine pieces turn collective responsibility into bedside duties, missed shifts and small accommodations. “A Chair Beside the Bed” establishes the patient scale; “The Relief Bicycle” briefly opens the windows with a buoyant folk-rock swing. Cello shadows the intimate exchanges of “Two Cups Cooling,” while “Copper Bowls” finds an unlikely ascent in bowed bass and tuned percussion. The closing “Leave the Light” earns its final harmony by withholding it.

albums.title: Credible Witness
albums.label: Proscenium Records
albums.notes: Released by Proscenium Records in 1982, Credible Witness tightens Benedict Spindle’s progressive pop until every interruption feels consequential. After Scarlet Demonstration’s sumptuous spectacle, Ada Pell’s mobile bass and Martin Quill’s gated snare leave the melodies less sheltered. The opening run snaps shut rather than spilling into connective flourishes; “Nothing but the Truth” makes that economy sound positively threatening. At the centre, “What I Told You at Home” admits backing voices only where certainty falters. Electric scale returns through the stubborn pulse of “The Terms of Your Release,” before “An Ordinary Account” exchanges theatrical proof for the vulnerable sound of fingers on strings.

tracks.title: What I Told You at Home

albums.title: Rootless Antiquaries
albums.label: Reed Court
albums.notes: Foxglove Abacus close their catalogue by letting the room answer back. Recorded in a converted schoolroom, Rootless Antiquaries pares their progressive folk to interlocking guitars, warm bassoon and double bass, with intricate metres carried as naturally as conversation. Martin Pell’s unusually plainspoken tenor leads accounts of disputed inheritances and confessed inventions; Elspeth Vane’s unisons gradually open into independent lines. “The Parish Model” briefly revives their bustling ensemble comedy, but the exposed “A Name for the Empty Bed” reveals the tenderness beneath it. The patient round of “All Our Authorities” and the bare farewell “Leave the Key” make an ending from shared breath, unresolved strings and audible space.

tracks.title: A Name for the Empty Bed

albums.title: Scarlet Parliament
albums.label: Meridian Crown
albums.notes: On their fourth album, Aurelian Voltage turn arena rock into a chamber of competing voices. Julian Vane’s hammering piano and Kit Arden’s argumentative guitar lines trade odd-meter challenges before finding choruses big enough to hold the room. Following Dangerous Splendour’s sharpened hooks, Scarlet Parliament makes the arrangements more theatrical without sacrificing physical momentum. “Permission to Speak” sets the terms with its interrupted seven-beat verses; “The Weight of Witness” brings the first side to a crowded, combustible close. The bare admission of “I Said Nothing” supplies the necessary human cost. By “Until Every Voice Is Heard,” the massed harmonies offer solidarity without pretending disagreement has disappeared.

albums.title: Zero Hourglass
albums.label: Vesper Sound
albums.notes: On their sixth studio album, Carmine Rookery set their handmade grandeur against an unforgiving electronic clock. Sequencers tighten the songs without taming Calder’s restless bass, Quill’s bodily drumming or Julian Vane’s percussive grand piano. “Borrowed Seconds” opens with clipped apprehension; “The Public Wants Blood” turns overlapping phrases into a merciless communal hook. At the centre, “Glass Committee” makes withheld cadences feel like institutional cruelty. Yet the guitars gradually recover room to breathe, especially on “A Crack in the Floodlights.” Released by Vesper Sound in 1983, Zero Hourglass advances beyond Satin Alibis’ cold surfaces without pretending that intimacy can simply switch the machinery off.

albums.title: The Prompter’s Revenge
albums.label: Meridian House
albums.notes: Released by Meridian House in 1983, The Prompter’s Revenge turns Dress Rehearsal’s precision into a linked backstage drama, with piano figures and rewritten refrains doing the work of dialogue. The counterpoint of “The Man Who Holds the Ladder” and “Madam Keeps the Keys” makes self-importance sound exhilarating before “Leave the Landing Light” reveals the household behind the borrowed costume. Gated drums and the seven-beat machinery of “Seven Steps to the Footlights” sharpen the threat without swallowing Adrian Venn’s audible breath. The expansive “We Can Carry the Evening” earns its grandeur by letting formerly competing melodies support one another.

tracks.title: The Man Who Holds the Ladder

albums.title: Chrome Confessional
albums.label: Red Rivet Records
albums.notes: Released by Red Rivet Records in 1984, Vesper Cavalcade's debut makes arena-sized promises from a room too small to contain them. Twelve-string guitars ring through amplifier buzz; cymbals bleed into piano microphones, and stacked choruses fray into papery distortion. “Leave the Landing Light” establishes the Toronto band's gift for turning a private ultimatum into a heavy-backbeat release. “Next of Kin” holds that release back, letting piano, breath and an unsigned form carry the drama until the drums finally arrive. Between the sharp shuffle of “Cheap Halo” and the gathering voices of “Room for One More,” their theatrical grammar takes shape: confession answered, disputed, then held by others.

albums.title: Picnic Astronauts
albums.label: Hearthglass Records
albums.notes: After Mercy Circuit’s exposed interiors, Picnic Astronauts carries The Damask Engine into the garden, where family ambitions mingle with wind, distant games and the clink of party glasses. Mandolin and twelve-string counterpoint give these songs their spring; a portable synthesizer supplies small, improbable horizons. “Room for the Moon” opens with unabashed lift, while “The Demonstration” finds tenderness in a public failure. Beneath the buoyant bass of “My Boy, the Architect,” parental pride acquires a revealing wobble. The communal release of “Everybody Bring a Chair” makes the closing retreat indoors feel earned: wonder survives, though nobody escapes embarrassment.

albums.title: Crown Machine
albums.label: Civic Sound
albums.notes: On Crown Machine, Velvet Meridian turn their hard-won arena command into a gleaming instrument of suspicion. Analogue sequences, gated drum rooms and immaculate guitar harmonies make success sound seductively efficient, while chromatic bass lines quietly sabotage the smiles. “Company Colours” and “Perfect Attendance” barely pause for breath; the piano-led “Borrowed Collar” finally counts the personal cost. The sprawling “The Hours We Keep” pits human time against programmed repetition, before “Teeth of the Crown” opens side two with abrasive force. Released by Civic Sound in 1985, this is their most tightly engineered record—and its closing “Leave the Hall Unlocked” earns grandeur by letting the machinery fall away.

albums.title: Satellite Teacup
albums.label: Vector Parlour
albums.notes: Released by Vector Parlour in 1985, Satellite Teacup turns a misdirected household transmission into the Astronauts' sharpest collision of domestic intimacy and technological spectacle. Sequenced bass, digital brass and gated drums propel the opening songs, but harpsichord and fingerpicked guitar keep interrupting the circuitry. “Please Hold for Outer Space” makes bureaucracy gloriously singable; “Dear Other Person” exposes the loneliness beneath the joke. The central sequence, from “The Station Sleeps” through “Without the Machine,” moves from crystalline repetition to mechanical overload and naked piano. After Adrian's close-room restraint, this is a bold reopening of the curtains—ending, on “Leave the Landing Light,” with two people rather than an answer.

albums.title: Turno de noche
albums.label: Muelle Sur Discos
albums.notes: Publicado por Muelle Sur Discos en 1986, Turno de noche encuentra a Faro de Cobre apretando una ambición enorme dentro de una sala pequeña. Las púas rozan las cuerdas, los amplificadores soplan y los coros multiplicados todavía dejan oír cada respiración. «Antes de que atraque» abre con urgencia de muelle; «Baja la escalera» descubre el diálogo entre Tomás Araya e Inés Mella. En el centro, «La taza» reduce la noche a unos pocos objetos domésticos. El estribillo de «Deja la luz» anticipa su futura escala, pero «Cadenas al alba» devuelve esa grandeza al suelo: metal, concreto y gente que vuelve a casa.

albums.title: A Table Set for Strangers
albums.label: Morrow Sound
albums.notes: Released by Morrow Sound in 1986, A Table Set for Strangers exchanges The Alder Parliament’s long-form designs for compact songs with little shelter between player and microphone. Clean guitar replies, firm electric bass and dry drums lend “Enough for Everyone” and “On Account” an almost cheerful efficiency; their lyrics count the cost of keeping up appearances. The piano-led “The Good Cups” exposes the hurt beneath that brightness before “Another Chair” opens into exuberant five-part harmony. As the record loosens, generosity becomes less an ideal than a difficult daily practice. “Leave the Table” ends their pre-hiatus years with overlapping voices and a guitar chord left to die naturally.

albums.title: Crimson Voltage
albums.label: Red Rivet Records
albums.notes: Vesper Cavalcade's 1986 Red Rivet Records debut full-length turns the scrappy theatre of Chrome Confessional into concise, widescreen rock. Doubled twelve-strings ring around gated snares, melodic bass and vocal choirs whose low objections meet soaring answers. “Say His Name Tonight” makes romantic candor sound monumental; “After the Last Streetcar” finds a looser, bass-led swagger. Piano ballads expose the private costs beneath the spectacle, especially “The Space for Next of Kin.” The closing sequence supplies the breakthrough: “If They Ask Me” nearly dissolves into voices before “Come Out with Me” converts a lonely plea into a jubilant invitation.

tracks.title: The Space for Next of Kin

albums.title: Bravura
albums.label: Candil Discos
albums.notes: Recorded over four evenings in a Buenos Aires dance academy, Palacio Fulgor’s Candil Discos debut makes a small room sound like the beginning of an arena. Twelve-string scrape, upright-piano hammers and audible breaths carry arrangements that grow without concealing their seams. Julián Varela’s grain-edged tenor turns everyday promises into public declarations, while Malena Costa’s suspended chords keep triumph slightly unsettled. “Salí a la luz” opens almost bare; “La silla junto a vos” finds its heart in Duarte’s answering lines. By the accumulating waltz finale, “Hasta que abran las puertas,” floorboards, brushes and friends singing together have become the spectacle.

albums.title: The Polished Impostor
albums.label: Proscenium Records
albums.notes: Released by Proscenium Records in 1986, The Polished Impostor turns Benedict Spindle’s theatrical progressive pop into a showroom of persuasive surfaces. Sequenced bass shadows electric bass, sampled orchestral blows advertise each chorus, and Jonah Venn’s programmed drums acquire unruly human edges through live cymbals and fills. After Credible Witness’s emotional directness, this immaculate machinery makes reassurance itself sound suspect. “A Wonderful Assurance” opens the doors with dazzling courtesy; the fingerpicked “Your Actual Hand” quietly checks the credentials. At the centre of the second side, “The Demonstration Will Continue” dismantles its own dance-floor certainty and finds a grand piano underneath. “Allow for Error” leaves both machine and conscience running.

albums.title: Trolley Oracle
albums.label: Blue Staple Records
albums.notes: Released on Blue Staple Records in 1986, Semaphore Custard's five-song debut makes a supermarket feel both theatrical and unnervingly personal. Borrowed eight-track equipment keeps the drums dry and the keyboards charmingly undersized, while upright piano and audible guitar strings give the elaborate writing a human scale. “The Bell Knows” finds revelation at the till; “Special on Pears” lets its walking rhythm stumble into waltz time. At the centre, “Under the Fluorescent Light” discovers vulnerability behind a promise of freshness. The patient, abruptly unfinished “Everything Must Go Home” establishes the band's enduring gift: making commercial language carry an intimate plea.

albums.title: Rookery at Wembley
albums.label: Vesper Sound
albums.notes: Recorded across two Wembley Arena nights in late 1985, Carmine Rookery’s first live album trades studio ceremony for muscular, fallible momentum. “Borrowed Seconds” shakes its sequencer grid loose; “Velvet Pretenders” arrives without its familiar overture, all pick scrape and lunging drums. Touring keyboardist Niall Fenwick widens the sound without smoothing its edges. At the centre, “A Room Above the Railway” opens into the complete closing suite from The Scarlet Wager, its competing melodies finally finding common ground. “No Witness but the Piano” briefly empties the arena around Julian Vane before the closing charge. The crowd sings out of tune; the amplifiers are allowed to die naturally.

tracks.title: The Scarlet Wager: Terms of Surrender
The Scarlet Wager: Nobody Leaves Crowned

albums.title: Encore Etiquette
albums.label: Parade Circuit
albums.notes: Released on Parade Circuit in 1986, Encore Etiquette folds Crown of Satellites’ elaborate stagecraft into their shortest, most immediate studio album. Sequenced pulses and tightly damped drums sharpen the surfaces, but Brand’s mobile bass and Adrian Venn’s audible breath keep the polish under pressure. “Save Your Applause” barely waits for its own chorus; “After You” and “Your Best Side” turn celebrity courtesy into nimble social comedy. The spare piano of “The Good Suit” exposes what all that brightness conceals. After “Coat on the Banister” restores twelve-string warmth, “Many Happy Returns” dismantles the celebration layer by layer, leaving an exquisitely courteous, deeply unsettling goodbye.

albums.title: After the Applause
albums.label: Civic Sound
albums.notes: After the sequenced gleam of Crown Machine, Velvet Meridian let the room back into the record. Their 1987 Civic Sound release opens with piano hammers, brushed snare and close acoustic strings, then earns its larger gestures through ensemble playing rather than studio spectacle. “Borrowed Coat” makes a homeward journey quietly monumental; “The Dressing Room” turns the aftermath of acclaim into a restrained guitar elegy. Even the tougher songs leave fingerprints: count-ins, amplifier hum, a bass line pushing against tired feet. From the sour accounting of “You Can Keep the Flowers” to the shared microphone of “Someone Left a Light,” this is grandeur learning to live with consequences.

albums.title: Concrete Horizons
albums.label: Meridian Crown
albums.notes: On Concrete Horizons, Aurelian Voltage bring their arena-sized convictions home to kitchens, job centres and late trains. Upright piano, acoustic guitars and compact string arrangements leave room around Julian Vane’s grain-edged tenor, while Martin Rook’s bass gives opener “Another Working Day” its stubborn forward motion. After Scarlet Parliament’s theatrical collisions, these songs find drama in ordinary negotiations: the family-table tensions of “A Place for Him,” the tender usefulness of “Leave the Landing Light.” “Not Yet Finished” supplies a necessary electric interruption, but the record’s greatest assurance arrives in “Under Our Own Roof,” where a small domestic promise earns an expansive, patiently unfolding chorus.

albums.title: Ceremony Unlimited
albums.label: Hearthglass Records
albums.notes: On their seventh album, The Damask Engine turn the bright surfaces of 1987 into both invitation and evidence. Digital bells, sampled orchestral punches and gated drums frame piano lines whose inner voices refuse the easy answer. “A Brighter Way to Live” is their sharpest pop overture; “Terms of Welcome” puts small print inside the hook. After the acoustic openness of Picnic Astronauts, this polished public address feels deliberately compromised. “A Place in the Photograph” punctures its own grandeur with an unvarnished exchange, while the title track sets synthetic brass against breathing human fanfares. The closing piano leaves optimism unfinished.

tracks.title: Leave the Light as It Is

albums.title: La mesa de todos
albums.label: Muelle Sur Discos
albums.notes: On their 1988 Muelle Sur Discos debut full-length, Faro de Cobre turn the rough ambition of Turno de noche into a language built for collective singing. Doubled bronze-string guitars give small amplifiers surprising breadth; stairwell harmonies make five people sound like a neighborhood. “La mesa de todos” finds grandeur in feeding another mouth, while “No salen en la foto” and “Lo ganado” let muscular bass hooks sharpen the record’s working-port perspective. The kitchen waltz “El plato junto al fuego” interrupts the charge with necessary tenderness. By the nearly unaccompanied “Dejamos un lugar,” shared breath carries the weight that louder records entrust to overdubs.

albums.title: Checkout Divinities
albums.label: Blue Staple Records
albums.notes: Semaphore Custard's first full-length turns a working day into intricate, warmly human progressive pop. Released by Blue Staple Records in 1988, Checkout Divinities expands the clipped machinery of Trolley Oracle with Celia Rusk's sampler, household percussion and luminous guitar stacks, without burying the fingertips on steel strings. “Automatic Doors” and “Buy One Heaven” make irresistible hooks stumble over announcements and missing beats; “Your Hands Are Warm” finds the tenderness beneath the sales pitch. The contrary motion of “Everything Must Rise” brings the shop-floor bustle to a head, before “When the Last Light Goes” gathers its workers into a radiant after-hours coda.

tracks.title: The Woman in the Window Display

albums.title: False Witnesses
albums.label: Red Ledger
albums.notes: After Wembley’s communal roar, Carmine Rookery make agreement sound dangerous. Released on Red Ledger in 1988, False Witnesses pares their grandeur to dry drums, abrasive piano and guitars that leave bruises rather than halos. “Everybody Knows” starts with the band already running; “The Approved Version” and “Swear It Again” turn answering harmonies into open dissent. The patient storytelling of “A Seat by the Aisle” exposes the wages behind the applause, while the grinding title track supplies the record’s fiercest confrontation. “I Was in the Room” finally slows the opening progression into an admission: the accuser was never outside the crowd.

albums.title: Boulevard Seraphs
albums.label: Meridian Soundworks
albums.notes: On their second full-length, Vesper Cavalcade widen the frame without losing sight of the people inside it. Grand piano now shares the load with Kessler's ringing twelve-string, while orchestral synthesizers and harmonized leads give these overnight encounters a panoramic glow. The rush of “Say It on the Boulevard” and “Room for One More” makes the seven-minute “The Brothers at St. Agnes” feel like a hard-won pause for breath. Its aftermath is quieter and less certain, especially on “What I Didn't Do.” By the extended closing answer of “Until the Streetlights Go,” the choruses sound communal—but belonging remains something these characters must keep choosing.

albums.title: El rugido azul
albums.label: Candil Discos
albums.notes: Con El rugido azul, Palacio Fulgor convierte el empuje acústico de Bravura en un espectáculo de estudio: cajas con compuerta, guitarras abiertas y coros que parecen responder desde la otra punta de un estadio. El piano de Malena Costa conserva peso y madera incluso cuando el arreglo se agiganta. «Que tiemble la avenida» abre la puerta de una patada; «Un lugar en tu mesa» encuentra una épica distinta en recibir a un amigo desalojado. Entre carreras, silencios y cambios de luz, Julián Varela mantiene la conversación dentro del gesto monumental. «Nadie sale solo» corona el ascenso; «Hasta que amanezca» devuelve la última palabra al grupo, sin instrumentos.

albums.title: Public Holiday
albums.label: Civic Sound
albums.notes: On Public Holiday, Velvet Meridian loosen their collars without forgetting who paid for the day off. Clipped piano, bright rhythm guitar and rubbery bass bring a funk-inflected bounce to their arena-sized choruses, while teasing backing voices puncture Nathaniel Vane’s public-address grandeur. Following After the Applause’s acoustic reopening, this is a brighter, more mischievous ensemble record. “Clocking Out” and “Borrowed Sunshine” make release feel almost effortless; the fairground machinery of “Round Again” turns toward the bruised family portrait “Rain at the Reservoir.” Later, “Nothing On Account” strips away the bunting before “Leave the Gates Open” closes with gloriously imperfect communal warmth.

tracks.title: A Little Longer in the Light

albums.title: La ciudad que responde
albums.label: Horizonte Austral
albums.notes: On their Horizonte Austral breakthrough, Faro de Cobre turn the harbor into a resonant chamber: bronze-bright twelve-strings, muscular bass and carefully tuned toms make every entrance feel earned. “Antes de la sirena” opens the doors; three rising major-key rockers carry the band toward the title track’s intricate, five-voice architecture. Crucially, the scale can contract. The instrumental “Entre dos luces” and Tomás Araya and Inés Mella’s intimate “Déjame la llave” restore the sound of hands, wood and breath. “Que pare la grúa” makes workplace safety an arena-sized demand, while “Mientras quede una luz” finds fresh meaning beneath an unchanged refrain.

albums.title: Electric Sanctuary
albums.label: Signal House
albums.notes: On their sixth album, Aurelian Voltage turn the sanctuary of the stage into something smaller, darker and open after midnight. Celia March’s programmed rhythms lock clipped piano and sequenced synthesizers into place, while Martin Rook’s bass keeps flesh against the circuitry. “Borrowed Light” and “No Questions at the Door” make precision feel welcoming; at the centre, “Stay Until I Sleep” strips that protection away to reveal the frightened person underneath. The spacious “After the Last Train” opens a stranger second half before Kit Arden’s guitars reclaim their reach. Released by Signal House in 1991, Electric Sanctuary finds solidarity in the imperfect human timing inside an electronic pulse.

albums.title: Eden Overtime
albums.label: Pattern Room Records
albums.notes: On their final studio album, The Damask Engine let the workshop doors stand open: piano action, amplifier hum and the slight drag of a shared downbeat become part of the writing. Eden Overtime exchanges Ceremony Unlimited’s bright surfaces for five players negotiating space in real time. “The Gates Still Open” advances without a victory parade; “Small Repairs” rediscovers their early acoustic sting. At the centre, “The Last Shift in Paradise” breaks a weary waltz against jagged electric counterpoint. The late harmonies offer fellowship rather than rescue, before “Leave the Light Unfinished” pares the ensemble back to two voices and a room unwilling to fall silent.

albums.title: Coupon Weather
albums.label: Counterfoil Records
albums.notes: On their second album, Semaphore Custard trade the crowded shop floor of Checkout Divinities for cleaner sampling and unsettling space. Coupon Weather makes conditional affection audible: piano chords wait for bass notes to explain them, consonants assemble into choirs, and silence interrupts the sales pitch. “While Stocks Last” opens in three unfolding rooms; “Your Signature Here” turns an intimate dispute into a refrigerated rhythmic puzzle. Mara Venn keeps these elaborate constructions conversational, especially on the bare “What I Kept.” The ascent towards “A Thousand Small Yeses” supplies their most sumptuous vocal architecture yet, before “After the Offer” leaves affection standing without its guarantees.

albums.title: Last Candles
albums.label: Red Ledger
albums.notes: Carmine Rookery's final album for Red Ledger brings their arena-scale instincts into a room small enough to hear the piano bench. Twelve-string scrape, breathing drums and Calder's melodic bass give these songs about cleaners, caretakers and late-shift households their physical weight. “The Guest of Honour” and “Put It on My Crown” briefly bare the old electric teeth; “The Good Cups” finds equally potent drama in an untouched piece of crockery. Following the bruised directness of False Witnesses, Last Candles allows warmth without disguising exhaustion. “Carry the Night” supplies one final surge before the title track leaves four voices, a piano and a patiently held resolution.

albums.title: Flesh & Thunder
albums.label: Meridian Soundworks
albums.notes: Released in 1992 on Meridian Soundworks, Flesh & Thunder tightens Vesper Cavalcade's panoramic rock into a pressure chamber. Twelve-string shimmer survives beneath sequencer loops, sampled metal and drums whose ambience shuts like a steel door. The opening triptych turns clipped anxiety into enormous choruses; “The Body Keeps the Hours” reveals the physical cost. Funk-driven “Chrome on Your Tongue” and the family confrontation of “Your Father's House” make success sound increasingly conditional. The title track delivers the communal spectacle, but the record's decisive gesture is quieter: “Don't Tell Me It's Morning” leaves Julian Vale alone with piano, a low pulse and reassurance he cannot accept.

albums.title: Instructions for Vanishing
albums.label: Red Baize Records
albums.notes: After the sequenced surfaces of The Polished Impostor, Benedict Spindle’s 1992 Red Baize release brings the microphone close enough to catch the cost of every assurance. Instructions for Vanishing begins with the bare patience of “Leave the Landing Light,” briefly recovers its ensemble footing, then retreats into rooms where marriage and illness resist theatrical solutions. “A Demonstration of Force” breaks that intimacy with a deliberately shocking electric eruption; “What the Doctor Didn't Say” finds greater tension in restraint. Small strings, fingerpicked steel strings and breathing piano replace machinery without renouncing harmonic intricacy. By “No Forwarding Address,” withdrawal sounds neither heroic nor final—simply possible.

albums.title: Chromium Smile
albums.label: Fivefold Recordings
albums.notes: After six years away, Crown of Satellites return with less armour and sharper hearing. Chromium Smile uses digital definition to reveal the grain of natural drums, spacious guitars and harmonies that no longer conceal every uneven edge. Brand’s melodic bass steers “A Face for the Morning,” while “The Good China” brings marriage into uncomfortably plain view. At the centre, “Your Side of the Bed” reduces their theatre to piano and breath. The closing run restores the fanfares without the old haste: “Room in the Chord” lets separate voices remain distinct, and “Before We Go” exchanges the expected victorious finish for a shared intake of air.

albums.title: Dinastía del deseo
albums.label: Astilla Sur
albums.notes: En Astilla Sur, Palacio Fulgor convierten la herencia en una disputa por quién cuida, quién reclama y quién abre la puerta. Tras la expansión eléctrica de El rugido azul, el piano de Malena Costa organiza un espectáculo de fanfarrias, percusión de salón y coros que intervienen como personajes. La entrada ceremonial de «Los nombres de la casa» desemboca en el galope de «Herederos del incendio»; «La parte que te toca» contrapone baile seco y resentimiento. Julián Varela encuentra su declaración más vulnerable en «Nadie hereda un abrazo». El cierre, «La mesa de todos», reparte la melodía y convierte la pertenencia en una tarea compartida.

albums.title: Names in Concrete
albums.label: Assembly House
albums.notes: Released by Assembly House in 1994, Names in Concrete strips Velvet Meridian’s civic grandeur back to dry drums, exposed guitar and the grain of Nathaniel Vane’s tenor. Redevelopment is heard through cleared benches, funeral clothes and rooms kept open after everyone leaves. The blunt title track and impatient “By Hand” refuse easy uplift; “Your Good Coat” and the fractured “Notice to Quit” make private loss and public erasure inseparable. Miriam Calder’s recurring piano figure quietly binds the record together. When the guitars finally stack on “What We Carry,” the release feels earned, before “Leave a Key” entrusts the ending to a small, imperfect choir.

albums.title: Los que faltan
albums.label: Horizonte Austral
albums.notes: After the widescreen breakthrough of La ciudad que responde, Faro de Cobre strip the walls bare. Los que faltan (1995, Horizonte Austral) sets overloaded guitars against dry drums and shoulder-to-shoulder voices, making every shared entrance feel contested. The opening rush of “No cuentan” and “La firma” gives way to the crooked six-beat insistence of “Seis pasos” and the fingerpicked roll call of “Inventario.” Grandeur returns in “En nombre de quién,” only to be interrupted by silence. Inés's exposed passage in “Lo que dijo Inés” sharpens the album's argument about representation; “Deja la llave” brings it home without offering resolution.

albums.title: Errata
albums.label: Margine Dischi
albums.notes: Daria Zorvelli's 1995 Margine Dischi debut makes the rehearsal hall part of its argument: harpsichord keys clatter, bows change direction, and breaths arrive before anyone has settled on the facts. Beneath the clipped strings of “An Honest Mistake,” acoustic guitar supplies a warmth the testimony cannot quite earn. The miniature social portraits give way to the exposed piano of “You Said I Never Cried,” while “At Your Sister's Table” turns vocal doubling into unreliable corroboration. These are the foundations of Zorvelli's chamber-pop language, already alert to class and desire. The percussion-free “What I Meant Was” closes on a suspended chord and an unfinished correction.

albums.title: Armillary
albums.label: Long Acre Sound
albums.notes: Returning after two decades, The Astrolabe Union make precision itself the subject of Armillary. Long Acre Sound’s sharply separated digital staging gives thumb-picked guitar, viola and piano fresh definition, while sampled bells and restrained synthesizer suggest the seductive order of a celestial model. “The Useful Sky” and “Bring the Ladder” offer an invitingly direct entrance before the central suite stretches from suspended harmony through “The Seventh Turning” to the full-band release of “Outside the Circle.” Domestic warmth returns with “A Measure of Apples.” On “Leave the Window Open,” the electronic frame gradually falls away: five people, one audible room, and no final claim to certainty.

albums.title: Saltwater Car Park
albums.label: Counterfoil Records
albums.notes: On their 1995 Counterfoil release, Semaphore Custard loosen the precision of Coupon Weather without abandoning its harmonic restlessness. Recorded largely in a rented coastal house, Saltwater Car Park gives fingerpicked guitars, fretless bass and brushed drums room to hesitate; softened sampler choirs drift like conversations through adjoining walls. The expansive opener, “The Sea Beyond the Loading Bay,” establishes its patient scale, while “Complimentary Sunshine” briefly restores the old bustle. Workers and stranded travellers inhabit the hushed centre. “Nothing Here Is Guaranteed” gathers the record into an unresolved electric swell before “Leave Your Shoes There” brings everything back to fingertips, floorboards and breath.

tracks.title: The Sea Beyond the Loading Bay

albums.title: A Machine for Remembering
albums.label: Contour House
albums.notes: Returning after twenty-seven years, Alderwake make the gaps in collective memory audible. Open-tuned guitars retain every fingertip scrape, but clean separation and long reverberation leave unfamiliar distances between the players. “The Missing Mile” gathers its rhythm almost imperceptibly; “Instructions for the New Man” sets practical knowledge against an unreliable account. At the centre, “Three Accounts of the North Road” unfolds one journey through three irreconcilable testimonies. The later songs find warmth in harmonium and steadier dance steps without pretending the intervening years can be recovered. “What I Can Tell You” ends the reunion with a single guitar and a voice unwilling to supply the missing facts.

tracks.title: Three Accounts of the North Road

albums.title: Mercy Flares
albums.label: Meridian Soundworks
albums.notes: Released in 1996 on Meridian Soundworks, Mercy Flares trades Flesh & Thunder's cold armor for the sound of people staying in the room. Piano hammers, twelve-string finger noise and Julian Vale's exposed breathing carry songs about hospital paperwork, groceries and the names families refuse to say. The nearly bare “Next of Kin” establishes the stakes; “Not Your Decision” gives grief a controlled electric edge without breaking the album's patient pulse. Organ and conversational harmonies gradually warm “Clean Sheets” and “Bring a Chair.” Only the closing title track summons Vesper Cavalcade's full vocal architecture—and its suspended ending offers company, not a cure.

albums.title: Velvet Procession
albums.label: Gable End Records
albums.notes: Municipal Swans’ 1997 Gable End Records debut finds civic ceremony in cupboards, kitchens and borrowed chairs. Recorded over two weekends in a rehearsal hall, Velvet Procession keeps picked guitar and Pieter Vervaet’s conversational baritone close, with cello and clarinet breathing in the room behind them. “Forty Chairs” gives the preparations a brisk snare-led bustle; “Your Name on the Envelope” finds the absence inside the occasion. Lotte’s harmonies gradually become independent melodies, culminating in the title track’s sole full-ensemble swell. “Leave It Till Morning” closes with two voices, guitar and a piano pedal’s release: an intimate foundation for the band’s later orchestral reach.

albums.title: After Applause
albums.label: Second Matinee
albums.notes: Released on Second Matinee in 1998, After Applause brings The Porcelain Astronauts back together without polishing away the years between them. Piano pedals, woody drums and warmly mobile bass place the five musicians in a shared room; their harmonies sound negotiated rather than perfected. “Come In, It's Open” makes a welcome out of understatement, while “The Moon on Hire Purchase” restores their earthbound space-travel humour. The six-minute “The House After Everyone” quietly shifts the floor beneath its melody. Organ and cello deepen the second half, leading to “Stay Until the Lights Go Out,” where gathering voices make companionship—not spectacle—the final event.

tracks.title: Your Name's Not on the List
Stay Until the Lights Go Out

albums.title: Sworn Sweetheart
albums.label: Margine Dischi
albums.notes: Released by Margine Dischi in 1998, Sworn Sweetheart turns Errata's close-miked chamber language into a miniature civic pageant. Harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet lend the brisk songs ceremonial swagger, while acoustic guitar keeps their emotional stakes within reach. “The Plaintiff Wore Apricot” stages three incompatible recollections on one melody; “Don't Repeat This” suddenly closes the doors on the spectacle. In the second half, slipping waltz meters and increasingly compromised harmonies make certainty harder to sustain. The lavish vocal convergence of “All in Agreement” offers a brilliantly untrustworthy climax, answered by the bare, deliberate withdrawal of “Without My Name.”

albums.title: Chalk Meridian
albums.label: Long Acre Sound
albums.notes: After Armillary's polished digital space, Chalk Meridian brings The Astrolabe Union back into a low-ceilinged room, with stool creaks, amplifier hiss and the friction of five musicians playing together. Astronomy becomes a practical language for boundaries, disputed rights and shared responsibility. The abrupt guitar-and-snare entrance of “The Path Is Not Yours” sets a compact, argumentative pace; “Her Father's Measure” opens a hushed clearing for viola and tenor. In the knottier second half, handclaps and bowed bass give the title track its stubborn momentum. “Room for Another Footstep” closes with communal warmth, leaving its final cadence—and the question of common ground—unsettled.

albums.title: Good China
albums.label: Sideboard Recordings
albums.notes: Recorded over three evenings with borrowed microphones, The Lacquer Picnic’s debut makes hospitality sound like a delicate negotiation. Nylon-string guitar sits close enough to catch fingertips; upright piano answers from across the room, leaving awkward silences intact. “Such a Lovely House” turns a brisk two-step into an exercise in swallowed objections, while “Until the Cheque Clears” reveals the dependence beneath the narrator’s wit. Bell’s sceptical clarinet on “The Spare Chair” introduces the ensemble’s gift for instrumental disagreement. By the closing “Good China,” guitar harmonics have gathered viola, bassoon and six voices: the first glimpse of their ability to turn private embarrassment into communal release.

tracks.title: Such a Lovely House
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
What a handsome little grate;
You let your sister shiver.
She asked if she could stay till eight;
You said you'd ring a driver.
The tiles are blue as borrowed plates.
She thanked you at the gate.

[Pre-Chorus]
I set my glass upon my knee;
You pass a little mat to me.
I lift it by the unchipped rim
And find another thing to mention.

[Chorus]
Such a lovely house you have,
Such a lovely house.
I put my cup down carefully
And leave the saucer out.
There's nothing here I'd dare to move.
You've thought of everything.

[Interlude]

[Verse]
What a useful serving hatch;
Your wife can hear us dining.
You praise the way she found a match
For all the curtain lining.
She starts to tell us what it cost;
