You ask her for the mustard.

[Pre-Chorus]
You say the place was going cheap;
I say you've made it yours to keep.
Beneath the table, with my shoe,
I push her fallen napkin through.

[Chorus]
Such a lovely house you have,
Such a lovely house.
I put my cup down carefully
And leave the saucer out.
There's nothing here I'd dare to move.
You've thought of everything.

[Bridge]
The cheque you wrote is in my coat;
The lining's coming loose.
I ought to mend that pocket seam
Before I put it through.
You ask if I have settled in.
I say the room will do.
You nod towards the second floor:
A tenant left that view.

[Interlude]

[Chorus]
Such a lovely house you have,
Such a lovely house.
I put my cup down carefully
And leave the saucer out.
There's nothing here I'd dare to move.
You've thought of everything.

[Outro]
Such a lovely house.

albums.title: Five Voices Under Brick
albums.label: Contour House
albums.notes: On their third album, Alderwake bring the reunion out of digital separation and into a room where breaths, scraped strings and competing accents become structural parts. The fleet opening pair gives way to the demolished terrace of “Fourteen Houses on Bell Lane,” its house numbers carrying more weight than any elegy. Dance figures thread through the middle, gathering force through rhythmic overlap, while the title track lets separate witnesses trouble a single account. “Subject to Purchase” supplies the sharpest electric edge. The closing pair retreats to fingerpicked strings and harmonium, leaving the last conversation—and its harmony—deliberately unfinished.

albums.title: The Distance Between Bells
albums.label: Salt Ledger
albums.notes: Released on Salt Ledger in 1999, The Distance Between Bells makes reunion sound like renewed attention rather than recovered youth. Double bass, brushed drums and Fenwick’s low viola leave generous air around the interlocking guitars; the five-part harmonies retain their breadth without concealing the grain of older voices. “Leave the Latch” opens with cautious repetition, while “The Ferry Steps” finds an easy bodily swing inside uneven bars. At the centre, “Each in Our Own Time” lets independent vocal lines slowly discover common ground. The closing “A Light in the Back Room” offers something smaller than triumph: warmth sustained through an unhurried guitar-and-piano exchange.

tracks.title: A Light in the Back Room

albums.title: Unarmoured
albums.label: Fourfold Records
albums.notes: On their first album in eight years, Aurelian Voltage trade spectacle for the tension of four musicians sharing a room. Released by Fourfold Records, Unarmoured keeps the piano hammers, bass slides and decaying toms close enough to touch. “Leave the Light Uncovered” establishes the dry, unhurried pulse; “No Permission Needed” proves that restraint needn’t mean surrender. At its centre, the interlocking acoustics of “Your Side of the Bed” give way to the patient piano lament “What We Didn’t Say.” Julian Vane’s lower register brings hard-earned intimacy to these songs of return, before “Here, Together” finds its resolution in four imperfectly joined voices.

albums.title: Aldermen
albums.label: Gable End Records
albums.notes: On their second album, Municipal Swans turn the village hall into a small orchestra without losing the scrape of a chair or the space between players. Cornet, tenor horn and trombone answer woody strings, while upright bass lends the brisk opening pair a new spring. “Deputy Mayor’s Daughter” hides social panic inside an irresistible refrain; “The Fish Course” finds affectionate comedy in ceremonial mishaps. The nearly bare sibling exchange of “How Many Are We?” marks the turning point. From there, familiar brass figures return slower and less certain, until “Leave the Side Door” closes with Pieter’s low baritone and a cello interval that declines to settle.

albums.title: Pulso argentino
albums.label: Astilla Sur
albums.notes: En Pulso argentino, Palacio Fulgor cambia el decorado por la proximidad: fieltro de piano, cuerdas de bajo y una caja seca sostienen canciones donde pedir ayuda cuesta tanto como ofrecerla. Publicado por Astilla Sur en 2001, el disco repliega la teatralidad de Dinastía del deseo sin renunciar a su escala emocional. «A fin de mes» retiene deliberadamente la resolución; «Lo que falta» deja a Julián Varela casi solo frente al piano. Desde «Una silla más», las voces amigas vuelven con cautela. El cierre, «Hasta mañana», encuentra dignidad en seguir andando, no en prometer que todo va a arreglarse.

albums.title: Sunday at Essendon
albums.label: Tramline Recordings
albums.notes: On Sunday at Essendon, Benedict Spindle brings his elaborate pop architecture home to Melbourne, leaving the chairs, count-ins and piano-room air audible. After the exposed reckonings of Instructions for Vanishing, these ensemble performances rediscover company without mistaking it for certainty. “Walking Distance” finds propulsion in fingerpicked guitar and an unhurried rhythm section; “The Good Plates” folds suburban brass-band warmth into a quietly barbed domestic scene. At the centre, “Sunday, With the Windows Open” follows a day through patient instrumental transformations. The closing “Room for One More” offers Spindle’s most generous kind of reassurance: a shared chorus, then musicians carrying on where words stop.

tracks.title: The Band in the Next Street
Leave the Light as It Is

albums.title: Cousins at Supper
albums.label: Sideboard Recordings
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Sideboard Recordings, The Lacquer Picnic turn a family supper into an ensemble comedy of uncertain loyalties. Springy upright bass and brighter percussion loosen the debut’s domestic hush, while backing voices offer corrections from every corner of the table. “Please Pass the Grievance” sets clipped piano against an irrepressible clarinet; the central portraits find subtler friction in carefully mismatched harmony partners. Even the brisk “Clearing Away” leaves something unsaid. By “Leave the Porch Light,” an unchanging guitar figure can accommodate strings, flute and a roomful of voices without making anyone concede their version of events.

tracks.title: The Long Way to the Dining Room

albums.title: La distancia doméstica
albums.label: Casa de Sal
albums.notes: On their 2002 Casa de Sal release, Faro de Cobre bring their widescreen instincts indoors. After years away from large stages, twelve-string attack, upright-piano hammers and brushed drums make work and household life feel close enough to touch. “Lo que alcanza” finds lift in small answering harmonies, while “Tu lado de la cama” lets the pulse dissolve around the ache of opposite shifts. The bass-led warmth of “Sopa para mañana” starts the return toward larger rooms. By “Hasta que estemos todos,” their arena scale has been patiently rebuilt: one enormous chorus, earned through restraint, before bare guitar brings everything home.

albums.title: Couture Perjury
albums.label: Carbon Copy Recordings
albums.notes: On her third album, released by Carbon Copy Recordings in 2002, Daria Zorvelli turns chamber-pop elegance into an instrument of pressure. Harpsichord locks against dry programmed drums; bowed strings arrive in blocks, and edited silences make every qualification audible. The immaculate attack of “The Perfect Account” gives way to the warmer guitar of “Allowance,” before “I Can Confirm” leaves its supposedly authoritative narrator unable to complete a sentence. Advancing beyond Sworn Sweetheart’s theatrical counterpoint, Couture Perjury makes the recording itself part of the dispute. “Dress Code” weaponizes stereo replies, while “Leave It as It Was” returns the opening melody at half speed, exposing the coercion beneath its poise.

albums.title: Suitable Attire
albums.label: Receipt Press
albums.notes: On Suitable Attire, Semaphore Custard turn respectability into a live-wire ensemble drama. Reunited after separate theatre work, the unchanged lineup lets Mara Venn steer the pulse: piano interjects, guitars answer, and choruses accelerate as though a difficult truth has finally escaped. “Good Shoes” and “The Approved Version” make that renewed attack exhilarating, while “Alterations” exposes the tenderness beneath the dress code. Sampler interventions are scarce and pointed; the real spectacle is musicians listening closely enough to change direction together. “Everyone Inside” brings percussion and communal voices into the room before “Sunday Best” sheds its ceremonial grandeur, ending with a guitar and an unadorned reckoning.

albums.title: The Room Above the Cut
albums.label: Sluice Lantern
albums.notes: Recorded at intimate room scale, The Room Above the Cut makes rearrangement part of Alderwake’s storytelling. Chairs scrape beneath the opening exchange; later, interlocking guitars and argumentative percussion turn recollection into a public hearing. Vale’s grain-edged baritone remains the narrative anchor, but other voices interrupt, qualify and inherit his accounts. The centrepiece, “Three Accounts of the Same Gate,” threads material from their first three albums through a new fiddle bridge before “The Empty Boat Race” releases the accumulated pressure. After that peak, “Two Cups Left” and the unaccompanied “Names for the Night Shift” bring the audience almost within touching distance. The encore earns its warmth one returning harmony at a time.

tracks.title: Three Accounts of the Same Gate

albums.title: Five Flights Up
albums.label: Assembly House
albums.notes: Recorded across three nights at Birmingham’s Assembly House, Five Flights Up turns Velvet Meridian’s catalogue into one sustained dramatic arc. Room chatter gives way to the headlong “The Gilded Shift,” while “Crown Machine” sheds its electronic armour without losing its bite. The close-miked pairing of “Borrowed Clothes” and “After the Applause” exposes piano hammers, fingertips and the effort behind Nathaniel Vane’s ringing phrases. From there, the band climb toward “Last Bus to the Palace,” making grandeur feel earned rather than imposed. An audience-led encore and the unresolved hush of “Leave the Landing Light” place the final emphasis on shared space, not spectacle.

albums.title: Bareknuckle Valentines
albums.label: Red Rivet Records
albums.notes: After the exposed grief of Mercy Flares, Vesper Cavalcade return by putting bodies in a room, not armor around the songs. Cut together in a converted broadcast space, Bareknuckle Valentines lets stick clicks, amplifier spill and shouted changes become part of its muscular warmth. “Come Out Swinging” shakes the hinges loose; the title track makes four unmistakably individual voices sound stronger than a seamless choir. “Keep Your Key” finds intimacy in unanswered questions, while “My Father's Hands” lets age complicate the old declarations. By “Leave the Lights On,” repeated refrains gather the force of people choosing to stay. The laughter beneath its last chord earns its place.

albums.title: Unmasked at Aston
albums.label: Fivefold Recordings
albums.notes: Recorded at their final Birmingham engagement, Unmasked at Aston brings Crown of Satellites’ monumental songs back within touching distance. Twelve-string guitar, piano and melodic bass carry arrangements once crowded with overdubbed harmonies; Sayer’s high responses leave revealing space around Adrian Venn’s tremulous tenor. The opening “House Lights, Heartbeats” gives way to familiar stomp before an extended acoustic passage makes “Please Don’t Say My Name” the evening’s emotional centre, its refrain passing into the audience. Early bravado and Chromium Smile’s measured unease prove unexpectedly compatible. Released by Fivefold Recordings in 2003, this farewell keeps the count-ins, applause and imperfect breaths—and ends with nothing left to amplify.

tracks.title: A Face You Can Come Home To
One More for the Coat Check

albums.title: Swanseal
albums.label: Lantern Stair
albums.notes: After the brass and widening counterpoint of Aldermen, Swanseal brings Municipal Swans back within arm’s reach. Released by Lantern Stair in 2004, these five pieces make a virtue of small sounds: fingertip percussion, upright-piano action, viola bow grain and the breath beneath Bram’s bass clarinet. “Borrowed Chairs” opens with an unusually fleet, conspiratorial shuffle; “The Fold in the Cloth” finds its drama in a major melody quietly darkened by a borrowed minor chord. The instrumental “Swanseal” tilts between dance steps before “Leave the Side Door” gathers the quintet into a tender, unresolved farewell. Nothing swells beyond the room.

albums.title: Cinder Circuit
albums.label: Oblouk Recordings
albums.notes: The Ninth Velodrome’s debut reconstructs a deserted sporting ceremony with borrowed amplifiers, patient feet and the acoustics of a former school assembly room. Released by Oblouk Recordings in 2004, Cinder Circuit establishes their vocabulary at its roughest: bowed-guitar abrasion, walking bass, percussion spill and collective breath. “Chalk on the Banking” opens with two dry bass notes; “Borrowed Flags” turns modest guitar canons into the record’s first substantial surge. The exposed harmonium of “Assembly Interval” makes that scale suddenly fragile. Six wordless singers enter the middle sequence without assuming the foreground, while “Bell Without an Official” threatens to derail the pulse that “After the Groundsmen” leaves running into tape flutter.

albums.title: Belfry Orchard
albums.label: North Aisle Recordings
albums.notes: After the compressed, roughened surfaces of Chalk Meridian, Belfry Orchard finds The Astrolabe Union working at lower volume and closer range. Piano and double bass carry the weight; viola bow pressure, harmonium breath, and Martin Vale’s undoubled tenor supply the grain. “All Hands at the Ladder” makes communal labor lightly danceable, while “Winding Day” reduces the ensemble to voice and harmonium, nearly still but never inert. The rippling “Clear Water Below” restores momentum without pretending grief has passed. Throughout, maintenance becomes a form of affection, and growth remains indifferent to permission. The title track ends not with resolution, but with a small chord disappearing into the room.

albums.title: The Executor’s Waltz
albums.label: Cordial House
albums.notes: Released by Cordial House in 2004, The Executor’s Waltz turns The Lacquer Picnic’s small-room chamber pop into an intricately contested family document. Following the sociable swing of Cousins at Supper, its live rhythm foundations support strings and woodwinds that argue rather than decorate. The bright manners of “A Generous Man” give way to the title track’s destabilising waltz and the subterranean bassoon of “Under the Carbon Paper.” Felix Ransome’s conversational baritone keeps every grievance human-sized. The thirteen-minute closing sequence, “All the Rooms We Leave” into “As We Remember Him,” gathers the album’s melodic claims into a crescendo before leaving the family singing without agreement.

tracks.title: The Blue Room Goes to Margaret

albums.title: A voz de puerto
albums.label: Casa de Sal
albums.notes: Recorded across two Valparaíso homecomings, Casa de Sal’s A voz de puerto makes Faro de Cobre’s scale feel physical: bronze-string scrape, descending bass, floor-tom thunder and five voices finding the same consonant. The dry opening pair yields to the debut-era drive of “Hasta el primer bus,” before “La luz de la cocina” brings the audience close through a single room microphone. “De mano en mano” stretches into a nimble bass-and-toms exchange; “Que responda la ciudad” restores the band’s widescreen harmonies. An early waltz, newly arranged, precedes “Nadie queda atrás.” Breathless entrances, premature audience choruses and untrimmed applause preserve the work behind the lift.

albums.title: Last Road to the Yards
albums.label: Ballast House
albums.notes: Recorded over two weekends in a borrowed rehearsal room, Switchyard Orchard’s Ballast House debut finds breadth without losing the scrape of chairs or the effort of playing together. “Keys to the Borrowed Van” moves from lone baritone to brisk, full-band resolve; “Friday Wages” establishes the stamping floor-tom pulse that anchors their early sound. At the centre, “After They Stack the Chairs” lets harmonium, fiddle and three distinct voices keep the lights on. The ringing refrain of “Past the Turnoff” opens the view before the title track hands its final chorus to the room. Leaving here is less a clean break than something people help one another attempt.

albums.title: Room Above the Yard
albums.label: Rivet House Records
albums.notes: Recorded over three winter weekends in a borrowed upholstery workshop, The Trestle Kin's 2008 Rivet House Records debut makes departure sound like another job that needs doing. Fingerpicked steel strings, circling bass, and restrained drums share audible space with chair noise and hard-floor reflections. Mara Venn's husky alto stays steady while Eli's late, crossing harmonies expose the strain beneath practical instructions. “Leave the Wrench” finds momentum in a halfway-arriving rhythm section; “Under the Saucer” nearly stops the room. By “Down to the Yard,” gathering guitar distortion gives those modest gestures weight. These five songs establish the band's enduring language of work, obligation, and unfinished leave-taking.

tracks.title: The First Bus Doesn't Stop Here

albums.title: Borrowed Driveway
albums.label: Brake Lamp Records
albums.notes: Recorded over two winter weekends in a borrowed rehearsal room, The Ochre Switch's 2008 Brake Lamp Records debut makes departure a household negotiation. Brisk acoustic friction and low baritone-guitar hooks give “Leave the Gate” its impatient momentum, while “Your Half of the Rent” strips the argument to voices and floor tom. Eli Venn's warm, grain-edged delivery and Mara's slightly delayed harmonies already carry the band's emotional weight. The loping “Past the Last Streetlight” opens their first broad horizon; “Boots by the Chair” brings it back to the kitchen. Narrow, woody and unvarnished, the EP closes with “Keep the House Standing,” its final chord left sounding in the room.

albums.title: Census of Porches
albums.label: Tussock Ledger
albums.notes: Recorded over two weekends in a borrowed community hall, Gorse Arithmetic’s 2008 Tussock Ledger debut makes absence audible through small acts of upkeep. Baritone-guitar strings spring against wooden reflections; shoe taps and shared-microphone harmonies remain inside the songs. “Keep the Hinges Oiled” establishes Ewan Bell’s plainspoken reserve and Mereana’s lingering vowels, while “Tuesday Run” puts cancelled services over an unexpectedly buoyant brush-and-mandolin pulse. The nearly bare “Your Side” brings their sibling alignment closest. On “A Light for the Meter Reader,” the opening guitar figure returns with the quartet behind it, establishing a musical vocabulary their later records would widen without abandoning.

tracks.title: A Light for the Meter Reader

albums.title: Where the Water Was
albums.label: Sluice Lantern
albums.notes: On Where the Water Was, Alderwake map a canal through what has replaced it: garden fences, diverted paths and houses whose deeds omit the working ground beneath them. Broadly spaced guitars and lingering room sound make this their most exposed studio record, extending the spatial experiments of their reunion years while easing the rhythmic pressure. “The Diverted Path” hides a missing beat inside its buoyant refrain; “Soundings on Dry Ground” suspends fiddle harmonics over patient guitar figures. Electric bass and low organ gather almost imperceptibly before the closing narratives draw the listener indoors. “Number Forty-Three” ends with a bare voice, then an ensemble heard as if through an open window.

albums.title: Basalt Psalms
albums.label: Pumice Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Pumice Recordings in 2008, Breakwater Atlas’s debut EP finds orchestral possibility inside a small Glasgow room. Fingertip scrape, amplifier hum and tightly framed strings remain audible even as the arrangements expand. “The Measure of a Day” establishes Eilidh Kerr’s steady contralto against patient acoustic picking; “Under the Crane” turns brushed percussion into a rolling, floor-tom-driven six. The nearly percussionless “Names in Chalk” brings the scale back to a single breath before “What We Leave Standing” gathers the record’s suspended harmonies into overlapping vowel calls. This is the foundation of their later breadth: handmade, unresolved and warmed by the sound of people listening closely to one another.

albums.title: Banquet Weather
albums.label: Lantern Stair
albums.notes: On Banquet Weather, Municipal Swans turn a reception into a continuous chamber-pop suite, following hired chairs, anxious speeches and the long collection of relatives into the night. Complete quintet performances remain audible beneath the expanded strings and returning brass: bows scrape, piano pedals lift, and grandeur never quite conceals the work involved. “Hired Furniture” opens with cello harmonics and a gathering march; “A Few Words Before We Eat” lets sibling counterpoint unravel the ceremonial toast. After the hushed “The Side Room,” “Everybody Take a Corner” delivers a hard-earned folk-rock release. The final pair withdraws that fullness, leaving affection suspended over a single reed note.

tracks.title: A Few Words Before We Eat

albums.title: Thumb Against String
albums.label: Hemstitch Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Hemstitch Recordings in 2008, Ansel Bellweather’s debut makes a duplex kitchen feel like an entire listening room. Borrowed four-track tape catches nylon-string scrape, refrigerator hum, and the small hesitations between closely doubled phrases. On “Leave the Water Running,” alternating bass notes turn rinsing a cup into an unfinished invitation; “The Loose Peg” finds a more restless rhythm without disturbing the hush. Cello enters as a tentative interlocutor, while “What I Meant by Stay” trusts harmonium and breathing space alone. By the unaccompanied end of “Room for Your Hands,” private practice has become an uncertain offer of company.

albums.title: Cantilever Hymnal
albums.label: Oblouk Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Oblouk Recordings in 2008, Cantilever Hymnal turns The Ninth Velodrome’s close-room abrasion into municipal-scale architecture. Twenty-four voices answer across a hall while centrally placed percussion and guitars sounding from adjoining rooms keep every crescendo physically grounded. The running bass of “Public Works” and interlocking accents of “Passing on the Banking” give its grandeur a working pulse. “A Sixth Above the Dust” introduces the radiant harmony that the later movements gradually erode. Larger than Cinder Circuit but scarcely more polished, this is music of collective strain: timpani can swallow the ensemble, yet the closing “Doors Left Open” finds its resolution in quiet chords, separate breaths and unhurried decay.

albums.title: Republic of Alibis
albums.label: Carbon Copy Recordings
albums.notes: Released in 2008 on Carbon Copy Recordings, Republic of Alibis expands Zorvelli’s chamber pop into an apartment building of competing testimonies. Harpsichord, brass and household percussion crowd the bright opening songs; after the nearly bare “I Left the Light,” bowed cello becomes the record’s uneasy center. The acoustic guitar keeps a human pulse beneath arrangements that interrupt, qualify and contradict her intimate mezzo. “Everyone Was Home” turns certainty into contrapuntal commotion, while “You Were Safe Here” bleeds into the possessive “For Your Protection.” Following Couture Perjury’s edited silences, these overlapping miniature scenes make ambiguity communal. “No Further Questions” gathers the evidence, then leaves only a voice and a moving chair.

albums.title: Vápenné ticho
albums.label: Dutina Records
albums.notes: Karstové Divadlo’s 2008 debut for Dutina Records finds orchestral breadth inside a cramped, audible room. Borrowed microphones catch dulcimer pedals, shifting chairs and the high ceiling’s lingering answer, while narrowly placed instruments retain their rough edges. “Než se ozve sklep” builds its five-beat guitar figure patiently; “Přenášení” turns dulcimer rattle into wiry forward motion. Between them, Tereza Vránová’s low alto brings thirst and ordinary effort into the music’s geological timescale. The near-bare harmonium song “Dlaň na vápenci” is its still centre. Later string counterlines enlarge the ensemble without overwhelming it, and “Ještě drží teplo” closes on a unison that refuses reassurance.

albums.title: Under Aldebaran
albums.label: North Aisle Recordings
albums.notes: Recorded at a single Canterbury theater engagement, Under Aldebaran strips away the idea of the Union as custodians of intricate studio constructions. These arrangements move through listening bodies: bass displaces the beat, drums provoke fresh turns, and piano and viola answer in real time. “The Ploughman's Astrolabe” opens with brisk confidence; “A Measure of Your Hand” reveals the tenderness beneath the rhythmic machinery. The reunion material gains particular weight in “Where the Meridian Breaks,” while the title track pushes the ensemble toward its fiercest collective playing. Breaths, untidy consonants, and proportionate applause preserve the room. The unaccompanied encore leaves its final harmony beautifully unsettled.

albums.title: Dress Code
albums.label: Carport Assembly
albums.notes: Recorded across two weekends in the Bellamys’ carport, The Juniper Detention’s debut makes enforced neatness sound gloriously untidy. Drum spill rattles the acoustic guitars, mandolin chops set the running pace, and six voices crowd a shared microphone without quite smoothing their edges. “Collar Check” establishes their gift for turning a reassuring harmony uneasy; “Property of the School” hides its accusations inside a bright twelve-string chorus. The hushed “Emergency Contact” reveals the vulnerability beneath the insubordination before “Fold the Chairs” delivers the first blown-open guitar climax. Six compact songs, already alert to who gets to leave and who has to clean up.

albums.title: Karori Sunday
albums.label: Cordial House
albums.notes: On Karori Sunday, The Lacquer Picnic let the room finish its sentences. Recorded around the demands of caring for older relatives, their 2008 Cordial House album exchanges the intricate disputes of The Executor’s Waltz for walking routes, shopping lists and visits that seldom produce news. Hall-recorded guitar and double bass give “The Long Way to the Gate” a generous, unforced gait; “Nothing Needed” finds gentle friction in a syncopated refrain. At the centre, “A Window on the Hills” lets outdoor wind interrupt the piano. The almost-instrumental “Curtain Reel” patiently restores movement before “Leave the Landing Light” opens into divided strings—and withholds its promised resolution.

tracks.title: The Long Way to the Gate

albums.title: Mercy Roster
albums.label: Rimu Tape Club
albums.notes: Released by Rimu Tape Club in 2009, Mercy Roster establishes Orin Pell's spare vocabulary across five songs shaped by a working week in home support. Guitar and grainy baritone share a microphone; felt and brass washers turn the piano into a soft clock whose irregularities leave room for speech. On “The Good Flannel,” a late-entering cello lends weight to an exchange about washing without resolving its awkwardness. “A Glass Left Full” goes further inward, surrendering its final verse to the voice alone. Recorded over two weekends in a borrowed rehearsal space, this debut finds its scale in practical gestures, ending with the viola and suspended second of “On the Way Home.”

albums.title: Cinderwake
albums.label: Tussock Records
albums.notes: Released by Tussock Records in 2009, Cinderwake introduces Pumice Choir through small sounds: steel strings catching fingertips, chairs shifting, two siblings drawing breath. The offset picking of “A Beat Behind” establishes a footing that the rhythm section quietly unsettles. These nine compact songs make family obligation feel physical, with held bass notes pressing against changing chords. At the centre, “Your Good Coat” and “Under the Kitchen” strip the quartet back to low, intimate singing and bowed resonance. Later, snare and tremolo widen the room without losing its edges. “Leave the Light Where It Is” turns a plainspoken verse into an electric ending—the first clear statement of the band's enduring method.

tracks.title: Leave the Light Where It Is

albums.title: Tinplate Summer
albums.label: Switchgrass Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Switchgrass Recordings in 2009, Tinplate Summer introduces The Copper Census at room scale: buzzing baritone strings, woody percussion, short organ blooms, and enough space to hear a chair shift. Across five songs, kitchen-table obligations become statements that might have to be made outside the house. “Leave the Porch Light” establishes Jonah Voss’s restrained narrative presence before Mara’s late entrance; “Bring It Back with Gas” gives their interlocking guitars a nervous, practical urgency. The title track gathers the full band without granting its anticipated final chorus. This is the spare foundation of their catalog, with the sibling harmonies’ breath and friction already essential.

albums.title: Cerchi graduati
albums.label: Traliccio Dischi
albums.notes: Atlante Obliquo’s debut makes symphonic post-rock from the practical sounds of people sharing a room: amplifier hum, bow friction, stick clicks and six guitars occupying unequal distances. Released by Traliccio Dischi in 2009, Cerchi graduati follows an observatory’s first, fruitless night of reactivation. On “Prima accensione,” a bare guitar exchange gradually acquires companions; “Livella” suspends the work entirely. Small, hummable motifs return in altered registers rather than giving way to fresh themes. The sole full-ensemble surge arrives in “Tutti ai sostegni,” its weight earned through accumulated parts. “A occhio nudo” then leaves cello, acoustic guitar and a barely separable human tone tending the silence.

tracks.title: Le stesse stelle, più in basso

albums.title: Borrowed Finery
albums.label: Assembly House
albums.notes: On their first studio album in sixteen years, Velvet Meridian make grandeur feel like something tried on rather than inherited. Chamber strings and harmonium gather around audible fingers, piano hammers and a rhythm section that knows when to leave the room alone. “Someone Else’s Jacket” opens the door gently; “The Wrong Fork” brings an overdue flash of mischief. The strings of “Alterations” expose the hurt beneath the good manners, while “A Room for Everyone” earns the record’s largest communal chorus well before the finish. Released by Assembly House, Borrowed Finery reconnects their architectural rock with the intimate human negotiations that always gave it weight.

albums.title: Bracken Index
albums.label: Sedge Editions
albums.notes: Released by Sedge Editions in 2010, Bracken Index introduces Euan Tern through five songs whose electronics still carry mud on their edges. One steel-string guitar provides the harmonic framework; borrowed-sampler edits turn gravel, fence wire and a distant pump into tentative accompaniments rather than a polished rhythm section. “Waterline Marks” establishes his push-and-pull thumb picking, while “What the Bank Remembers” lets a seven-beat pattern trouble an inherited account of the reservoir’s construction. The nearly spoken “Leave the Gate” offers no tidy resolution. Hiss, uneven microphone distance and exposed breaths make this Bristol debut feel less like a finished portrait than an attentive first encounter.

albums.title: Splitlip
albums.label: Shalehouse Records
albums.notes: Released by Shalehouse Records in 2010, The Quarry Hours' debut makes collective effort audible: brittle acoustic downstrokes, round bass, scuffed percussion and voices finding their footing together. Recorded largely live in a former upholstery workshop, Splitlip establishes Ewan Calder's weathered baritone and Mara Teviot's independent, questioning alto as its central tension. “Leave the Latch” turns a solitary invitation into a roomful of support; “Shale in the Cuffs” and “What We Owe” uncover a darker viola-led undertow. The rushing title track supplies the bruises, while “Stay Till It's Light” offers companionship without pretending anything has been fixed.

albums.title: Towpath Diagrams
albums.label: Dovetail Tapes
albums.notes: Released on Dovetail Tapes in 2010, sluice/09’s debut EP makes a small, tactile world from steel strings, borrowed harmonium and canal-side mechanisms. Loops catch and restart rather than disappear into the mix; suspended guitar voicings hold their ground while bass notes quietly change the weather. “Catch on the Gate” establishes the method with an exposed picking pattern and an awkwardly persuasive latch rhythm. “Leave the Chain Loose” briefly opens the circle to communal singing, while “Your Landing Light” finds its weight in an unanswered doorstep visit. On “Until the Rings Stop,” electronics withdraw beneath an uninterrupted guitar take: an early statement of the group’s refusal to edit the hands out.

albums.title: Pronósticos desiertos
albums.label: Discos Aguafuerte
albums.notes: Released by Discos Aguafuerte in 2010, Pronósticos desiertos introduces Las Falsas Magnolias at domestic scale: nylon-string guitar, interlocking strings and a rehearsal room whose walls answer every pause. Inés Valdés’s low, clear mezzo keeps the promises conversational, even when the arrangements start questioning them. “Para el jueves” walks forward on answering cello plucks; “La señora del fondo” quietly trips its own waltz. The brisk “Cuando llenemos la sala” turns backing vocals into dissenting witnesses. After the near-stillness of “No te pido señales,” the closing round gathers warmth without achieving agreement—a debut already wary of confusing affection with evidence.

albums.title: Everyone Who Stayed
albums.label: South Window Records
albums.notes: Switchyard Orchard’s first full-length makes leaving town sound like something everyone has a stake in. Recorded largely live in a rented community hall, Everyone Who Stayed keeps acoustic strum, melodic bass and dry drums within touching distance, then lets its choruses spill into the room. The fiddle and electric guitar trade sharp answers on “Borrowed Ute,” while “Notice on the Fridge” finds drama in a kitchen conversation nobody wants to finish. After the near-whispered “Your Side of the Table,” the band rebuilds patiently toward the title track’s overlapping voices: a shared history held open rather than neatly resolved.

tracks.title: Leave the Light Above the Sink

albums.title: The Weight We Borrow
albums.label: Rivet House Records
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Rivet House Records, The Trestle Kin give their close, woody acoustics a deeper rhythmic foundation without losing the sound of people sharing a room. Mara Venn’s husky alto holds steady while Eli’s harmonies arrive sideways, turning household negotiations into communal refrains. “Everybody Puts In” and “Payday Windows” supply the early lift; “The Mill Road” delivers the first electric surge. The quieter center makes inherited responsibility feel tangible in keys, floorboards, and unpaid bills. By the loping “What the House Takes,” obligation has become momentum. “Leave the Landing Light” ends without settling the account—or the harmony.

albums.title: A Key for Every Door
albums.label: Brake Lamp Records
albums.notes: Released by Brake Lamp Records in 2011, The Ochre Switch's debut album opens their homemade sound into a broader stereo frame without tidying away its friction. Doubled acoustics chatter against clipped snares, while corridor-recorded electric guitar gives the low hooks room to ring. Eli Venn's grain-edged baritone and Mara's late-arriving harmonies make leaving Newcastle sound like a family discussion with bills attached. The quick opening pair meet their practical reckoning on “The Fridge on the Landing”; the title track turns that tension into a communal chorus. “Keep the Engine Running” closes with gathering momentum, leaving the decision itself unmade.

albums.title: No Service Beyond Here
albums.label: Tussock Ledger
albums.notes: Gorse Arithmetic’s first full-length gives their workshop folk a road beneath it. Ewan Bell’s springy baritone guitar stays close and dry while bass and kick establish forward motion; Mereana’s harmonies become replies, opening space around his plainspoken accounts of shrinking settlements. The accelerating opening run crests at “No Service Beyond Here” before “Names on the Roll” leaves an empty classroom almost untouched. Tape grain, lightly driven electric guitar and communal choruses carry the central stretch, especially “Saturday Roster.” By “Leave the Gate,” momentum has become something quieter: a farewell allowed one final chorus, and no victory lap.

tracks.title: Keep a Light at the Junction

albums.title: Magnificent Mortals
albums.label: Fourfold Records
albums.notes: On their eighth album, Aurelian Voltage find grandeur in leaving room. Recorded with warm strings, occasional woodwind and a choir whose four members remain individually audible, Magnificent Mortals gives Julian Vane's grain-edged tenor longer lines and the quartet's interplay greater weight. “Room Enough for Us” broadens at walking pace; “Good Shoes” and “Still Taking Up the Street” quickly dispel any notion of retreat. The spare bereavement study “The Number I Still Know” finds its muscular answer in “Lean on Me for Once.” Released by Fourfold Records in 2011, this is arena rock attentive to lasting love, practical care and the power of a quiet ending.

tracks.title: Room Enough for Us
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
The knee goes first on the station stair;
You stop and pretend to straighten your hair.
I know that trick. I invented it, love.
Give me the case. Let the others shove.
We've tickets enough for the journey ahead;
There's time for a sit when we get there instead.

[Pre-Chorus]
Your hand in mine, by the booking hall,
Still draws a look. Let it draw them all.

[Chorus]
There is room enough for us,
For the years we carry in.
Keep your hand upon my arm;
Let the whole bright evening in.
We need longer now to rise,
But we're rising. Here we come.
Move the chairs and leave the lights:
There is room enough for us.

[Verse]
Your glasses lie by the kitchen bread;
You read me the bill with mine instead.
The tailor has let my good coat out;
It fits who I am when we go about.
You fasten the cuff that my fingers refuse;
I kneel, with a grunt, for the knot in your shoes.

[Chorus]
There is room enough for us,
For the years we carry in.
Keep your hand upon my arm;
Let the whole bright evening in.
We need longer now to rise,
But we're rising. Here we come.
Move the chairs and leave the lights:
There is room enough for us.

[Bridge]
I used to shake your fingers free
When footsteps followed you and me.
Tonight, beneath the foyer glass,
I let the hurried people pass.
You take my elbow. I let you.
Such a small thing, so late to do.

[Chorus]
There is room enough for us,
For the years we carry in.
Keep your hand upon my arm;
Let the whole bright evening in.
We need longer now to rise,
But we're rising. Here we come.
Move the chairs and leave the lights:
There is room enough for us.

[Outro]

albums.title: Mending Sunday
albums.label: Hemstitch Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Hemstitch Recordings in 2011, Mending Sunday opens Ansel Bellweather’s kitchen-door folk into a close, breathing trio. Nylon-string guitar retains its fingertip scrape and rounded bass; cello answers unfinished phrases while harmonium makes small harmonic shifts feel momentous. “Come In Quietly” offers a bare invitation, and “The Sleeve” turns a post-argument repair into a flowing six-beat melody. The interlocking lines of “Room for Both” briefly promise an easy reconciliation before “What Holds” exposes the strain beneath it. By “Leave the Lamp,” warmth returns without certainty: three quiet voices share the room with the audible labor of the bellows.

albums.title: Seven Against Nine
albums.label: Blue Spindle Records
albums.notes: Released by Blue Spindle Records in 2011, Luvo Nqolase’s six-song debut makes rhythmic independence feel companionable: the thumb keeps rocking while treble figures wander across it. Close microphones catch fingertips, breath and the borrowed room itself, with concertina and handclaps offering just enough company. “Bring Your Hands” turns shared work into a brisk invitation; “The Stone Beside the Path” slows to a boundary dispute neither melody nor narrator can settle. The nested voices of “Between Windows” point toward his later ensemble thinking, while “What We Leave Standing” ends with an unaccompanied promise and the room still listening.

albums.title: Bilhete Picotado
albums.label: Cavalete Discos
albums.notes: Recorded over two winter weekends in a borrowed Porto rehearsal room, Tomás Nespereira’s Cavalete Discos debut finds a fairground still closed to the public. Steel-string guitar, conversational baritone and bassoon trace five workers through small, necessary jobs, with chair creaks and ensemble breaths left intact. “Trocos para Abrir” establishes the unhurried intimacy; “Apertar à Mão” turns a plucked-sounding bassoon figure into an ingenious working rhythm. The bruised tenderness of “Por Cima da Fenda” gives way to “Antes de Ferver,” whose late-arriving violas reveal the orchestral breadth Nespereira would explore without abandoning this close human scale.

albums.title: Bus Evacuation
albums.label: Red Clay Relay
albums.notes: On their first full-length, The Juniper Detention turn a threatened school closure into an argument with no empty seats. Mandolin strikes and scraped acoustic strings retain Dress Code’s cramped immediacy, while roomier drums and widely panned electric twelve-strings give six interlocking voices space to disagree. “Portable Classroom” supplies the irresistible refrain; “The Man with the Keys” and “Minutes of the Meeting” find obligations beneath official titles. By the extended closing pair, “County Line After Dark” and “Leave One Light,” departure has become something larger and less reassuring than escape. This is communal folk-rock with its hands still on the folding chairs.

albums.title: After Forty Winters
albums.label: Spindlebank
albums.notes: Released by Spindlebank in 2011, After Forty Winters returns Bracken Dial to their acoustic centre without trying to recover their younger selves. Lower keys, generous silences and largely live performances expose the grain of bass wood, crumhorn breath and bow changes. “The Key Still Turns” quietly reveals the old rhythmic ingenuity beneath its plain surface; “The Adjourned Match” lets an unfinished contest gather force through instrumental counterpoint. Later, “Their Father's Hand” and “Your Letter in November” weigh inherited obligations against belated remorse. The closing “Leave the Lamp” reduces the ensemble to voice and fiddle before one unresolved collective cadence: a reunion, but no easy settlement.

albums.title: Forked Bearings
albums.label: Sundspor
albums.notes: Svalevev’s debut learns departure by ear: ferry horns travel through floorboards, wings stir outside a window, and a household wakes to someone already gone. Recorded largely in one room, Forked Bearings makes the friction between low-string ostinatos and suspended upper guitar figures its quiet engine. On “Before the Landing Light,” a second picking pattern shifts the ground without raising the volume; “Seven Across” turns that instability into a communal, seven-beat refrain. Thumb scrapes, harmonium breath and slightly delayed harmonies remain exposed throughout. The percussionless “Leave the Window Latched” closes without settling its final interval—a precise beginning for a band concerned with how departure sounds to those who stay.

albums.title: Moraine Teeth
albums.label: Skare Editions
albums.notes: Iver Ruskedal’s debut sets steel-string intimacy against Bergen’s rainlit electrical glare. Thumbnail scrapes and fret buzz remain audible as short guitar loops splinter into coarse, luminous grains; narrow drum samples and muted bass move around the picking rather than flattening it. “Borrowed Current” and “Under the Flyover” turn uneven phrases into quietly insistent hooks, while the instrumental “Drainpipe Harmonics” finds a resonant chamber in rehearsal-room runoff. The closing “Leave the Low String” dismantles that brightness layer by layer. Released by Skare Editions in 2012, Moraine Teeth establishes Ruskedal’s central tension: the body admitting what its inherited habits cannot yet accommodate.

albums.title: Chromatic Rime
albums.label: Pumice Recordings
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Pumice Recordings, Glasgow’s Breakwater Atlas turn the close quarters of Basalt Psalms into spacious, carefully scored architecture. Pump organ and fingerpicked guitar remain the human measure, while strings, distant trombones and a twelve-person wordless choir widen the horizon. “The Weight of Seven” establishes the patient rhythmic language; “Counterweight” breaks into ride-driven motion without sacrificing detail. Eilidh Kerr’s grounded contralto gives “No Word for Leaving” its exposed gravity, and the acoustic “Thread Ends” makes the closing sweep feel earned. Across rehearsal-room intimacy and municipal-hall resonance, Chromatic Rime finds grandeur in work, endurance and futures still undecided.

albums.title: Cizalla
albums.label: Sello Ladera
albums.notes: Released by Sello Ladera in 2012, Isóbara’s debut EP keeps the room close: string buzz, dragged fingertips and short reflections are part of the arrangements. “El peso del pulgar” establishes their interlocking rhythmic language, letting treble figures in three pull against a thumb cycle in five. On “La pared,” Amalia Véliz’s intimate Spanish delivery meets an oscillator felt almost before it is heard. The bowed charango of “Entre dos superficies” makes acoustic friction and electronic sustain seem continuous. “Manga gastada” briefly tightens the pulse before “Lo que queda debajo” dismantles it, introducing a quartet already more interested in persistence than climax.

albums.title: Unhurried
albums.label: Pale Current Records
albums.notes: Released in 2012 on Pale Current Records, Orin Pell's first full-length gives the spare language of Mercy Roster room to hesitate. Thumbpicked steel-string, dry prepared piano and answering viola lines retain the intimacy of players seated together; damper lifts and instrumental bleed become part of the phrasing. “A Pear in the Sun” offers a lilting patch of daylight before “The Long Wash” and “Still in the Chair” stretch into bass-clarinet shadow and near-stationary cello. These songs measure the distance between completing a task and attending to someone. The closing “When You're Ready” makes that distinction audible, shedding instruments until waiting itself seems to resonate.

albums.title: Basalt Horses
albums.label: Tussock Records
albums.notes: Released by Tussock Records in 2012, Basalt Horses expands Pumice Choir’s close-grained debut into music built around distance, resistance and shared air. Sharply divided acoustic guitars frame drums and amplifiers resonating through a converted community hall; the room becomes another instrument. “Borrowed Gate” and “Your Brother’s Car” find propulsion in bass-led refrains, while “Six Steps Back” establishes the album’s patient six-beat undertow. The nearly bare “What I Can Swear To” interrupts that gathering force. From there, the arrangements climb toward the bruising release of “The Weight We Kept,” before “After the Hooves” lets clean harmonics carry the record out.

tracks.title: No One Takes the Lower Road

albums.title: Return Ticket
albums.label: Second Matinee
albums.notes: Released on Second Matinee, The Porcelain Astronauts' final album makes coming back sound as consequential as taking off. Spacious electronics frame acoustic guitars, chamber strings and the returning harpsichord, while Adrian Vale's weathered tenor finds a grounding presence in Celia Rook's increasingly prominent lower harmonies. “Two for the Coast” offers a flash of syncopated brightness; the extended “Junctions” lets their chamber instincts roam without becoming a retrospective. The intimate negotiation of “A Drawer for Your Things” leads toward the choral welcome of “There Is Still a Place.” Then “Here, Then” brings everything indoors, leaving a piano chord to finish speaking.

albums.title: Pep Rally
albums.label: Switchgrass Recordings
albums.notes: The Copper Census turn up the lights on their first full-length, but the brighter room exposes deeper divisions. Hard-panned acoustics, picked bass, compressed drums, and overdriven organ carry clipped verses into sibling choruses that sound welcoming until everyone starts wanting something different. “Temporary Flags” and “Home Side” make obligation feel almost danceable; the handclapped “Cakewalk” turns a town fundraiser into an irresistible trap. At the record’s quiet hinge, “Your Half of the House” strips that collective confidence down to two breathing voices. The closing “All the Lights Stay On” restores the full band without settling the argument, its jubilant coda outlasting the people who began it.

albums.title: Propwork
albums.label: Sump Room Records
albums.notes: Borrowed Viaduct’s 2012 Sump Room Records debut makes togetherness sound like a practical negotiation. Recorded over two weekends in their Christchurch workshop rehearsal unit, Propwork leaves bow scrape, bass spill and a loose drum fitting inside the songs. Mara Bell’s grainy alto holds the centre while Eli Sutherland tests its edges with contrary melodies. “A Key That Turns” establishes that uneasy companionship; “Cups by the Sink” finds tension in borrowed domestic space. The overdriven closing stretch of “Carry It Level” hints at the band’s future reach, but “Leave a Light in Here” supplies the defining gesture: four voices gathering, then an unresolved chord and the room itself.

albums.title: Dripline
albums.label: Leafbed Recordings
albums.notes: Recorded between a rented Bengaluru bedroom and a cooperative tool shed, Neem Circuit’s 2012 Leafbed Recordings debut makes small sounds carry questions of work, access and shared time. On “Hours We Keep,” a full verse of bare fingerpicking precedes the first granular shimmer; “Common Tap” turns hose fittings into a dry, off-centre rhythm section. The brisk two-step of “After My Shift” supplies the EP’s physical peak without dislodging its stubborn acoustic pedal note. Kavya Rao’s close, lightly husky alto keeps the English and Kannada lyrics conversational. Worker testimony and passing traffic remain audible on “Before Six,” while “Leave It Running” finds its ending in the room after the music stops.

albums.title: Podzemní poledne
albums.label: Dutina Records
albums.notes: Released by Dutina Records in 2012, Podzemní poledne turns the physical distance between a struck string and its returning echo into chamber-scale drama. Karstové Divadlo’s second album separates dry Brno performances from passages recorded anew in a quarry service gallery; the underground responses arrive as counterlines, not atmosphere pasted over everything. “Šest kroků ke světlu” gives the opening stillness a measured pulse, while “Než dopiješ” brings Tereza Vránová’s conversational alto almost within touching distance. At the centre, “Spád” entrusts the record’s descending theme to strings alone. Its eventual return in “Co unese strop” earns the ensemble’s full weight before the exposed, patient closing song.

albums.title: Diesel Arithmetic
albums.label: Latchwork Recordings
albums.notes: On his 2012 Latchwork Recordings debut, Nairobi’s Kito Mwangala makes the journey home feel like an intimate negotiation between money, time and nerve. Thumb-piano mechanisms and fingers dragging across muted guitar strings sit closer than the street outside; rounded bass and irregular scraps of metal provide just enough footing. “Enough for One” establishes the descending motif that quietly binds the EP, while “Ticket Teeth” finds a tentative pocket in punched-metal clicks. The nearly motionless “Will You Be There?” turns a practical question into an exposed emotional wager. “Leave the Latch” brings another guitar into the room, offering company rather than an easy answer.

albums.title: Someone Is Listening
albums.label: Acacia Wire Records
albums.notes: Released by Acacia Wire Records in 2012, Cassian Mothusi’s debut makes a carpeted outbuilding feel like the last room awake in Pretoria. Ringing acoustic strings hold steady above moving bass notes; brushed drums and distant electric replies never obscure the fret noise or the catch in his tenor. “Leave the Landing Light” introduces the close three-part harmonies, while “Your Street, Before Rain” briefly puts restless waiting into motion. The spare “A Small Correction” breaks that gathering warmth. By “Someone Is Listening,” affection has become an uncomfortable vigil, carried into an unresolved electric ending. It establishes the intimate vocabulary his later records would expand and interrogate.

albums.title: Piecework
albums.label: Bobbin House Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Bobbin House Recordings in 2012, Piecework finds Manchester trio Twillphase building a small, tactile world from nylon strings, machinery and the air between takes. Shuttle strikes keep their rough edges; guitar figures repeat without quite settling into the percussion. Ellis Rook’s conversational low tenor makes these accounts of wages, nicknames and bodily wear feel overheard rather than proclaimed. “Mind Your Fingers” introduces that intimacy, while “First Pay” gives a remembered purchase room to carry its own weight. The intricately crowded “Keeping Up” hints at the rhythmic possibilities ahead, but “Leave It There” closes with the modest gravity of people finally stopping work.

albums.title: Corrections in the Margin
albums.label: Towpath Recordings
albums.notes: After the spacious absences of Where the Water Was, Alderwake pull their chairs up to the kitchen table. Released by Towpath Recordings in 2013, Corrections in the Margin makes page turns, tapping feet and uneven room reflections part of its documentary grain. “Sixpence Carried Forward” hurries into its chorus; the fiddle-led pair “The Short Measure / Across the Landing” tests the same small phrase against different steps. At the centre, “Hours Not Entered” gives unpaid labour the weight of a bare voice and harmonium. A brief communal flare yields to “Names on the Reverse,” where two guitars leave the final accounting open.

tracks.title: The Short Measure / Across the Landing
That's Not How He Said It

albums.title: Linho Elétrico
albums.label: Agulha Discos
albums.notes: On her 2013 Agulha Discos debut, Inês Valdouro makes relocation audible in trouser hems, bus times and coins counted twice. Nylon-string bass patterns carry short Portuguese songs whose apparent simplicity conceals crooked bars and suspended endings. Recorded together, guitar and mezzo retain the give of conversation; the overdubbed sextet contributes grain, counterpoint and the occasional protesting chair. “À Hora dos Autocarros” opens the room into lilting chamber folk, while “Trocos” tightens it around five-beat arithmetic. The nearly bare “Ainda Digo Rega” provides the evening’s still point. “Linho à Janela” gathers the ensemble upward, then leaves the guitar—and the new life—unsettled.

albums.title: Spillway Psalms
albums.label: Sedge Editions
albums.notes: Released by Sedge Editions in 2013, Euan Tern’s first full-length gives the disturbances of Bracken Index a physical centre: rounded sub-bass, displaced kicks and percussion cut from chains, boots and breath. “At the Gauge” makes a solitary guitar figure change shape simply by adding a beat; “Accounts of the Leaving” strips that machinery away to let incompatible memories stand. Throughout, his close, husky tenor keeps reservoir folklore grounded in questions of access, ownership and loss. “The Weight of the Wall” brings the record’s fullest release before “What the Water Keeps” leaves only an increasingly unsteady guitar figure.

albums.title: Ochre Parade
albums.label: Shalehouse Records
albums.notes: On their second album, The Quarry Hours carry their close-miked folk-rock into a community hall without losing the scrape of pick against string. Brass, divided strings and a twelve-person chorus enlarge the songs while leaving audible space between their players. “Hall Doors” opens in harmonium breath; “Day Wages” turns a clipped working-week rhythm into an immediate communal refrain. The unsettled procession of “No Flag for This” tests the pageantry, while “A Chair Beside the Bed” brings everything back to two people. Released by Shalehouse Records in 2013, Ochre Parade finds its scale in the softer, returning promises of “Stone Still Warm.”

albums.title: Apricot Republic
albums.label: Copper Kettle Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Copper Kettle Recordings in 2013, Apricot Republic trades Banquet Weather’s connected orchestral scenes for ten distinct songs played with the doors open. Guitar, double bass, strings and reeds breathe together in a converted schoolroom, their small hesitations becoming part of the rhythm. The opening run is unusually radiant: “All the Windows Open” and the title track give Lotte’s upper melodies room above Pieter’s conversational baritone. Hospitality’s hidden workload surfaces in “Steam at Midnight” and “The Last Collection,” before “Schoolroom Shuffle” loosens the ensemble’s shoulders. “Those Who Stayed” turns cleanup into communal celebration; “Leave Two Chairs” preserves the breaths and furniture noises after it.

albums.title: Tenants Wearing Gold
albums.label: Folded Stage Records
albums.notes: Parlor Cartography’s debut makes a small rehearsal room feel like an entire apartment building. Close-recorded strings interrupt, sympathize and occasionally expose the light baritone at the center, while uneven upright piano and audible bow changes keep its miniature dramas human. “Company on the Landing” opens the door with bare guitar and a buoyant refrain; “What the Cello Knows” finds tenderness through the wall. The borrowed-jacket trilogy, beginning with “A Jacket for the Evening,” turns social aspiration into accelerating operetta. Then the bustle recedes, leaving “A Room of Ordinary Size” to discover dignity in an unadorned melody. Released in 2013 by Folded Stage Records, this is their intimate foundation.

tracks.title: Whose Name Is in the Lining?

albums.title: Confeti en los bolsillos
albums.label: Fulgor Cooperativa
albums.notes: On their 2013 Fulgor Cooperativa release, Palacio Fulgor recover communal warmth without pretending the years haven't happened. Twelve-string scrape, exposed piano hammers, open drums, and audible amplifier hum give these arena-sized songs the intimacy of five musicians sharing a room. Julián Varela's rougher tenor remains proudly declamatory, but the answering voices sound like friends, not an immaculate choir. “Lo que nos queda” opens with buoyant resolve; “Dejame la luz” and the expansive “Los años de la casa” locate devotion in everyday care. By “Nos vemos abajo,” celebration belongs to everyone present—including the late entrance and laughter left on the tape.

albums.title: Latch Choir
albums.label: Dovetail Tapes
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Dovetail Tapes, Bristol trio sluice/09 turn homemade mechanisms into a rhythm section without polishing away their awkward little hesitations. Open-tuned guitar, bowed fiddle and harmonium carry songs about spare keys, shared entrances and the people paid to keep passage possible. “Someone Left the Catch” sets a brisk pace; “All the Names on the Bell” crowns the opening run with interlocking vocal syllables and a genuinely welcoming refrain. The miniature “Spare Room” changes the light. From there, clipped beats and patient ballads reveal the isolation behind these everyday arrangements, until “Leave It on the Latch” brings three unedited voices into the same room.

tracks.title: All the Names on the Bell

albums.title: Request Line
albums.label: Cable Basket
albums.notes: Released by Cable Basket in 2013, Request Line introduces kitenge/64 through five intimate dedications carried on dry guitar, buzzing thumb piano and percussion pieced together from claps, string noise and digital slips. Room hiss and chair creaks keep these loops within arm’s reach. “If You're Still There” establishes the EP’s patient, off-centre pulse; “The Other Cup” strips it back to two chords and Nyambura Kibe’s low, conversational alto. On “Windows Still Lit,” three overlapping vocal figures make the small room feel suddenly inhabited. Before the broader arrangements of Antenna Orchard, this debut finds its lift in modest means—and in leaving space for an unheard reply.

albums.title: Podium Grass
albums.label: Oblouk Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Oblouk Recordings in 2013, Podium Grass turns The Ninth Velodrome’s architectural crescendos into close listening. Piano hammers, double-bass finger noise and eight singers’ shared breaths bring the ensemble within arm’s reach; fencing rattles and wind under empty benches occupy the space beyond. “Under the Benches” opens almost without weight, while “Groundsman’s Measure” finds a walking pulse that never becomes a march. The cello-and-piano duet “A Place to Sit” offers an unusually direct melody before “Gate Load” briefly tears the quiet open. This is their most restrained record: ceremony remembered through maintenance, silence and the effort of staying.

albums.title: Corrections Desk
albums.label: Witness Room
albums.notes: After the fractured miniature scenes of Republic of Alibis, Corrections Desk brings Zorvelli back into a room with other players—and leaves their hesitations intact. Piano, upright bass, brushes, viola and bass clarinet give these songs a conversational elasticity, with harpsichord deployed like a sharply worded footnote. The easy walk of “The Story We Liked” conceals a painful retraction; “Good Silver” and “Below the Fold” turn social polish into rhythmic friction. At the center, “The Empty Chair” lets instruments answer where stacked voices once interrupted. The closing “No Reply Required” makes accountability sound neither triumphant nor complete.

albums.title: Manual of Astonishment
albums.label: Tramline Recordings
albums.notes: On his 2013 Tramline Recordings release, Benedict Spindle makes precision feel companionable. Whole piano performances and gently elastic drums anchor vocal constructions whose intricate joins are almost invisible. “The First Thing You Believe” opens a trapdoor beneath an apparently plain melody; the central “A Demonstration of Kindness” turns contrapuntal ingenuity toward an unexpectedly tender promise. This is the synthesis his earlier records anticipated: acoustic confession and electric machinery sharing the same room. As “Ordinary Evidence” and “Leave the Door on the Latch” reduce the spectacle to individual voices and instrumental lines, persuasion becomes less a public triumph than a private responsibility.

tracks.title: Leave the Door on the Latch

albums.title: Mandíbula
albums.label: Sello Remache
albums.notes: En su debut para Sello Remache, León de Alambre convierte el cuarto de ensayo en una arena sin borrar sus huellas: uñas sobre nylon, tacones contra el piso y respiraciones entre dientes. Mandíbula presenta la voz pública como conquista y hambre peligrosa. «Abrir la boca» fija el contraste entre intimidad acústica y golpe eléctrico; «Dientes de oro» lo acelera con brillo glam y palmas secas. En el centro, «Lo que debo» desnuda el costo familiar de hacerse escuchar. Las guitarras se multiplican sin alisar sus bordes, hasta que «Que tiemble el nombre» entrega el protagonismo a cuatro voces que ya pueden sostenerse sin amplificación.

albums.title: Dientes de prestidigitador
albums.label: Discos Aguafuerte
albums.notes: En su primer larga duración, editado por Discos Aguafuerte en 2013, Las Falsas Magnolias convierten el oficio de ilusionista en un teatro de cámara lleno de cuentas pendientes. El clave deja oír sus mecanismos; las cuerdas y el clarinete bajo agrandan la escena sin borrar su escala doméstica. «Respetable público» presenta una figura ascendente que el disco irá despojando de autoridad. Las baladas enlazadas «La mujer que falta» y «Desde adentro de la caja» disputan una misma desaparición mediante voces contradictorias. Entre valses truncados y estribillos bulliciosos, la precisión del arreglo vuelve más incómodo el engaño. «Después de la función» deja apenas voz, cello y una promesa sin resolver.

tracks.title: Una moneda detrás de tu oreja

albums.title: An Unclaimed Teaspoon
albums.label: Sideboard Recordings
albums.notes: Between Karori Sunday’s open-ended conversations and Seating Arrangements’ interlocking rhythms, The Lacquer Picnic make a virtue of withholding. Nylon strings, piano pedals and the scrape of a viola bow sit almost uncomfortably close; arrangements widen only when the household negotiations can no longer stay polite. The opening miniatures find comedy in inventories and conditional generosity, before “Who Said You Could Have It” makes ownership sound indistinguishable from grief. “The Empty Rectangle” is the exposed heart of the record, while “An Unclaimed Teaspoon” finally admits the full ensemble. Its accumulating verses turn a negligible piece of cutlery into something nobody can bear either to keep or relinquish.

tracks.title: Who Said You Could Have It

albums.title: Pocket Current
albums.label: Platform Glass
albums.notes: Released on Platform Glass in 2014, Relayweather's debut makes the journey home feel like a sequence of small negotiations. You hear fingers, fabric and wood before their electronic afterimages: guitar harmonics spread into chords, clipped plucks become hooks, a knock learns to keep time. Elliot's husky tenor holds these handmade arrangements close, even when “Still Lit” opens into the EP's first expansive chorus. The uninterrupted fingerpicking of “Fold the Blanket” offers its most exposed moment; “I'll Leave It On” finds momentum, then removes its rhythmic reassurance. Across five tracks, the Melbourne trio establish a language of suspended harmony, audible sampling seams and care expressed through practical gestures.

albums.title: Glitter Mutiny
albums.label: Red Rivet Records
albums.notes: On their 2014 Red Rivet Records release, Vesper Cavalcade put theatrical pleasure to work: fuzzed twelve-strings scrape against dry drums, melodic bass and choruses crowded with distinctly different voices. The melodic sweep of their earlier records survives, but the stakes are local and concrete. “The Last Night at the Mercury” turns a venue's closure into a furious communal hook; “Clock Out Together” finds dance-floor momentum in the logistics of a walkout. The exposed piano of “Our Name on the Poster” refuses the band an easy moral victory. Rather than build another monument, “Thursday, Seven” sends everyone back out with a meeting time and a collective shout.

tracks.title: The Last Night at the Mercury

albums.title: Soft Reset
albums.label: Latch Audio
albums.notes: Released by Latch Audio in 2014, Soft Reset introduces morrow// FM through the grain of a steel string and the small imperfections of a laptop pushed to its limits. Narrow, close-miked verses suddenly unfold into stereo, but Eli Venn’s breath and fret noise remain inside the circuitry. “When It Loads” establishes their intimate acoustic-to-electronic grammar; “Passenger Window” gives it a skipping, quietly infectious lift. The near-dissolution of “You Were Saying” makes the patient closing surge of “Leave It Till Morning” feel earned. Across five songs, unfinished conversations become something unexpectedly hopeful: another chance to say it tomorrow.

albums.title: Cobalt Alias
albums.label: Counterseal Records
albums.notes: Released by Counterseal Records in 2014, Ivara Sorel’s debut EP makes a dressing room of the chamber ensemble: every hammer strike, valve click and collective breath registers at close range. “The Name I Give” unfolds from near-spoken piano intimacy into a three-part trumpet refrain, while “Good Cuffs” lets a buoyant tune trip over its own extra half-bars. At the center, “Without the Clasp” finds vulnerability in felt-muted resonance and mechanical rattle. The gallery standoff of “The Visitor Will Remain” supplies the theatrical summit; “Hello” quietly dismantles it. These five economical arrangements establish Sorel’s early language of borrowed identities, singable refrains and conspicuously human effort.

albums.title: Everybody Upstairs
albums.label: Sump Room Records
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Sump Room Records, Christchurch’s Borrowed Viaduct turn shared quarters into a gathering. Recorded mostly live in a hired hall, Everybody Upstairs gives kick drum and plucked double bass a firm centre without losing bow scrape or the air around a ringing guitar. Mara Bell’s grainy alto stays at the heart of the songs, with Eli Sutherland’s contrary tenor making “Bring Your Boots” especially immediate. The temporary rooms of “Until the Room Is Ready” give way to the practical devotion of “Call Again Tomorrow.” By the accelerating, distant-choir finish of “Leave the Chairs,” togetherness feels earned rather than assumed.

tracks.title: The Long Way to the Dairy

albums.title: La distanza esatta
albums.label: Traliccio Dischi
albums.notes: On their second album, Bologna’s Atlante Obliquo bring their six-guitar architecture within touching distance. Nylon strings creak, bows catch, and Elia Vannini’s wordless tenor emerges from behind a chamber trio sharing an audible room. Released by Traliccio Dischi in 2014, La distanza esatta trades the amplifier haze of Cerchi graduati for warmth, interruption and patient human exchange. “Il panno sulle lenti” opens with domestic simplicity; “Registro delle riparazioni” builds an ascent that quietly dismantles itself. After the harmonic miniature “Vetro fermo,” the closing sequence finds dance, friction and release, ending with “A turno,” whose melody belongs to nobody for long.

albums.title: Contrapesos
albums.label: Cavalete Discos
albums.notes: On his first full-length, Porto’s Tomás Nespereira turns a fairground family’s working day into chamber folk of unusual physical precision. Steel-string guitar keeps time while bassoon steps forward to lead an eleven-player ensemble; heel taps, brushed drum and struck wood make labour audible without turning it into spectacle. The unaccompanied opening of “Antes do Sol” releases into the record’s quickest stride, while “À Vez” finds a precarious dance in interlocking pizzicato. “Horas por Pagar” brings the withheld wages—and the strings—to breaking point. More interconnected than Bilhete Picotado, Contrapesos closes by stripping its arrangements back until even the evening’s arithmetic becomes a matter of perspective.

albums.title: Splitlane
albums.label: Sump Audio
albums.notes: Released on Sump Audio in 2014, kitevault's debut EP makes a bedroom feel as enclosed and resonant as a training pool. Hammered dulcimer supplies hooks and splintery percussion, while guitar harmonics, rounded bass and Ellis Mercer's close, grain-edged tenor keep every small gesture audible. “Next Lane” begins with a squeaking bench; “Count Me Out” builds its pressure through counted subdivisions and crowded vocal doubles. The beatless “The Spare Chair” interrupts that ascent with devastating restraint. Even the luminous drop of “Wait Outside” leaves daylight between its wooden strikes. “No More Lengths” closes this miniature introduction with humming voices and the sound of dampers lifting.

albums.title: After the Shift
albums.label: Breakwater Assembly
albums.notes: On their second full-length, The Trestle Kin make amplifier bleed part of the writing: chords linger across bar lines, counter-melodies resist the lead, and drums arrive only when restraint becomes unbearable. Recorded live in a former union meeting room, After the Shift deepens the rhythmic weight of The Weight We Borrow without losing the shared air of their debut EP. Mara Venn's husky alto keeps its plainspoken center through the delayed release of “Still in My Work Clothes” and the gathering pressure of “Second Shift Weather.” “Hold This End” offers a small, necessary kindness before the closing three-song sequence breaks open and leaves two voices standing.

tracks.title: All the Lights Along the Yard

albums.title: The Weight of Leaving
albums.label: Sounding House
albums.notes: Released by Sounding House in 2015, The Weight of Leaving turns Gorse Arithmetic's widening folk-rock inward. Ewan Bell's baritone guitar rasps through a small amplifier; Ruth's bass supplies answers the lyrics withhold, while clipped room sound makes Tom's drums feel abruptly bounded. “Someone Has to Stay” delivers their fiercest chorus without breaking Bell's vocal reserve. The domestic bargaining of “Good Towels” and “Before You Cancel the Power” makes migration tangible rather than abstract. Uneven metres gradually restore momentum, culminating in the slow accumulation of “What the House Holds.” The bare closing duet, “Leave the Gate,” offers closeness without pretending the obligations have been settled.

albums.title: Nadie al otro lado
albums.label: Casa de Sal
albums.notes: On their return to the studio, Faro de Cobre make instant contact sound strangely lonely. Sampled guitar harmonics and filtered organ flicker around twelve-string patterns, but every programmed rhythm meets a human reply: woodblock, handclap, palm against drumhead. “Avísame al llegar” turns concern into a taut rock refrain; “De este lado” brings Tomás Araya and Inés Mella from opposite stereo edges into one exposed center. The closing stretch gradually switches the circuitry off. By the live-room surge of “Que nadie quede afuera” and the distant harmonies of “Una taza más,” their familiar grandeur rests on something simpler—and harder—than connection: being present.

tracks.title: La luz del aparato
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]
Ah, a la sal.
Ah, al azar.

[Verse]
Me llega apenas la mitad,
la otra mitad me nombra.
Hay una sílaba de cal
pegada al aire de tu boca.
Digo presente y suena mar.

[Interlude]

[Verse]
Hora de sal, demora azul,
mi voz trabaja sin relevo.
Queda una erre donde tú
ibas abriendo el aire nuevo.
No desamarres todavía.

[Pre-Chorus]
Pasa despacio por la voz.
Hay gente abajo.
Hay gente abajo.

[Chorus]
Alumbra, aparato, alumbra.
Dame la a de acá.
Que no se cierre lo que zumba,
que quede abierto el umbral.

[Interlude]
Ah, a la sal.
Ah, al azar.

[Chorus]

[Outro]
Acá.

Todavía.
Ah.

albums.title: Satin Arithmetic
albums.label: Falter Editions
albums.notes: Oskar Bellwether’s 2015 debut for Falter Editions makes domestic embarrassment sound quietly consequential. Thumb-picked nylon strings and close upright piano anchor a small ensemble whose viola, cello and reeds behave like skeptical dinner guests. Breaths, pedal creaks and short room reflections keep the intricate writing within touching distance. The nimble comedy of “Excellent Credit” gives way to the exposed financial dread of “The Amount Remaining,” while uneven waltzes turn good manners into precarious choreography. “A Toast to Solvency” briefly gathers the players into something triumphant; “What I Can Afford” leaves that promise unresolved. Throughout, Bellwether’s intimate baritone lets precise jokes dissolve into admissions.

albums.title: Wage for the Rain
albums.label: Leafbed Recordings
albums.notes: Neem Circuit's first full-length turns the scale of Dripline outward without losing the sound of hands at work. Open-tuned steel strings, dry low alto and contact-miked tools anchor arrangements that widen almost imperceptibly: bass arrives late, keyboard tones linger, and breakbeats emerge when the songs can no longer contain their pressure. “Day Rate” makes a wage calculation quietly piercing; “Carry the Water” converts shared labour into the record's sharpest rhythmic release. An interview interrupts that momentum before the final three songs find strength in answering voices. The title track closes with a settled melody over harmony that still won't grant permission.

albums.title: Seedtime Atlas
albums.label: Hedgerow Assembly
albums.notes: On Seedtime Atlas, The Astrolabe Union recover the saturated ensemble color of their earlier records without losing the patience acquired along the way. Recorded largely with the quintet playing together, these songs let cello, oboe, and bass clarinet become fellow thinkers rather than decorative guests. The luminous piano repetitions of “The Light in the Seedhouse” open onto nimble planting songs; the title suite makes teaching and correction audible through interlocking lines and changing meters. From there, the arrangements gradually loosen their grip. “The Younger Hand” finds feeling in withheld answers, while “A Tune for Keeping” passes its melody around the band before gathering everyone into song.

albums.title: Domewake
albums.label: Parallax Works
albums.notes: Released by Parallax Works in 2015, Aperture Republic's debut turns a disused planetarium into a resonant civic chamber. Live rhythm-section takes anchor six-player strings, close piano and guitars whose distortion preserves scrape and amplifier breath. Naledi Maseko's grain-edged alto hangs deep in the room, while a former attendant's recollections interrupt the spectacle with ordinary detail. “An Unofficial Opening” establishes the walking pulse; “Where the Ceiling Opens” pushes its patient architecture toward rupture. After the near-stillness of “House Lights,” uneven figures rebuild the ensemble. “Until the Room Is Empty” finds its resolution not in conquest, but in unaccompanied humming—a first statement of hope as upkeep.

tracks.title: A Small Repair to the Sky

albums.title: Velcro Devotion
albums.label: Latchwork Recordings
albums.notes: On his first full-length, Kito Mwangala expands Diesel Arithmetic’s spare loops into songs large enough to hold an answer. Muted steel strings bite against thick sub-bass; buckles, straps and workshop taps keep their uneven spacing. “Hold This End” announces the change with an immediate, generous chorus, while “Not After Closing” turns a postponed call into syncopated friction. The bare guitar of “Unpick” interrupts the central rush without offering easy release. Released by Latchwork Recordings in 2015, Velcro Devotion finds its confidence in practical negotiations—fare saved, repairs attempted, weight shared—and closes with “Fasten It Again,” whose voices outlast the beat.

albums.title: Gymnasium Voltage
albums.label: Red Clay Relay
albums.notes: On their loudest studio album, The Juniper Detention turn the recreation hall into a pressure chamber: cupboard-isolated amplifiers roar while mandolin chops and six-part harmonies retain the scrape of people playing together. Released by Red Clay Relay in 2015, Gymnasium Voltage finds yesterday’s dissenters signing the forms themselves. “Emergency Contact” and “Dress for the Weather” sprint through clipped, argumentative changes; “Planning Period” answers with an exhausted teacher’s near-spoken reckoning.
