At the center, “The Partition” lets organ, floor toms and splintering twelve-string overwhelm the room. The closing “Last Key” strips that authority back to six exposed voices—and the obligation to stay.

albums.title: Personal Best
albums.label: Split Level Records
albums.notes: Podium Static’s 2015 debut for Split Level Records makes modest means sound expansive: hammered dulcimer rings through borrowed-room ambience while rounded bass and gated snares sketch out a pop-sized horizon. Personal Best introduces Lena Voss’s conversational intimacy and the band’s enduring fascination with recognition, expectation and showing up anyway. “Borrowed Kit” lets bare strings establish the stakes before its buoyant beat arrives; “Runner-Up Smile” turns second place into the EP’s biggest, most conflicted refrain. The handclap rush of “Put Me In” briefly feels unstoppable, but “Our Own Record” offers the more revealing finish: three imperfect voices holding a chord that refuses to declare a winner.

albums.title: Borrowed Hours
albums.label: Small Current
albums.notes: Released on Small Current in 2016, Lumen Relay's debut EP turns the journey home after an argument into five closely connected electronic miniatures. Guitar-string friction, felted piano and household percussion remain audible inside Theo Sayer's granular chords and Felix Orr's rounded low end. Mara Venn's husky alto makes apology sound tentative, never triumphant. “Leave a Light” establishes their signature passage from near-mono confession to a broad instrumental refrain; “If You're Still Up” finds equal force in unanswered space. The title track gathers those textures into a luminous release before returning to the room itself, establishing a language of connection the Melbourne trio would keep testing.

albums.title: Rooms Facing Weather
albums.label: South Window Records
albums.notes: On their third release, Switchyard Orchard make returning home sound less like arrival than another unsettled arrangement. The Dunedin band trade communal room ambience for distinct planes of tremolo guitar, harmonium and brushed percussion, leaving air around Riddell’s dry-grained baritone. “Key Under the Meter” saves its full chorus for a late, earned opening; “The Loan Car” answers with muscular guitars and a stubborn backbeat. At the record’s uneasy centre, “Curtains in Daylight” sets a wandering fiddle against lilting chords that refuse to reassure. Even the bright hooks of “Someone Left the Light” carry doubt. The closing “One Beat Behind” reduces belonging to a voice, amplifier hum and an imperfectly timed answer.

albums.title: The Hours We Keep
albums.label: Turnout Recordings
albums.notes: On their third release, The Ochre Switch turn touring’s displaced hours into patient, tightly wound folk-rock. Repeating baritone-guitar lines hold the floor beneath suspended electric textures, organ and strikingly dry drums; Eli’s grain-edged warmth remains intact as Mara’s harmonies arrive slightly out of step. “Clocking Off” and “Your Side of Tuesday” give that restraint a muscular pulse, while “Are You Still There?” leaves a telephone conversation painfully open. Longer instrumental stretches make tiny chord changes matter. The brisk “Borrowed Ladder” briefly recalls their homemade beginnings before “Until the Kettle Clicks” carries the record toward daylight, its final bass note lingering after the drums stop.

albums.title: The Weight of Leaving
albums.label: Sundspor
albums.notes: On their first full-length, released by Sundspor in 2016, Svalevev make irregular metre feel like shared physical work. Thumb-led guitars and suspended upper figures remain close enough to hear fingers lift, but deeper bass, ceramic percussion and three-part refrains widen the room. “Carry It Together” gives seven beats an inviting swing; “Until the Ferry” finds equal weight in harmonium air and waiting. Ingrid Velde's dusky alto keeps departures practical: cups counted, belongings carried, roofs tended. The bowed strings gathering through “Names for the Crossing” and “What We Keep Dry” bring breadth without grandstanding. “Enough Hands” closes not with resolution, but with everyone breathing together.

albums.title: What the Harbour Holds
albums.label: Salt Ledger
albums.notes: On their eighth album, The Alder Parliament turn from crossings to upkeep: roofs, keys, linen and promises that still require attention. Close steel strings and audible piano mechanisms sit inside a dark, generous acoustic, while Vale’s woody baritone anchors harmonies that now gain force by arriving sparingly. The restless five-beat tread of “Five Steps to the Landing” opens into the long, breathing instrumental spaces of “The Work Between Tides.” A descending figure quietly binds the sequence, but the closing songs need progressively less scaffolding. On “Leave the Light as It Is,” the ensemble falls away until only Vale remains: older, steady, with no grand resolution required.

tracks.title: Leave the Light as It Is

albums.title: Duración oblicua
albums.label: Sello Ladera
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Sello Ladera, Valparaíso's Isóbara widen the handmade language of Cizalla without losing the sound of fingers meeting wood. The brisk “Hacer lugar” and “Otra vez la distancia” set rounded sub-bass beneath interlocking guitars, with vocal canons slipping between their accents. “Lo que tarda” suspends that momentum; “Lijar la mesa” brings it back through uneven, quietly insistent cycles. Throughout, affection is measured in repeated journeys and shared physical work. The massed voices and saturated oscillators of “Mientras sostenemos” make the record's largest gesture, answered by the single voice and unresolved nylon-string resonance of “Todavía aquí.”

albums.title: Basalt Receiver
albums.label: Sounding Line
albums.notes: Released by Sounding Line in 2016, Sólveig Kambdal’s debut EP finds an unusually tactile language for folktronica: steel strings scrape, cable knocks become meter, and submerged machinery keeps imperfect time. “Through the Hull” draws a fingerpicked song out of underwater ticking; the brisk “Not at Your Door” makes nervous hesitation almost propulsive. At the center, “I Let It Ring” strips away rhythmic camouflage for an undoubled confession. These five recordings establish the intimacy-against-distance contrast she would later expand, but their power lies in restraint. On “Before You Wake,” even the guitar loses its footing, leaving a breath where resolution should be.

albums.title: January Dogs
albums.label: Lantern Track
albums.notes: After the broad stereo spaces of Basalt Horses, January Dogs brings Pumice Choir almost uncomfortably close. Muted steel-strings, clipped bass and an old reed organ frame Mara Vale's grain-edged alto; family history emerges through shopping arrangements, disputed dates and the stubborn evidence of photographs. “Who Took the Picture” begins without cover, while the loping “Back Seat, January” gives way to the broken footing of “On the Back in Blue.” At the record's quiet centre, “Bathroom Light” finds devotion in work no camera recorded. Electric guitar returns as a wavering thread, not a release. “Keep This One” leaves the siblings suspended together, with only the organ motor following them into silence.

albums.title: Copper Metronome
albums.label: Small Measure Records
albums.notes: On his third release, Ansel Bellweather lets household rhythms turn argumentative. June Calder’s dry brushes, struck wood, and muted percussion catch against paper-prepared guitar, while his warm baritone sometimes trails the machinery it helped set running. “A Place for Everything” makes a missing beat feel like a small correction; the title track tightens that impulse into something more troubling. At the center, the percussion-free “The Basin” leaves cello and silence to carry the aftermath. Leaner than Mending Sunday, Copper Metronome finds its release not in a grand reconciliation but in “Leave It There,” a bare nylon-string performance willing to leave its last chord unanswered.

albums.title: Sidereal Cotton
albums.label: Blue Spindle Records
albums.notes: On his first full-length, Makhanda's Luvo Nqolase opens the room without losing the sound of fingers on strings. Opposite-channel guitars trade uneven accents, Anelisa Mbane's harmonies move between intimacy and distance, and Sive Dondolo's low percussion gives the music weight without a fixed backbeat. Sewing, cultivation and family negotiations meet the patient measurements of the sky. The six-entry round of “Six Before Sunrise” makes collective work exhilarating; “What You Said at the Table” leaves room for disagreement. After the crossing rhythms of “Carry the Water Level,” instrumental spaces widen toward “Until Each Name Is Called,” whose departing voices leave a suspended chord—and responsibilities still unfinished.

tracks.title: What You Said at the Table
A Field Is Not an Answer

albums.title: Petites cérémonies
albums.label: Disques Menue
albums.notes: Released by Disques Menue in 2016, Petites cérémonies introduces Les Escaliers de Poche through five small negotiations of shared space. Nylon-string guitar, upright piano, cello and clarinet leave room for radiator ticks, chair creaks and the soft knock of a pedal. Anaïs Venne’s close, lightly husked mezzo makes each request sound both practical and consequential. The returning clarinet figure in “La moitié des poires” establishes the EP’s conversational scale; “Sans faire de bruit” strips it back to sibling voices whose closeness cannot quite conceal disagreement. The brisk waltz “Les assiettes du dimanche” offers a flash of levity before “Tu peux laisser la lumière” closes on two separate breaths.

albums.title: Diesel Vigil
albums.label: Fallow Circuit
albums.notes: On their second full-length, The Copper Census let the night stretch around their songs. Recorded together in a large room, Diesel Vigil preserves amplifier hiss and the space between instruments, then fills that space with tape-delayed baritone guitar and gathering organ. Jonah Voss’s measured tenor follows loading crews, late drivers, and partners speaking past one another. “County Lights” waits almost two minutes for its drums; “Separate Receipts” brings the record back to two siblings and bare strings. From there, melodic bass steadily tightens its grip, driving toward the immense “Until the Yard Goes White.” This is their most patient record, and their least certain that staying means belonging.

albums.title: Antenna Orchard
albums.label: Cable Basket
albums.notes: On their 2016 Cable Basket debut album, kitenge/64 widen the handmade circuitry of Request Line without polishing away its seams. Mugo sets dry nylon-string guitar and woody thumb piano inside broad synthesizer harmonics, deep bass and crisply displaced drums. Nyambura Kibe’s grain-edged alto keeps these songs about misdirected dedications intimate, even as refrains become small gatherings. “Wrong Number, Stay” and “Next Door Radio” establish the momentum; the title track turns overlapping syllables into the record’s brightest lift. After the quietly destabilizing instrumental “Cable Basket,” “Whoever Hears This” finds resolution in shared repetition rather than a closing chord.

albums.title: Perigeo
albums.label: Cúpula Discos
albums.notes: Released by Cúpula Discos in 2016, Amalia Zorzán’s debut EP finds its scale in the distance between a plucked string and a held breath. Recorded over three evenings in an observatory’s former lecture room, these six songs keep nylon guitar, viola, cello and occasional brushed bombo close enough to hear their friction. “Más cerca” earns its late cello entrance; “Dejá la luz” and “La taza de mi madre” let six and three quietly overlap. The near-still “Lo que tarda” forms the emotional centre, before “Antes del último colectivo” briefly quickens the pulse. “Quedar a mano” closes on voice, viola and an unresolved interval—the intimate foundation of her later orchestral reach.

albums.title: Yoru no Sukima
albums.label: Komorebi Editions
albums.notes: Released by Komorebi Editions in 2016, Yoru no Sukima introduces kasane/84 through the small sounds left behind when a room empties: nylon-string resonance, sleeve friction, tape joins and a voice held close. Across five songs, Emi Kuroda’s tangible performances meet Sota Nishimura’s gently dislocated loops, with little bass or stereo spectacle to soften the encounter. “End Roll” lets an eighty-four-second cassette cycle surface beneath an exposed guitar figure; “Hanbun no Seki” finds its strength in almost-dry folk simplicity. The suspended center, “Iki no Nokori,” makes breathing itself harmonic material. By “Mada Koko ni,” electronics fall away, leaving the EP’s quiet act of companionship unmistakably human.

albums.title: Tin of Thunder
albums.label: Receipt Press
albums.notes: On their sixth release, Semaphore Custard make endurance sound intricate rather than monumental. Felted piano, woody guitar and harmonium leave room for brushed rhythms and rehearsal-tape choirs that flicker like remembered colleagues. Mara Venn’s reedy mezzo keeps the scale personal even as the harmonies take improbable turns. “The Renewal Notice” opens three successive doors inside one chorus; “Good Knee” answers with a brisk, furniture-rattling shuffle. The patient labour portraits at the record’s centre give way to the dry machinery of “Exact Change,” before “Leave the Light for Us” gathers separate voices into an unforced unison. Tin of Thunder extends the band’s handmade pop language without polishing away its age.

albums.title: Kisses by Telephone
albums.label: Acacia Wire Records
albums.notes: On his second album, Cassian Mothusi takes the intimacy of Someone Is Listening into a studio with sharper edges: dry snares, roaming bass lines and electric guitars that leave long afterimages. The acoustic pick noise remains close enough to touch, even as the arrangements widen. “Your Number by Heart” opens with an almost reckless brightness; “The Distance We Invent” lets that confidence unravel across an extended coda. Between them and the hushed “Receiver,” telephone intimacy starts to sound like a substitute for shared life. By the guitar-swamped “All the Windows Lit,” the trio’s harmonies are fighting to remain audible. “Morning Without Coordinates” finally loosens the record’s grip without resolving it.

albums.title: Doble identidad
albums.label: Sello Remache
albums.notes: On their second album, Monterrey quartet León de Alambre turn arena-sized hooks into disputes over names, loyalty and the right to speak for others. The production is dry and sharply divided: syncopated bass needles straight kicks, guitars answer across the speakers, and recognizable backing voices interrupt Mateo Sada’s grain-edged tenor. “Quién habla por mí” and “La otra cara” establish the combative pace; “Apellido prestado” plants a nylon-string descent that returns, electrified, in “La firma del padre.” Between the stalking “El dueño de la cuadra” and handclap-driven “Sin pedir permiso,” vulnerability keeps breaking through. “El mismo suelo” offers solidarity before the closer quietly pulls its harmonic foundation apart.

albums.title: Selvedge Weather
albums.label: Weft Register
albums.notes: On their first full-length, Manchester trio Twillphase widen Piecework’s close acoustic room without sanding away its splinters. Nylon-string figures rub against shuttle knocks, rounded analogue bass and keyboards that breathe like tired bellows; Ellis Rook’s warm, frayed low tenor holds the centre as other accounts gather around him. “Learning the Ends” and “Two Envelopes” find dance-floor momentum in apprenticeships and household arithmetic, while “Mrs Vale’s Account” lets testimony interrupt the machinery. The exposed duet “What We Kept” makes the eventual gathering on “Leave the Light Unfinished” feel earned. Memory here is neither monument nor consensus: it is work passed between people.

albums.title: Borrowed Voltage
albums.label: Platform Glass
albums.notes: On their 2017 Platform Glass debut, Relayweather turn Pocket Current’s exposed sampling seams into dance-floor architecture. A thumb against guitar wood becomes the kick in “Borrowed Voltage”; brushed strings and felted piano feed luminous, breathing synth beds. The central run crests with “I’ll Come Get You,” where a lift home carries the emotional weight of a declaration. “Your Blue Shirt” punctures that momentum with bare piano before “Temporary Address” introduces deeper bass and wider silences. Throughout, Elliot’s breath-frayed tenor keeps the scale personal. “Room for One More” brings the opening melody back among handclaps and overlapping voices, choosing an unresolved added ninth over easy closure.

albums.title: Ablation Studies
albums.label: Skare Editions
albums.notes: On his second album, Iver Ruskedal loosens the tightly chopped vocabulary of Moraine Teeth into long guitar performances and exposed stretches of weather. Steel strings scrape, bass notes linger, and outdoor recordings preserve the awkward intimacy of a microphone being carried. “Walking the Former Shore” finds a crooked, patient stride; “Each Day Less” turns seven beats into the record's strongest propulsion before dismantling its own percussion. Throughout, Ruskedal's close baritone connects glacial retreat to inherited silences and bodily change. The closing “Where We Measured From” leaves its melody unfinished, surrendering the remaining space to meltwater and barely vibrating strings.

albums.title: Saltlung
albums.label: Ferric Hymnal
albums.notes: Released by Ferric Hymnal in 2017, Saltlung turns Breakwater Atlas’s orchestral reach toward friction and bodily limits. Dry drums, clipped strings and painfully close metal percussion unsettle the spaciousness of Chromatic Rime, while Kerr’s dark contralto brings composed working lives into unusually sharp focus. “Wash at the Elbow” opens mid-stride; the title track makes exhaustion almost physically measurable. Two angular instrumentals interrupt the compact songs before sustained harmony cautiously returns. The five-member refrain of “We Can Keep This Open” earns its communal warmth without polishing away the strain, and “Leave Your Boots Here” closes with cello, voice and no rescuing crescendo.

albums.title: Cartilage Halo
albums.label: Mica Bloom
albums.notes: Released on Mica Bloom in 2017, Avelune's debut builds precarious chamber pop from prepared upright piano, woody strings and household percussion. Felt, paper and metal clips make every attack tangible; the clear mezzo remains close enough to catch a mouth opening before a line. “Good Teeth” and “An Extra Mouth” find brisk comedy in maintenance and obligation, while “Bathwater” and “Keep the Landing Light” slow into care's awkward, sleepless hours. The instrumental “Room Above the Room” briefly enlarges these domestic dimensions. “Leave Some” brings everything back to voice, piano and an interval that refuses to settle.

albums.title: Anatomia da Amendoeira
albums.label: Agulha Discos
albums.notes: On her first full-length for Agulha Discos, Inês Valdouro turns an almond plot into a family chronicle, expanding her debut’s modal miniatures into supple, through-composed chamber folk. Nylon-string guitar anchors a sextet whose violas argue, remember and quietly redirect the songs; bow grain and shared breaths remain audible throughout. The sunny gait of “Flor de Fevereiro” gradually unravels into the divided loyalties of “A Parte de Cada Um”. At the centre, “Inventário das Árvores” and “Carta de Lyon” stretch speech-like intimacy across quick instrumental crossings. “O Que Fica de Pé” closes without insistence, entrusting its once-sung melody to the strings.

albums.title: Peachbuffer
albums.label: Small Current
albums.notes: Released on Small Current in 2017, Peachbuffer introduces elayra.exe through pop hooks with the seams left showing. Steel-string attacks bounce like rubber, ukulele chords splinter into bright grains, and tiny mouth clicks keep the machinery companionable. “Two Straws” wastes no time announcing its melody; “Soft Launch” turns a falsetto refrain and tumbling sample riff into the EP’s giddiest exchange. At the center, “Without Ice” lets an untreated guitar expose the loneliness beneath the sugar. These five compact songs establish a defining instinct: make the chorus feel bigger by opening the melody, while keeping every fret squeak close enough to touch.

albums.title: Flannel
albums.label: Pale Current Records
albums.notes: On Flannel, Orin Pell widens the room without sacrificing the grain of his chamber folk. Double bass and brushed drums bring buoyancy to thumb-picked guitar and prepared upright piano, while viola, cello and bass clarinet keep their own patient counsel. Following Unhurried’s longer forms, these songs find movement in the practical choreography of care: a sleeve negotiated, a wrist tested, an apology felt before it is spoken. “Warm Water” opens with an easy lift; “Washers” lets metallic piano and low woodwind wander beyond language. The brisk, rueful “Quick Enough” supplies an unexpected jolt before “Leave It There” closes with guitar, one voice and no grand resolution.

albums.title: Passenger Heat
albums.label: Night Fare Recordings
albums.notes: On their 2017 debut for Night Fare Recordings, Bergen duo silt//signal make a late bus journey feel both communal and profoundly private. Steel-string thumb patterns, close-miked consonants and handheld street recordings occupy the foreground; electronics gather around their edges like residual warmth. “Request Stop” lets a pulse emerge from near-free time, while “Change in My Palm” and “Last Connection” find stumbling momentum without smoothing away the guitar’s friction. The harmonium-led “Someone Else’s Coat” offers a hushed interior before “Seat Fabric” returns to the road. These five songs establish the duo’s essential tension: a small, tangible performance trembling inside a much larger city.

albums.title: Stairwell Revue
albums.label: Folded Stage Records
albums.notes: On their second album, Parlor Cartography turn a residents' celebration into chamber pop with entrances, interruptions and consequences. Harpsichord sharpens the rhythmic machinery, celesta illuminates private corners, and a wider stereo image gives the quartet room to argue around Tomáš Vorel's articulate baritone. “Committee of Three” makes counterpoint sound like administrative warfare; “Minutes of the Celebration” stretches that comedy into a miniature operetta, punctured by the hushed “Behind the Coats.” Compared with Tenants Wearing Gold, the staging is more ambitious but the scale remains human. By “Leave the Landing Light,” communal triumph has become something gentler: an imperfect household choosing to remain hospitable.

tracks.title: The Landing / Bring Your Own Chair

albums.title: Overdrive Hearts
albums.label: Latch Audio
albums.notes: On their 2017 Latch Audio debut full-length, Melbourne's morrow// FM make hesitation move. Acoustic pick attacks survive festival-sized kicks, metallic percussion sparks around dry handclaps, and bass lines talk back to Eli Venn's vulnerable tenor. The opening climb peaks with “Median Strip,” but the close-room apologies of “Say It Properly” reveal what powers the spectacle. Guitar-tuning miniature “Between Stations” quietly rebuilds the dance floor before the final ascent. Where Soft Reset wore its laptop seams openly, Overdrive Hearts turns those handmade details into communal architecture—culminating in the title track's unprocessed, two-person final chorus.

tracks.title: What You Left on the Bench

albums.title: Sepal
albums.label: Rookery Editions
albums.notes: Tamsin Quillory’s debut EP makes mourning audible in the work of keeping things alive. A felt-muted upright sets the scale: pedal creaks, dry seed rattles and breaths remain exposed as finely cut electronics begin to gather around them. “Wash the Tools” establishes the descending figures and suspended harmonies that anchor these five songs; “Rootbound” opens their intimacy into a viola-framed chorus. Even at its fullest, Sepal leaves room for words and touch. Released by Rookery Editions in 2017, it establishes the handmade acoustic-electronic vocabulary Quillory would expand on Germination Index. The closing “What Will Take” finds a walking pulse without mistaking forward motion for resolution.

albums.title: Veselé závrtě
albums.label: Oblouk Editions
albums.notes: On their third album, Karstové Divadlo discover lift without losing their weight. Papery drums, handclaps and felt-muted dulcimer turn uneven metres into inviting walking rhythms, while trumpet and bass clarinet bring daylight into the ensemble’s chamber-scale post-rock. The easy melody of “Po sedmi domů” conceals its seven-beat footing; “Oběh drobných věcí” unspools that buoyancy into interlocking instrumental loops. At the centre, “Pod jazykem” strips everything back to cello and Tereza Vránová’s unvarnished alto. By the expansive closer “Ještě chvíli nesme,” brass has become breath rather than celebration, and the pulse carries on after language gives out.

albums.title: Domingo sin prodigios
albums.label: Discos Aguafuerte
albums.notes: On their second full-length, Las Falsas Magnolias leave the theatrical entrance empty. Electric piano, low synthesizer tones and lightly damped drums replace much of the previous album's ornate machinery; strings hold their ground one line at a time. Inés Valdés's dry, intimate mezzo brings failed wonders home to the people who paid for them. “Nadie espera nada” establishes the exposed scale, while “La comida se enfría” begins a devastating three-song stretch of household negotiations. The brisk resignation of “Que atienda otro” offers release without absolution. Finally, Valdés and Berón close “Con lo que queda” together, without an instrumental afterword.

albums.title: Every Gate Opens Twice
albums.label: Towpath Recordings
albums.notes: Alderwake’s final studio album moves with elbows out and windows open. Dry, interlocking guitars, lightly amplified fiddle and bright harmonium give these songs a spring that never conceals the weather in Vale’s baritone or the grain of the ensemble voices. “It’ll Hold Until Tuesday” turns makeshift repair into rhythmic comedy; “Behind the Goods Yard” finds freedom in a disputed shortcut. At the centre, “The Same Water, Differently” lets competing accounts run separately before finding a shared tune. Released by Towpath Recordings in 2018, Every Gate Opens Twice closes not with leave-taking but with “Leave the Long Key Here”: a practical instruction becoming a communal promise.

albums.title: Aseptic Bloom
albums.label: Papillary Records
albums.notes: Odile Marchand-Lowe’s debut EP makes the examination room feel disarmingly domestic: nylon strings, felted piano, and close-miked woodwinds share space with tape hiss and shifting chairs. Released by Papillary Records in 2018, Aseptic Bloom introduces her chamber-scaled art pop through songs about permission, exposure, and the embarrassment of accepting care. “Before You Touch” opens on a naked inhale; “Six Small Permissions” turns uneven breaths into a suspended vocal chord. The lilting “Tender to Pressure” offers the first glimpse of a more buoyant songwriter, while “Leave the Window” closes without harmonic reassurance. Its tenderness comes from attention, not consolation.

albums.title: Vowel Atlas
albums.label: Pärl Editions
albums.notes: Released by Pärl Editions in 2018, Liisi Orvek’s debut EP makes family correspondence audible in the spacing of a phrase rather than the telling of a story. Nylon strings, plucked viola and close-recorded woodwinds leave every intake of breath exposed in a small Tallinn rehearsal room. “Tere, jälle” finds its meter only after an unaccompanied greeting; “Ümbriku serv” lets flute and guitar exchange quick, unfinished thoughts. At the center, “Aa, ee” turns vowels into a quietly abrasive canon. The harmonium-supported “Sinu käekiri” supplies the emotional crest before “Veel üks rida” walks toward a final guitar harmonic, leaving the room—and its breathing—intact.

albums.title: Capillary Hymns
albums.label: Lichen Index
albums.notes: Myrglass’s debut makes a room feel as expansive as a valley: steel-string fingerpicking, harmonium air and unprocessed ice recordings share the foreground with breath and fingertip noise. Released on Lichen Index in 2018, Capillary Hymns establishes the Bergen trio’s grammar of drifting loops, suspended harmony and deliberately incomplete cadences. “Where Your Wrist Was” barely raises its voice before percussion arrives; “Contour Interval” finds a crooked walking rhythm inside repeated guitar passes. At the center, “Palm Room” strips proximity down to wood and diction. The closing “Separate Plucks” opens outward, then disassembles itself, leaving intimacy unresolved rather than diminished.

albums.title: Sepal
albums.label: Petiole Recordings
albums.notes: Released by Petiole Recordings in 2018, Sepal establishes Elspeth Rooke’s chamber pop at speaking distance. Recorded largely live in a borrowed Wellington rehearsal studio, its nylon strings, upright piano and woodwinds retain fingertip scrape and audible breath. Letters between her grandmother and a younger sister supply the everyday particulars; identifying details stay withheld. “The Weather There” waits until its final verse to admit a clarinet, while “Two Cups Short” finds unexpected lift in walking pizzicato cello. The exposed voice-and-flute miniature “Name Omitted” makes discretion audible. “Leave the Gate” offers the warmest melodic release before “Until Your Next” leaves the exchange gently, deliberately unfinished.

albums.title: Contour Bloom
albums.label: Marl Array
albums.notes: On Contour Bloom, Euan Tern lets the landscape breathe. The Bristol songwriter’s third release trades Spillway Psalms’ compressed impacts for open-tuned guitar, bowed viola and reed organ, with harmonies changing almost imperceptibly beneath his close, husky tenor. “Intake Path” and “White on the Wire” establish the patient scale; “Gate Teeth” briefly brings back the sampler’s bite before human hands loosen its machinery. Family memories rub against contested ground on “What My Aunt Kept,” while “Volunteer Willow” finds growth without easy consolation. The closing “Room for the Water” makes sympathetic strings feel communal: a place held open rather than claimed.

albums.title: Dimanche chez Lucie
albums.label: Éditions Coudrier
albums.notes: On her 2018 debut for Éditions Coudrier, Montréal’s Céleste Vaudrel makes a Sunday visit audible through its pauses, evasions and small courtesies. Recorded over two weekends in a borrowed rehearsal room, these five chamber-folk miniatures preserve chair creaks and bass-clarinet key clicks without borrowing recorded family voices. “Avant le café” begins almost alone; “Qui a commencé” gives an unclaimed argument to viola and clarinet. The gently crooked waltz of “La nappe à fleurs” and the dry wit of “Garde le reçu” establish her gift for letting conversational rhythm shape a composition. By the unresolved close of “On laissera la lumière,” affection means knowing where to stop.

albums.title: Tender Defiance
albums.label: Cairn Signal
albums.notes: On their third album, released by Cairn Signal in 2018, The Quarry Hours trade the procession-sized arrangements of Ochre Parade for the uncomfortable intimacy of a room where someone finally asks for help. Muted electric guitar, exposed upright piano and low viola leave Ewan Calder’s dry baritone little cover; Mara Teviot’s brief replies make the silences more consequential. “Casual Hours” puts insecure work against a stubborn backbeat, while “Turn You Over” measures caregiving in small, repeated actions. The distortion of “Stone Keeps Warm” feels earned rather than triumphant. Only “Room at the Table” opens into an extended communal refrain, offering company without pretending the trouble has passed.

albums.title: Tinsel Referendum
albums.label: Copper Kettle Recordings
albums.notes: On their sixth album, Ghent’s Municipal Swans trade some orchestral breadth for clipped drums, electric bass and electric-piano glints, without losing the grain of woodwind and bow. Tinsel Referendum makes public ceremony newly danceable—and newly awkward. “A Show of Hands” turns disputed applause into percussion, while “Your Name on the Ribbon” lets sibling counterpoint puncture the official version. At the center, “The Fundraiser Waltz” clears the room with exquisite tact. The closing “All Those in Favour” offers a communal refrain, then withdraws its support. Released by Copper Kettle Recordings in 2018, this is their sharpest, most rhythmically economical account of affection under civic pressure.

albums.title: Lydspor
albums.label: Stillhet Utgivelser
albums.notes: On her debut EP for Stillhet Utgivelser, Tromsø’s Eira Solhavn makes the quiet flat an audible collaborator: piano felt, shifting furniture and imperfect loop joins all stay in the frame. Lydspor begins with the nearly dry, two-note address of “Er du der” before edited pedal thumps give “Kjøkkenlys” a hesitant footing. At its center, “Litt mer lys” opens into a briefly luminous choir, its major harmony shadowed by a stubborn minor note. These are small songs about keeping someone company, not pristine ambient miniatures. By “Før du går,” the accompaniment is disappearing beneath an unfinished sentence—a modest introduction to Solhavn’s enduring balance of bodily closeness and expanding space.

albums.title: Reedbed Oscillations
albums.label: Spindle Index
albums.notes: On their 2018 Spindle Index release, sluice/09 pare back Latch Choir’s fuller refrains without losing the hands behind the machinery. Guitar strings decay into low synthesizer tones; fiddle harmonics hover where replies should be. The spacious opening pair makes the muted dance pulse of “Missed Connection” feel unusually bodily, before its rhythm gradually falls away. At the centre, “At Mum’s Table” finds extraordinary weight in an almost untreated voice and an ordinary family conversation. The closing songs recover movement, not certainty: “Until We Sound the Same” ends with instruments meeting on one note, then quietly slipping out of agreement.

albums.title: Gilt Etiquette
albums.label: Counterseal Records
albums.notes: Released by Counterseal Records in 2018, Ivara Sorel’s debut album enlarges the prepared-piano world of Cobalt Alias into an evening of strings, bass clarinet and answering brass. An unnamed attendant moves between reception rooms, measuring the distance between impeccable manners and genuine welcome. The hall blooms around the instruments while Sorel’s alto remains startlingly close. “Your Name on the List” makes social recognition a clipped, pizzicato negotiation; “In the Cloakroom” strips away the ceremony. By the expansive “A Place Beside You” and the forceful “Do Not Call Me Grateful,” borrowed roles give way to personal demands. “Leave the Ribbon Untied” closes with the grandeur of a small, private decision.

albums.title: Lateral Drift
albums.label: Cantilever Recordings
albums.notes: On their second full-length, Christchurch’s Borrowed Viaduct make togetherness sound difficult, necessary and unfinished. Dry drums, narrowly placed guitars and exposed bow scrape pull apart the communal warmth of Everybody Upstairs, letting disagreements remain audible. “The Version You Keep” sidesteps its promised chorus for a bass-led detour; “Spare Key” turns brisk strumming into unstable footing. The hushed exchange of “If Thursday Works” sits directly against the splintered electric attack of “Load-Bearing.” Throughout, Mara Bell’s grainy alto holds the room without settling the argument. “Leave a Light Where It Was” finally opens into a generous refrain, then removes the drums before anyone can mistake it for resolution.

tracks.title: Leave a Light Where It Was

albums.title: Germination Instructions
albums.label: Propagation Records
albums.notes: Adjoa Kessiri’s debut EP makes wanting sound like something learned by hand. Nylon-string figures catch against workbench taps; a borrowed viola holds notes that the harmonies refuse to settle. Across five songs, her intimate, grain-edged mezzo becomes a small, fallible community, with answering parts arriving from different corners of the room. “Leave a Little Space” introduces that circular conversation, while “Good Light” turns an overflowing guitar pattern into the record’s most immediate hook. Released by Propagation Records in 2018, Germination Instructions establishes the exposed, domestic scale of Kessiri’s botanical vocabulary: care is an action, proximity is a negotiation, and growth offers no guarantee of belonging.

albums.title: Terreno Baldio
albums.label: Dobradiça Edições
albums.notes: On Terreno Baldio, Tomás Nespereira lets the winter silence around a stranded fairground family become part of the arrangement. His steel-string guitar remains close enough to catch the fingernails, but bassoon, divided violas and a low harmonium breathe across a newly spacious room. Following Contrapesos, the writing turns from coordinated labour toward rent, school admissions and work borrowed from strangers. “Morada Provisória” gives these negotiations a walking pulse; “O Peso do Inverno” and “Enquanto a Roda Não Anda” build orchestral crests that offer no easy release. By “Ficamos Até Amanhã,” almost everything has fallen away except a voice, a guitar and the time needed to finish speaking.

albums.title: False Start
albums.label: Split Level Records
albums.notes: On their debut full-length for Split Level Records, Melbourne trio Podium Static turn struck wood and wire into an arena-sized nervous system. Resampled dulcimer flashes through glassy synths, enormous gated snares and bass that seems to lift the floor without swallowing the room. The countdown of “On Your Marks” opens into the breathless promise of “Within Reach,” but recognition rarely arrives without a flinch: “One Bar Late” deliberately wrong-foots its own payoff. At the centre, “Your Side of the Car” strips ambition back to parental silence. The communal roar of “Everybody Gets a Name” earns its scale before “Walk Home” leaves one wooden note hanging.

albums.title: Trophywater
albums.label: Sump Audio
albums.notes: On Trophywater, Bristol’s kitevault scales the handmade intricacy of Splitlane into electropop built for larger rooms. Hammered dulcimer strikes become rhythmic hooks; guitar harmonics flicker beneath rounded subs and choirs that buckle against the kick. “Personal Best” makes the expansion startling, moving from mouth-close confession to the record’s most forceful release. Yet achievement rarely brings comfort: the uneasy major chords of “Good for You” leave congratulations hanging unanswered. Through the final ascent of “Lane Lights,” Ellis Mercer’s grain-edged tenor remains within touching distance. “Pack Down” finally refuses the drop, finding something like relief in the ordinary work of leaving.

albums.title: La Part des objets
albums.label: Petite Mesure
albums.notes: Sur ce premier EP paru chez Petite Mesure en 2019, Éloïse Carreau fait de cinq objets hérités les témoins imparfaits d’une histoire familiale. La guitare, enregistrée au plus près dans son appartement montréalais, laisse entendre les ongles et les déplacements de la main; alto et clarinette répondent sans encombrer le silence. « De la main de qui » installe cette attention aux traces, tandis que « Hors cadre » entrouvre une fenêtre lumineuse avec sa voix doublée et sa caisse claire brossée. Entre valse décentrée et confidence presque parlée, Carreau pose déjà les fondations de son écriture : une émotion portée par les détails, jamais par l’emphase. « La Tasse recollée » laisse le dernier mot au piano, sans résoudre l’accord.

albums.title: What We Keep
albums.label: Small Current
albums.notes: On their 2019 Small Current debut album, Melbourne’s Lumen Relay turn the private exchanges of Borrowed Hours into music with room for other people. Felt piano, fingerpicked guitar and audible breaths become broad electronic structures, anchored by clipped drums and rounded sub-bass. “Here Again” finds an early rush without pushing Mara Venn’s husky alto away from the listener; “Objects in the Hall” then removes the beat and exposes the unfinished conversation beneath it. The title track rebuilds through syncopation, while “Carry It With Me” makes reconciliation sound collective. Even at its most expansive, What We Keep measures repair in actions rather than declarations.

tracks.title: Stay Until
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
You turn your cup against the grain
Your thumb keeps finding where it split
I hear you say you're sorry twice
I haven't found an answer yet
The fridge clicks off; we let it sit

[Pre-Chorus]
You needn't make another speech
Or put your keys beyond your reach
There's room beside what you have said
For something we haven't tried yet

[Chorus]
Stay until the kettle cools
Till there's nothing left to prove
Let the next small thing be ours
Move your chair; I'll make you room
Stay until, stay until
We know what staying asks us to do

[Interlude]

[Verse]
I called your sister back today
And let her finish for a change
She asked if you were coming round
I said I couldn't speak for you
Then set another saucer down

[Chorus]
Stay until the kettle cools
Till there's nothing left to prove
Let the next small thing be ours
Move your chair; I'll make you room
Stay until, stay until
We know what staying asks us to do

[Interlude]

[Bridge]
I used to leave the washing up
For you to find when you came in
You used to sleep with one shoe on
As if departure might begin
I'll take the plates; you dry the cups
We don't have to call that fixed

[Chorus]
Stay until the kettle cools
Till there's nothing left to prove
Let the next small thing be ours
Move your chair; I'll make you room
Stay until, stay until
We know what staying asks us to do

[Outro]
Move your chair; we'll make you room
Stay until, stay until
Pass the cups from hand to hand
We'll make room; we'll make room

tracks.title: Leave the Light As It Is

albums.title: Velvet Intercom
albums.label: Falter Editions
albums.notes: On his second album, Vienna’s Oskar Bellwether turns apartment-house acoustics into bright, rhythmically alert chamber pop. Electric bass and brushed drums give his nylon-string guitar and upright piano firmer footing, while harpsichord, argumentative woodwinds and layered harmonies complicate every assurance. An ascending three-note figure first heard in “Press Twice” travels between rooms; “Your Laugh Through the Plaster” answers its nervous economy with a wonderfully expansive chorus. The uncomfortable intimacy of “What I Owe You” anchors the quieter center before “Everybody Knows the Host” restores the social bustle. Released by Falter Editions in 2019, Velvet Intercom makes being overheard sound easier—and less satisfying—than being understood.

tracks.title: The Long Way to the Door

albums.title: Le sucre craque
albums.label: Disques Menue
albums.notes: On their first full-length, released by Disques Menue in 2019, Les Escaliers de Poche give their apartment-sized chamber pop a brighter, more brittle mechanism. Harpsichord, interwoven clarinets and mobile electric bass animate songs in which hospitality quietly becomes work. The clipped refrains of “Mets-toi à l’aise” and “Il manque une tasse” yield to the generous sway of “Deux cuillères,” before caregiving exposes the ledger beneath the tablecloth. Anaïs Venne’s intimate mezzo keeps every negotiation close. The title track supplies a rare rhythmic confrontation; “Je laisse la lumière” closes with a kindness suspended over an unanswered piano chord.

albums.title: Mulch Dance
albums.label: Furrow Editions
albums.notes: On their second full-length, Neem Circuit turn the patient expansions of Wage for the Rain into compact, bodily arguments. Mulch Dance opens with the wrong-footed snare of “After Six,” then makes elastic bass, swung breaks and overloaded gardening-tool microphones feel inseparable from fingerpicked steel strings. Kavya Rao’s dry alto keeps English and Kannada verses conversational even as the edits bite. “Four Months, Then” suspends the momentum for uninterrupted worker testimony; “Keep a Chair” finds equal force in almost bare wood and breath. The long, scuffed crescendo of “An Evening Owed” earns every layer before “Leave the Cup” brings the record home, its dance still faintly audible through headphones.

albums.title: Oathless
albums.label: Witness Room
albums.notes: After Corrections Desk restored the ensemble's room sound, Oathless pares that room down to breath, gut strings and low piano. Released on Witness Room in 2019, it makes restraint an ethical choice: these songs will not turn suffering into a public explanation. “Leave the Landing Light” briefly recalls Zorvelli’s crooked waltzes, but withholds the rhyme that might make its scene feel settled. The conflicting doubles of “Not Like That” disturb an otherwise almost entirely acoustic surface; “Closed Hearing” gathers the record’s fiercest bowed-string tension. From there, accompaniment and certainty recede together, until the title track stops just short of the cadence a listener might mistake for an answer.

albums.title: Testimony Engine
albums.label: Parallax Works
albums.notes: On their second album, Aperture Republic pull testimony out of Domewake's reverberant distance and place it squarely in the room. Released by Parallax Works in 2019, Testimony Engine couples clipped bass and gated drums with bowed-string ostinatos, abrasive guitar edges and Naledi Maseko's warm, grainy alto. “Enter the Record” establishes its urgent machinery; “The Recreation Center” slows down enough to hear what a closure actually removes. The restless middle peaks with “No Further Action,” before the percussionless “Before Anyone Answers” clears a path to “We Can Still Gather.” Its cumulative finale locates hope in continued attendance—and leaves the last word to one exposed cello note.

albums.title: Unsent Receipts
albums.label: Latchwork Recordings
albums.notes: On Unsent Receipts, Kito Mwangala withdraws the bass weight of Velcro Devotion and leaves the evidence on the table: a fare paid twice, a washed uniform, a message nobody sends. Stretched thumb-piano tails hang behind dry guitar, while percussion stops just short of offering reassurance. The exposed opening of “Carbon Copy” makes every breath consequential; “Before You Finish” lets a distant answer interrupt the question itself. Only “Leave the Shutter Open” sustains a communal pulse. Released by Latchwork Recordings in 2019, this is Mwangala’s most searching record yet, closing with the unfinished breath of “The Screw You Left.”

tracks.title: Keep the Change, Bring the Lid

albums.title: Pawl Choir
albums.label: Small Hours Press
albums.notes: Released by Small Hours Press in 2019, spoke/27’s debut makes a working bicycle sound like a chamber ensemble heard at arm’s length. Prepared acoustic guitar, pitched pawl clicks and brake-spring offbeats support Nao Mibu’s intimate Japanese alto, with room noises left intact. “Chain Grease” takes half its length to find a pulse; “Apron on the Handlebars” turns that tentative motion into an easy, conversational hook. Between them, the duo finds rhythmic detail without crowding the people in the songs. The instrumental “Coasting” opens a pocket of suspended breath before the arrangements shed their mechanisms, ending with the unprocessed tenderness of “Someone Still Sweeping.”

albums.title: Calendula Hours
albums.label: Cichy Pokój
albums.notes: Released by Cichy Pokój in 2019, Tomasz Zawrel’s debut EP locates recovery in washed cups, garden work and the return of appetite. Nylon-string guitar and viola da gamba share a close, papery room sound; his low baritone lets sentences determine their own length. “Calendula Hours” walks in gently uneven triple time, while “An Appetite” finds a brighter pulse without mistaking energy for resolution. The exposed gratitude of “You Needn't Have” leads into “Steadily, Again,” whose staggered vocal entrances turn a private instruction into company. These five songs establish the intimate ensemble language that Breathing Lessons would later expand.

albums.title: Seating Arrangements
albums.label: Sideboard Recordings
albums.notes: On Seating Arrangements, The Lacquer Picnic loosen their collars without losing their ear for domestic friction. Electric piano glints between nylon-string figures, while shakers and rim-clicks make the chamber arrangements unusually supple. Following the exposed intimacies of An Unclaimed Teaspoon, these songs accommodate stepfamilies, spare keys and friendships that outlast invitations. “Your Side of the Table” makes conversational counterpoint sound effortless; the percussion-free “A Room We Could Keep” finds tenderness in an unfinished negotiation. Guest cellos deepen the second half, cresting in “Everyone Can Stay” before “Leave the Cups” brings the ensemble back into one warm, audible room.

albums.title: Instructions for Returning
albums.label: Mellomrom Records
albums.notes: On their third release, Svalevev make returning sound less like retracing a path than learning to hear it again. Thumb-led guitars remain close enough to catch every scrape, but clipped breaths, unstable loops and low synthesizer tones rearrange the ground beneath them. “The Missing Step” gradually shortens its stride; “Water Under the Floor” gives the trio’s electronic experiments their deepest weight. At the centre, “What We Left Standing” and “Kitchen Window” recover the vulnerability of uninterrupted performance. Released by Mellomrom Records in 2020, Instructions for Returning turns the departures of The Weight of Leaving toward altered shorelines, inhabited rooms and the patient work of staying.

tracks.title: The Missing Step
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
The lower gate still lifts to the right.
I catch its weight against my knee.
The wire has grown into the birch;
I turn where someone cut it free.
My thumb comes black from the iron latch.
I wipe it where the cloth is patched.

[Chorus]
I know the turn, I know the stone.
I lift my foot for a step that's gone.
Leave me room to set it down.
The path goes on. The house is gone.

[Verse]
The currant stems have split the bed.
One tap stands crooked in the clay.
I reach the place we kept the salt;
there's rain enough to wash it away.
Below, a pump runs through the night.
They've raised the road above the tide.

[Chorus]
I know the turn, I know the stone.
I lift my foot for a step that's gone.
Leave me room to set it down.
The path goes on. The house is gone.

[Interlude]

[Bridge]
I'll clear the leaves beneath the grate.
The water needs a little room.
You hold the sack. I'll lift the plate.
We'll leave before the ferry's due.

[Outro]

albums.title: Peripheral Sunshine
albums.label: Small Current
albums.notes: On Peripheral Sunshine, elayra.exe lets the room into the circuitry. Steel-string fragments and thumb-piano notes expand around trolley-wheel rattles, ventilation hum and the soft reflections of public spaces. Released by Small Current in 2020, the album trades Peachbuffer’s compact, conspicuous edits for warmer bass, patient suspensions and choruses that open like a view through glass. “Plastic Cup Sweat” supplies the brightest hook; “One Seat Between” makes interruption feel equally consequential. By “Past the Last Gate,” percussion has nearly disappeared, leaving an acoustic figure to outlast the voice. These are songs about waiting with your habits still arranged for someone else.

albums.title: Milímetros por siglo
albums.label: Sello Ladera
albums.notes: On their third release, Isóbara bring geological time into the kitchen: a kettle’s cutoff, a dance count and fragments of family messages become parts of the rhythm section. The direct seven-beat melody of “La casa cede” opens an increasingly percussive first stretch before “Lo que sostiene” pares everything back to nylon-string harmonics and Amalia Véliz’s intimate mezzo. The second half loosens the relationship between hands and programmed clicks, preserving the small negotiations of ensemble playing. Released by Sello Ladera in 2020, Milímetros por siglo finds its emotional summit in the generous refrain of “Todavía cabe,” then settles into the low-register farewell of “Hasta que enfríe.”

albums.title: Elastic Mercy
albums.label: Night Fare Recordings
albums.notes: On their first full-length, Bergen duo silt//signal turn the spare transit sketches of Passenger Heat into music with weight and give. Steel-string attacks snap into crooked ostinatos; rounded sub-bass presses against dry palms and knuckles. Domestic negotiation supplies the stakes: exchanged shifts, an apology left unfinished, room made in a crowded bed. “Swap the Late” and “Soft Catch” establish the fractured stride, while the unedited singing on “Say It Without Then” makes its tenderness explicit. After the miniature acoustic clearing of “Cupboard Light,” the arrangements open outward, culminating in “Your Version,” where the machinery recedes and two imperfectly aligned voices remain.

albums.title: Elastic Islands
albums.label: Sounding Line
albums.notes: On her 2020 Sounding Line debut album, Tórshavn's Sólveig Kambdal turns the submerged textures of Basalt Receiver into a nimble pop language. Guitar fragments catch against rubbery bass, hydrophone clicks lag deliciously behind the beat, and her close, dark mezzo keeps every bright arrangement tethered to a human breath. The title track offers the broadest release; “Sticking Gate” makes an awkward meter feel like everyday movement, while “One Stone Over” turns a boundary dispute into understated exhilaration. The closing stretch gradually withdraws the electronics, until “Still Water Moving” returns an earlier melody to untreated underwater rumble: escape remains possible, but never complete.

albums.title: Sizigia
albums.label: Cúpula Discos
albums.notes: On Sizigia, Amalia Zorzán expands the close-grained ensemble of Perigeo without losing the scrape of a nail against nylon. Guitar and voice remain dry and near; chamber responses carry the observatory lecture room's audible depth. “A la salida” finds lift in chacarera's shifting accents, while bass clarinet gives “La luz de la cocina” its tender weight. Harp opens “El mismo meridiano” toward the first long orchestral ascent. Throughout, celestial alignment becomes a language for missed shifts, caregiving and negotiated time together. The title track gathers the fullest ensemble before “Te dejo la luz” reduces that reach to an intimate exchange between mezzo-soprano and cello.

albums.title: Hikari no Aida
albums.label: Komorebi Editions
albums.notes: On their first full-length, Kyoto duo kasane/84 let daylight into the handmade rooms of Yoru no Sukima. Nylon-string guitar retains its nail clicks and cloth rustle, but rounded electronic pulses, bass clarinet and bowed strings give the songs a wider horizon. “Mado no Mukou” and “Hanbun no Kotoba” find quietly memorable refrains inside loops that never quite meet their starting points. The nearly motionless “Shiroi Isu” makes the surrounding movement feel newly tender. By “Kasanaru Hibi,” breath chords and overlapping choruses become a gathering rather than a veil. Released by Komorebi Editions in 2020, Hikari no Aida preserves the duo’s intimacy while making room for others.

albums.title: Si sale seis
albums.label: Sello Aljibe
albums.notes: On her 2020 debut for Sello Aljibe, Buenos Aires songwriter Malena Urdavia turns private superstitions into intimate chamber pop. Nylon strings scrape, bass clarinet exhales, and clipped Spanish phrases establish rhythms before the brushes arrive. The counted opening of “¿Y si no?” introduces a record where every small gesture seems to influence an unseen outcome. “No lo nombres” knots domestic instructions into restless counterpoint, while “La parte que te toca” lets suspended harmony expose the cost of bargaining with someone you love. After the crooked bounce of “Tres veces madera,” “Hasta que salga” withdraws instrument by instrument, leaving disagreement tenderly unresolved.

tracks.title: La llave del lado de adentro

albums.title: Compás ausente
albums.label: Hebra Discos
albums.notes: Released by Hebra Discos in 2020, Lucía Bermejal’s five-song debut makes chamber scale feel close enough to touch. Charango plectrums snag, bows change direction, and silence carries the hesitation of addressing a former teacher. “Antes de decirle” lets an entire verse pass before viola enters; “El dedo señalado” finds tension in bombo strokes answered by cello pizzicato. The exposed “Al margen” turns a handwritten annotation into an unsettled recollection. Recorded with close microphones in a borrowed rehearsal room, Compás ausente establishes Bermejal’s orchestral folk language without gloss. Its closing title track gathers a quartet around repetition, then withholds the percussion that might have settled everything.

albums.title: Never Whistle Here
albums.label: Šiv Records
albums.notes: Vitrajune’s 2020 Šiv Records debut turns backstage rules into intimate acts of care. Felt-piano hammers, chair taps and a wheezing organ sit within touching distance, while bass clarinet and string trio negotiate crooked waltzes and sharply interrupted phrases. Her close-miked mezzo makes each instruction sound personally entrusted; granular vocal traces suggest people working just beyond the scenery. “The Spare Pair of Hands” breaks the miniature scale with stacked voices and jubilant brass. After the exposed hush of “Pencil Dust,” “Carry the Room Outside” brings everyone into an exuberant, beautifully fallible procession. These compact theatrical songs establish the tactile vocabulary that Hands Without Heirs would later give more space.

albums.title: A Cup Left Cooling
albums.label: Latchlight Records
albums.notes: Nell Harrowby’s debut measures a household day in kettle clicks, prescription slips and unfinished conversations. Recorded largely live in a timber-lined room, these chamber-folk songs let fingerpicked guitar, dry viola and bass clarinet answer one another without obscuring the grain of her alto. “Before the Kettle” opens alone; “Thirty Days” turns upright-piano repetitions into the uneasy arithmetic of a prescription. The brushed walking pulse of “Your Turn to Buy Milk” makes room for irritation and wit alongside tenderness. Released by Latchlight Records in 2021, A Cup Left Cooling establishes Harrowby’s intimate ensemble language, then gradually dismantles it, leaving “Landing Light” suspended between guitar harmonics and an unfinished night.

albums.title: The Chair Beside the Bed
albums.label: Palier Records
albums.notes: On her 2021 Palier Records debut, Montreal songwriter Sabine Desrochers makes the kitchen itself part of the arrangement: refrigerator hum under nylon strings, a thumb catching a bass note, silence held until a sentence finishes. These five chamber-folk songs study care without making a virtue of it. “With Food” finds a tentative routine in alternating bass, while “Don’t Thank Me Yet” lets a grainy bass clarinet answer back rather than console. The brisker “The Good Chair” preserves the jokes and friction of shared rooms. Before the wider ensemble writing of Rooms Still Listening, this is Desrochers learning how much two or three voices can leave unsaid.

albums.title: Public Tenderness
albums.label: Soft Circuit Records
albums.notes: On their third release, Relayweather make visibility sound less like connection than a demanding rhythm. Public Tenderness tightens husky, close-miked vocals against clipped nylon samples, stern bass figures and choruses that arrive with barely a breath to spare. “Green Dot” turns availability into dance-floor tension; “In Front of Everyone” withholds the release its build appears to promise. At the centre, the untreated piano of “Milk in the Fridge” exposes what the machinery cannot disguise. Released through Soft Circuit Records in 2021, this is a sharper, less reassuring successor to Borrowed Voltage, finding its eventual warmth in human hands and the spacious closing admission of “Leave the Light Where It Is.”

tracks.title: Leave the Light Where It Is

albums.title: Capillary Ballet
albums.label: Papillary Records
albums.notes: On her first full-length, Montreal’s Odile Marchand-Lowe enlarges the intimate vocabulary of Aseptic Bloom into chamber music with a pulse. Released by Papillary Records in 2021, Capillary Ballet sets close, conversational singing against bass clarinet, divided strings, and modular patterns that turn uneven meters into bodily habits. “Permission to Turn” opens the room one piano note at a time; “Your Weight, Distributed” introduces a firmer electronic undertow. The increasingly intricate arrangements make caregiving audible as repetition, negotiation, and fatigue. After the exposed guitar of “No Good Arm,” “Leave the Landing Light” gathers the ensemble into a resolution its wavering oscillator quietly complicates.

tracks.title: The Long Way to Your Room

albums.title: Juniper Syntax
albums.label: Pärl Editions
albums.notes: Released by Pärl Editions in 2021, Juniper Syntax enlarges Vowel Atlas’s intimate handwriting without losing the grain of guitar strings or the breath before a word. A fourteen-player ensemble, recorded in sections around largely untouched vocal and guitar takes, keeps woodwinds forward and strings in a short, luminous distance. “Kadaka keel” finds lift in five beats; “Kolm sammu, viis tagasi” turns irregular measures into an almost-dance. The woodwind hinge “Vahemärk” opens onto colder, less reliable family memories before “Üle lahe” supplies the great orchestral release. By “Veel üks vokaal,” breadth has become space: alto flute and voice leave the final thought unresolved.

albums.title: Moraine Syntax
albums.label: Lichen Index
albums.notes: On their second album, Myrglass bring the cutting room into sharper focus: gated steel-string figures, ice recordings sliced into percussion, and a dry tenor placed close enough to hear each withheld breath. Moraine Syntax turns measurement and memory into rhythmic problems, finding danceable momentum in displaced accents and uneven phrases. “What the Water Kept” anchors its clearest refrain to a five-beat figure, while “Without a Scale” suspends the machinery almost entirely. The forceful “No Fixed Point” makes the final harmonium-led retreat of “Your Hand, Unmeasured” feel earned. Released by Lichen Index in 2021, this is a more sharply articulated, emotionally exposed successor to Capillary Hymns.

albums.title: Kinpost
albums.label: Petiole Recordings
albums.notes: On her first full-length, Wellington’s Elspeth Rooke opens the windows of Sepal’s close chamber folk without losing its tactile detail. Brushed snare and rounded electric bass give family correspondence a walking pulse; clarinets, flute and cello make disagreement audible inside otherwise welcoming harmonies. “Two Versions of the Orchard” turns competing memories into nimble counterpoint, while “Permission” nearly empties the room around a confidence that cannot safely be repeated. The gently syncopated “Keep the Bowl” begins the return toward company. By the full-ensemble “Under Both Names,” warmth has become a way of holding contradictory testimony, not settling it.

albums.title: Velvet Metabolism
albums.label: Mica Bloom
albums.notes: On her second album, Avelune turns the handmade language of Cartilage Halo into elastic electronic pop without losing the grain of the room. Prepared-piano fragments bounce against rounded bass and percussion fashioned from cupboards, scissors and running water; sampled vowels retain the breaths that made them. “Your Cup, My Hands” makes unequal labor unexpectedly singable, while “Soft Work” lets affection and resentment share a slow pulse. The accumulating requests of “Could You Just” push that tension toward overload. Released by Mica Bloom in 2021, Velvet Metabolism closes with “Enough for Everyone,” where imperfectly aligned voices make cooperation sound possible, not automatic.

albums.title: Altitude de Agosto
albums.label: Semente Oblíqua
albums.notes: On her third release, Inês Valdouro lets silence enter the sextet. Nylon-string guitar, bow grain and sharply articulated Portuguese sit in a dry room, with reed organ supplying breath rather than grandeur. The widely spaced opening of “A Sombra Não Dá Salário” makes each bass note feel earned; “À Jeira” briefly turns seasonal work into an uneven dance. At the centre, “Palavras de Regadio” pares agricultural memory down to voice and cello harmonics. These first-person songs transform conversations about heat, wages and vanishing vocabulary without borrowing documentary authority. Pulse returns cautiously, until “O Nome que Falta” leaves a final viola interval hanging beyond the last verse.

albums.title: Porcelaine rouge
albums.label: Éditions Coudrier
albums.notes: On her 2021 Éditions Coudrier debut album, Céleste Vaudrel turns family etiquette into exacting chamber folk. Where Dimanche chez Lucie left stories unfinished, Porcelaine rouge makes the interruption itself audible: dry guitar strokes, isolated piano chords and bass-clarinet patterns meet across sharply cut silences. The brisk “Après toi” gives courtesy a nervous momentum; “Ce n’est rien” worries reassurance into something less innocent. At the center, the nearly naked “Ai-je le droit” questions the telling itself. Strings gradually lengthen the later songs’ horizons, until the title track gathers the fullest ensemble—and relinquishes it for a breath and a sentence no arrangement can resolve.

albums.title: Sundmerki
albums.label: Eyrafold
albums.notes: Saltbréf’s debut, released on Eyrafold in 2021, makes orchestral folk from small acts of attention: a towel left ready, a delayed shift, a message sent across town. Nylon-string guitar, upright bass and harmonium anchor performances whose chair creaks and horn breaths remain audible. On “Sundkort,” viola completes what the voice leaves unsaid; “Þegar flóðið snýr” earns the record’s first sustained ensemble swell through patient bow pressure and brass. Rather than building toward a grand finale, Sundmerki slows into the night. “Handan rúðunnar” leaves voice and cello at the window, a distant brass chord dissolving into outdoor air.

albums.title: Almost Awake
albums.label: Nightjar Circuit
albums.notes: On Almost Awake, morrow// FM let the spaces between destinations become the subject. Completed in separate home studios after prolonged touring, their second album loosens the grid around upright piano, brushed strings and percussion assembled from everyday rooms. Eli Venn’s intimate tenor stays exposed even as Mara Keane stretches his doubles into suspended electronic weather. “Pedal Down” opens with barely a pulse; “Nothing Happens Yet” turns an anticipated drop into a naked admission. The warmth returns incrementally, reaching its brightest chorus on “Somewhere We Can Stay,” before “Leave the Light” closes on breath rather than certainty. It’s their least resolved record, and their most revealing.

albums.title: Afterimage Studies
albums.label: Stillhet Utgivelser
albums.notes: On her first full-length for Stillhet Utgivelser, Tromsø’s Eira Solhavn enlarges the handmade intimacy of Lydspor without polishing away its friction. Felt-piano mechanisms, breath and domestic noise remain audible inside granular vocal clouds, viola harmonics and low electronic pressure. “Bus Stop, 15:40” offers the clearest refrain, its answering piano figure giving an interrupted conversation somewhere to settle. The displaced percussion of “Leave the Line Open” briefly disturbs that equilibrium before “Ved stolen” brings the room close again. Across ten songs, an ordinary sunless day expands and contracts in emotional scale, ending with ensemble warmth stripped back to one plainly spoken-in-song assurance.

albums.title: Germination Index
albums.label: Rookery Editions
albums.notes: On her first full-length for Rookery Editions, Melbourne’s Tamsin Quillory turns Sepal’s solitary acts of tending into music built for collective breath. Felt-muted piano, rattling seed capsules and scraped strings become rhythmic machinery, anchored by rounded sub-bass and sharply gated drums. The spring-loaded “Room for Roots” makes that enlargement immediately tangible; “Unequal Light” folds irregular phrases into an unexpectedly adhesive refrain. At the centre, “Wash the Tools” pares everything back to the physical particulars of loss. From there, the record grows outward toward the sweeping “Another Season,” without mistaking momentum for recovery. Its final instruction—“Leave Some Water”—keeps sounding after the voices withdraw.

albums.title: Grafting Season
albums.label: Propagation Records
albums.notes: On her first full-length, Accra’s Adjoa Kessiri lets the intimate constructions of Germination Instructions grow complicated roots. Nylon-string patterns meet deep synthesized bass, while viola, cello and bass clarinet turn private admissions into crowded negotiations. Her independently sung vocal layers retain their breaths and friction: the buoyant “Room for Two” makes togetherness sound irresistible; “Your Mouth, My Answer” reveals its price. At the center, “What I Stopped Saying” almost empties the room. The ensemble returns by degrees, reaching the spacious, unsettled generosity of “Enough Light” before “Not Your Rootstock” closes with a refusal that needs no raised voice.

albums.title: Treino de Terça
albums.label: Bancada Discos
albums.notes: Released by Bancada Discos in 2021, Clube dos Cometas’ debut EP makes Tuesday training feel like a small weekly opening in ordinary life. Dry guitar, audible bow changes and brushed snare keep the borrowed rehearsal room within reach; pizzicato strings and clarinet exchange glances across a narrow, central rhythm section. “A Camisola Emprestada” sets off at a jog, while “Lugar no Banco” finds the band’s melodic confidence without making its attraction any less bashful. Tomás Seabra’s reedy tenor lets hesitation shape the phrasing. After the halting conversation of “Vais Direto para Casa?”, “Até Terça” pares everything back to bass and two imperfectly aligned voices: an invitation, not a declaration.

albums.title: Touchmove
albums.label: Klaaspind
albums.notes: Käigukuma’s debut makes discipline danceable: dry chamber strings click against clipped kicks while granular synths turn their overtones into airborne glitter. Released on Klaaspind, Touchmove introduces Liise Vaher’s silvery soprano as both a measuring instrument and a vulnerable presence, its carefully placed consonants giving way to unguarded breaths. “Your Move” sets adolescent desire inside a brisk, unforgiving grid; “Good Passenger” finds the loneliness beneath perfect manners. The almost weightless “Between Rounds” opens a seam through the album’s center. By “Hands Above the Keys,” suspended harmonies and unfinished piano suggest that refusing a tidy resolution might be its own first choice.

albums.title: Chlorine Halo
albums.label: Pale Basin Records
albums.notes: On her 2021 debut for Pale Basin Records, Kyoto's Sayo Nerihata turns a swimming pool into a room for things almost said. Nylon-string figures, wheezing organ and fingertip taps remain close enough to touch; breath-led Japanese vocals open into tiled reverberation, with ventilation and distant splashing left audible. “Chlorine Halo” makes bodily self-consciousness strangely weightless, while the central “Under My Tongue” lets stacked vowels swallow its confession. The gently lilting “Your Towel on the Chair” offers the clearest glimpse of the more direct folk writing to come. By “After Everyone,” guitar and language have receded, leaving a voice, its reflections and the organ's final breath.

albums.title: Les Adresses provisoires
albums.label: Petite Mesure
albums.notes: With Les Adresses provisoires, Montreal’s Éloïse Carreau expands the apartment-scale intimacy of her debut EP into a quietly mobile chamber-folk language. Fingerpicked guitar anchors string-quartet exchanges, bass-clarinet shadows and muted-cornet replies; brushed drums give the family’s successive relocations a walking pace. “Le deuxième palier” finds momentum without sacrificing hesitation, while “Les noms sur l’interphone” lets competing recollections overlap without resolving their differences. The nearly bare “Sans numéro” marks the record’s emotional hinge. From that silence, the ensemble rebuilds toward the generous release of “Une fenêtre pour chacun,” before “La chaise près de la porte” leaves an address audible chiefly through what is missing.

tracks.title: La chaise près de la porte

albums.title: Small Repairs
albums.label: Breakwater Assembly
albums.notes: On their fourth release, The Trestle Kin trade the amplifier spill and long ascents of After the Shift for dry, deliberate songs about living with what won't mend. Mara Venn's warm, husky alto stays at the center; Eli's late-arriving harmonies make small changes feel consequential. “Leave the Hinges” sets an easy two-step, while “Day Rate” finds daylight in syncopated acoustic guitar. The slow heart of “What the Floor Will Hold” and “Winter Water” gives way to the scuffed urgency of “Not a New Roof.” From there, the arrangements shed their tools until “As It Stands” leaves two voices and one lingering electric note.

albums.title: The Last Good Key
albums.label: Assembly House
albums.notes: On The Last Good Key, Velvet Meridian make grandeur a matter of attention rather than scale. Recorded largely face-to-face, their 2022 Assembly House release lets drum shells ring, bass notes settle and Miriam Calder’s modest piano voicings carry unexpected harmonic weight. “A Key That Still Turns” opens with a spring in its walking stride; “The Rooms We Keep” stretches into triple time without losing its conversational intimacy. Nathaniel Vane’s tenor wears its effort openly, while Elias Rook saves his guitar harmonies for moments that earn them. By the practical tenderness of “Leave the Light Above the Door,” this is neither retreat nor farewell, but an argument for remaining useful.

tracks.title: A Key That Still Turns
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
He rubs the morning from his thumb
A little brass comes through
The counter grows another inch
He lets it have the room
An apprentice folds the alphabet
And leaves the vowels loose

[Pre-Chorus]
The landing has arrived downstairs
There's room for everyone in pairs

[Chorus]
We can come through sideways
We can bring the rain
Let the doorway learn our shoulders
Till it opens out again
We were never in the marble
We were always in the grain

[Verse]
The foreman has a borrowed face
It fits him round the eyes
He takes his praise in narrow strips
And hangs them out to dry
At noon his hands become two birds
Too heavy for the sky

[Chorus]
We can come through sideways
We can bring the rain
Let the doorway learn our shoulders
Till it opens out again
We were never in the marble
We were always in the grain

[Bridge]
Leave a little of the crooked
In the measure of the square
There are people in the turning
There is turning in the stair
I was taller when they drew me
You can rub me smaller there

[Chorus]
We can come through sideways
We can bring the rain
Let the doorway learn our shoulders
Till it opens out again
We were never in the marble
We were always in the grain

[Outro]

tracks.title: Leave the Light Above the Door

albums.title: Acequia mineral
albums.label: Sello Greda
albums.notes: Released by Sello Greda in 2022, Inés Talavera’s debut follows an inherited irrigation share from kitchen-table recollection into the language of official claims. Close charango and dark alto sit forward of breathing, imperfect strings; the former tailoring workshop remains audible in every creak and uneven decay. “El turno del agua” finds fleeting fellowship in cueca-derived accents, while “Nombres y medidas” turns a spoken inventory into the record’s emotional center. By “Hasta donde dice el papel,” independent string lines gather without forcing a climax. “La mano se retira” leaves both harmony and entitlement unsettled: inheritance here is something to answer for, not simply receive.

albums.title: Harestep
albums.label: Rushbed Records
albums.notes: Released by Rushbed Records in 2022, Oisín Keld’s debut makes uneven metres feel like practical movement: stepping over wire, testing a bank, stopping to look again. Recorded largely live in a borrowed rehearsal hall, Harestep keeps the nail noise and low-string buzz beside viola lines that seem to grow from the guitar’s overtones. “Leave the Wire Loose” sets its seven-beat cycle against an unhurried vocal; “Before You Pull” nearly abandons accompaniment altogether. Bass clarinet and close-stacked harmonies deepen the later songs without enlarging their volume. The jagged “Where the Bank Gives” supplies the rhythmic peak before “Leave It Loose” returns the record to an unfinished, resonating quiet.

albums.title: Chlorine at Four
albums.label: Pale Tile Recordings
albums.notes: Ultravellum’s debut follows a sleepless night through motel rooms, chemical air and the first unhelpful light of morning. Nylon-string guitar remains within touching distance while quarter-inch loops stretch its harmonics into an uncertain horizon. “Dry Mouth” begins with a lucid picking pattern; by “Please Leave the Key,” delayed doubles and low electronic knocks have loosened the floor beneath it. The central “Until” suspends an unfinished sentence inside mismatched tape cycles. Melody gradually returns on “Curtain Gap,” but there is no restorative sunrise: “Pool Pump” ends with untreated strings and distant machinery, leaving Mara Venn’s intimate alto suspended between bodily fatigue and time without edges.

albums.title: Nightjar Assembly
albums.label: Cable Basket
albums.notes: On their third release, Nairobi's kitenge/64 make availability sound like a daily practice: a spare key, a late light, an unanswered dedication. Released by Cable Basket in 2022, Nightjar Assembly pares back Antenna Orchard's expanded electronics, giving low-tuned nylon strings, woody thumb piano and room hum space around Nyambura Kibe's grain-edged alto. “Buffering Your Name” briefly fractures that quiet with syncopated glitch pop; “A Place at the Table” and “Hewa” find rhythm in brushed surfaces and decay. The late songs gather strength through staggered voices, culminating in “Until Our Hours Meet,” where separate farewells lose their pulse and resolve into a shared breath.

tracks.title: The Long Way to Your Door

albums.title: Oolong Frequencies
albums.label: Moth Dial
albums.notes: Released by Moth Dial in 2022, petalcodec's debut EP finds the Taipei project building songs from the evidence of exchange: cassette motors, caught breaths and fingers moving across strings. Nylon guitar and harmonium stay within touching distance, while radio interference and granular replies suggest another room, another waking hour. “Your Morning, My Sink” makes domestic routine quietly rhythmic; “Seven Small Things” slips seven beats beneath an effortless melody. The warm, plainly stated chorus of “Keep a Light” points toward the firmer songwriting of Eight Hours East. Here, though, intimacy remains spare: “When You Get This” dismantles its accompaniment until only a voice and the recorder's final click remain.

albums.title: Nine Laps Uncounted
albums.label: Oblouk Recordings
