albums.notes: Returning after nine years, The Ninth Velodrome trade the monumental climb for something more companionable: twelve linked movements recorded to tape in a wood-paneled hall. Harmonium, bowed guitars and close-recorded choir share the same breathing space, while bass and percussion discover momentum without demanding collapse. “Inside the Banking” makes an uneven meter feel welcoming; an ascending phrase travels through “Handrail,” “Passing Light” and “Room for Another.” The spare percussion of “Felt and Copper” opens onto the radiant rounds of “Common Air.” Even the orchestral surge of “The Open Grandstand” eventually yields, leaving “Until We Differ” to measure togetherness in unequal breaths.

albums.title: Les Poignets vides
albums.label: Disques Contrepoids
albums.notes: On her 2022 debut for Disques Contrepoids, Montréal’s Mireille Dorsenne makes chamber pop out of an inventory: cuffs, blades, receipts and the space a missing magician leaves behind. Harpsichord quills, bow changes and chair movements stay inside the frame, giving these French-language songs the intimacy of a demonstration performed across a table. The brisk accounting of “Tout est dans le double fond” gives way to the wounded waltz “La Femme sciée parle,” where the assistant finally claims the story. As percussion recedes, close harmonies leave suspensions hanging between viola and cello. “Manche vide” closes without an answer, only a voice continuing after the instruments have stopped.

tracks.title: Tout est dans le double fond

albums.title: Attrito celeste
albums.label: Raccordo Edizioni
albums.notes: On their third album, Bologna’s Atlante Obliquo make resistance audible: bow hair catches, drum figures stumble without losing the pulse, and six separately amplified guitars refuse to merge into one monumental wash. Following the spacious chamber intimacy of La distanza esatta, Attrito celeste restores force through shorter, more sharply articulated forms. “Cuscinetto grippato” starts mid-struggle; “Il turno delle mani” pits the full guitar ensemble against an immovable cello figure. Between them, “Finché tiene” suspends the machinery around Elia Vannini’s barely embodied, wordless tenor. Released by Raccordo Edizioni, this is symphonic post-rock measured in friction, fatigue and the small adjustments that keep people playing together.

albums.title: Herederos del ruido
albums.label: Sello Remache
albums.notes: On Herederos del ruido, León de Alambre make inheritance sound less like a monument than a room full of people negotiating where to stand. Live rhythm-section takes give the Monterrey band's arena rock a yielding pulse, with scraped nylon strings and distinct backing voices surviving every electric surge. “La armadura” sets bright hooks against suspended harmonies; “Sin romper la mesa” saves its heaviest, crooked riff until the acoustic conversation can no longer contain it. The title track turns refusal into collective resolve. Across the closing march, guitar lament and hushed “Con otro sentido,” release comes through shared responsibility rather than a bigger chorus.

albums.title: Good Hands, Bad Timing
albums.label: Ballast House
albums.notes: On their self-produced Ballast House return, Switchyard Orchard put more daylight into their folk-rock without sanding away its working edges. Bright piano, wiry guitar and sharply articulated bass carry the clipped opening of “Good Hands, Bad Timing,” while “Borrowed Van” turns mechanical uncertainty into quick-footed momentum. At the centre, “The Things That Still Work” quietly inventories a parent's belongings, refusing an easy swell of consolation. From there, endurance becomes something shared: passing tools, repairing roofs, stacking chairs. Riddell's grainy baritone remains the anchor, but Keane and Bell increasingly answer back, finally taking turns with the refrain of “There's Still a Way Home.”

tracks.title: Leave the Kitchen Light
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]

[Verse]
You kept your coat on at the sink,
I rinsed the cups before you'd finished.
You asked if work had picked up much;
I said enough, then changed the subject.
Your teaspoon ticked against the rim.
We let the fridge come cutting in.

[Pre-Chorus]
You left the chair a little out.
I haven't pushed it back.
There's nothing clever left to say
Across a gap like that.

[Chorus]
Leave the kitchen light,
Let it reach the road.
Past the houses stepping down,
Past the last late load.
You can still be angry,
You can still come by.
We don't have to call it settled.
Leave the kitchen light.

[Verse]
You said the money wasn't why;
I put the folded notes between us.
You slid them underneath my plate
And asked if I'd been up to see her.
I watched your sleeve catch on the latch.
You freed it without looking back.

[Chorus]
Leave the kitchen light,
Let it reach the road.
Past the houses stepping down,
Past the last late load.
You can still be angry,
You can still come by.
We don't have to call it settled.
Leave the kitchen light.

[Interlude]

[Verse]
The bulb above the stove runs warm.
A moth keeps tapping at the ceiling.
I dry your cup and put it down,
Then turn the handle where you'd reach it.
I could have asked you once to stay.
I found the words too late that day.

[Chorus]
Leave the kitchen light,
Let it reach the road.
Past the houses stepping down,
Past the last late load.
You can still be angry,
You can still come by.
We don't have to call it settled.
Leave the kitchen light.

[Outro]
Not the hall one.
Not the stair.
Leave the kitchen light.
I'll leave it there.

albums.title: Room Enough to Stay
albums.label: Turnout Recordings
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Newcastle’s The Ochre Switch make staying put sound like an active commitment. Recorded largely live, Room Enough to Stay keeps the spaciousness of The Hours We Keep while clearing room for travelling bass lines, woody acoustic rhythms and Mara Venn’s independently timed harmonies. Eli’s grain-edged baritone remains the steady centre. “Leave the Side Gate” opens in gently turning six-eight; “Saturday Rate” finds lift in a brisk working-week shuffle. The neighbourhood study “The Shop Below” lets instruments carry part of the story, while “Room Enough” reaches the record’s emotional summit without raising its voice. These are generous songs with obligations still attached.

albums.title: All the Rooms Lit
albums.label: Sounding House
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Gorse Arithmetic make room for brightness without mistaking it for certainty. Ewan Bell’s springy baritone guitar anchors clean electric figures, hand percussion and compact upright piano, while Mereana’s harmonies increasingly determine where a sentence lands. The full-band entrance of “Keys for Everyone” opens onto the communal choruses of “Working Bee” and “Put Your Name Down.” At the centre, “Another Plate” and “The Hall Roof” find belonging in practical gestures rather than homecoming promises. The late electrical push of “What We Can Carry” earns its release; the closing title track brings the siblings into unison, with the piano pedal still audible beneath them.

albums.title: Celuloide Azul
albums.label: Edições Fita Clara
albums.notes: On their 2023 debut for Edições Fita Clara, Porto’s Teatro das Marés trace a cinema’s working day through nylon-string grain, audible bow changes and celesta light. Duarte Seabra’s precise, lightly reedy tenor keeps the songs conversational even as accompaniment becomes architecture: the quartet begins by coloring a room and ends by determining its dimensions. “Bilhetes para Hoje” turns queue management into buoyant counterpoint, while “Intervalo Técnico” lets an exposed viola hold the building’s fatigue. The luminous “Sessão das Nove” supplies the largest release; “Depois da Última Imagem” closes without resolution, leaving communal pleasure suspended between the final reel and tomorrow’s paperwork.

albums.title: Moth Dialect
albums.label: Soft Ceramic
albums.notes: On hushrelay’s debut album for Soft Ceramic, the apartment becomes a resonant chamber: extractor-fan hum, nylon strings, and cassette flutter open onto unexpectedly deep bass and suspended keyboard harmony. Expanding the guitar-and-hiss intimacy of the earliest sessions, Moth Dialect traces one sleepless night without turning its small gestures into spectacle. “把電視轉小聲” finds a supple pop refrain inside clipped consonants and muted taps; “風扇的背面” lets the room itself carry the melody. Later, the interlocking guitars of “留一瓣給你” make tenderness feel slightly unsteady. By “天快亮,” almost everything has fallen away except breath, a plainly audible splice, and the reassurance of someone still nearby.

albums.title: Fluorescent Company
albums.label: Latchpin Records
albums.notes: On their debut album for Latchpin Records, Leeds quartet Ladderwake turn the hours after work into quietly expansive folk-rock. Dry, interlocking acoustics make room for melodic bass, brushed snare and clean electric inversions; the room stays audible even as the amplifiers bloom. Compared with their brisk early rehearsals, these songs trust withheld resolutions and the space between replies. “Yellow Tabard” finds exhilaration in a shared-microphone chorus, while “Borrowed Sleeves” makes an uneven phrase feel like a difficult admission. The wiry release of “Last Bus Argument” earns its volume. By “The Long Way Round,” companionship needs only guitars, footsteps and voices that never quite land together.

albums.title: Taffeta Republic
albums.label: Pleat Editions
albums.notes: On their third album, Prague’s Parlor Cartography turn evening dress into a small political system: who gets admitted, who pays, and who recognizes the borrowed coat. Taffeta Republic gives their chamber pop a firmer floor, with weighty bass and dry drums beneath wide-screen strings. “Hired Evening” and “The Compliment” arrive with unusually immediate hooks, their harpsichord accents cutting like cufflinks. At the center, “Without the Jacket” exposes Tomáš Vorel against suspended quartet chords before “Everybody at Once” floods the room with competing melodies. Released by Pleat Editions, this is their most spacious record, but its final, bare piano chord keeps the human scale intact.

albums.title: Unbroken Teeth
albums.label: Lantern Track
albums.notes: On their fourth album, Pumice Choir recover the acoustic weave of their earliest recordings without retreating into it. Live-room drums give these songs weight, while the retained tempo shifts and vocal spill make endurance sound like work shared between people. “The House Still Moves” opens in unison before its guitars find separate paths; “Unbroken Teeth” turns a taut refrain into a genuinely new instrumental argument. Mara Vale's restrained alto anchors the exposed sibling harmonies of “Your Version.” After the near-silence of “Still Here,” “What We Hold in Place” gathers the quartet into a long, unsentimental plateau—and a single collective stop.

albums.title: Ordinary Arithmetic
albums.label: Small Measure Records
albums.notes: On his fourth release, Ansel Bellweather lets more daylight into his close-miked chamber folk. Nylon-string guitar and softly doubled baritone remain the center, but clarinet, bouncing piano, plucked cello, and handclaps give domestic negotiations a newly buoyant pulse. “Carry the One” starts mid-stride; “The List You Left” finds comedy in the grocery budget. The exposed middle stretch, especially “At the Kitchen Door,” preserves the fatigue beneath that brightness. By the gloriously crowded “All the Chairs,” shared life sounds worth the inconvenience. “Leave It Here” closes with one guitar and distant friends: intimacy expanded, not abandoned.

albums.title: Parallax
albums.label: Blue Spindle Records
albums.notes: On his third release, Parallax, Luvo Nqolase makes electronics feel like another property of wood, wire and breath. String attacks become restless sequences; guitar harmonics spread into grainy light, while his thumb keeps human time beneath elastic bass. Released by Blue Spindle Records in 2023, the album extends Sidereal Cotton’s overlapping arrangements without sacrificing Seven Against Nine’s room-level intimacy. “The Peg in the Ground” and “Nine Miles by the Map” supply its sharpest propulsion. At the centre, “My Father's Version” and the argumentative “You Were Not Here” strip perspective back to testimony. “Here, Still” closes with no technological distance left: just one voice, finishing its obligation.

albums.title: Velvet Mile
albums.label: Fallow Circuit
albums.notes: On Velvet Mile, The Copper Census retain Diesel Vigil’s long sightlines while bringing every gesture closer: thumbed baritone strings, soft floor toms, and sibling harmonies with the breath left in. Connection takes practical forms here—the exchanged key, the school pickup, the drive shared after work. “Your Turn to Drive” finds lift in a restless bass line, while “Leave the Line Open” makes silence part of the conversation. The accumulating force of “The Long Grade” supplies the lone full-volume release. From there, the record sheds weight until its title track leaves an organ note and the sound of the room.

albums.title: Summer's Northern Edge
albums.label: Hedgerow Assembly
albums.notes: On their most spacious studio album, The Astrolabe Union make a summer journey north feel both geographical and bodily. The differently tuned guitars of “The Long Light” establish a language of overlapping resonances; “White Nights at the Ferry” lets viola and piano carry what the lyric leaves unsaid. Vale's audible breaths and the ensemble's lower-set harmonies give these songs their unforced gravity. “Dance at the Turning Place” briefly restores the full band's dancing force, but restraint defines this late chapter. The title track and “Leave the Window Open” allow silence to become structural, finding endurance in attentive company rather than any promise of permanence.

albums.title: Permission Slips
albums.label: Carport Assembly
albums.notes: On their first full-length since Gymnasium Voltage, The Juniper Detention make room for the breath before an answer. Released by Carport Assembly, Permission Slips keeps acoustic pick scrape, shifting chairs and six closely woven voices audible inside complete ensemble takes. “Leave the Porch Light” begins alone; by “You Signed It,” twelve-string distortion and snapping drums turn family negotiation into a brisk confrontation. The spacious title track finds unease in a harmony note held against changing chords, while “Out of District” restores their forward rush. “Somebody Has to Lock Up” closes without spectacle: six people singing softly, accepting that leaving and responsibility can coexist.

albums.title: Unseeded
albums.label: Split Level Records
albums.notes: On their third release, Melbourne’s Podium Static stop chasing the finish line and listen to the room. Unseeded keeps the rounded bass and suspended-chord lift of their electropop, but loosens the compression around ringing dulcimer, clipped synths and Lena Voss’s quietly catching mezzo. “Nobody’s Timing” opens at walking pace; “Local Favourite” finds a generous chorus inside the fear of disappointing everyone. At the centre, “Wood and Wire” strips ambition back to breath and mallet strikes. Live toms gradually restore momentum before “Room for One More” turns the record’s hardest question into an invitation. Persistence has rarely sounded so physical, or so companionable.

albums.title: Blue Apron at 04:12
albums.label: Small Hours Press
albums.notes: Released by Small Hours Press in 2023, Blue Apron at 04:12 widens the close, friction-rich world of Pawl Choir without losing its human scale. Stereo prepared guitar and rounded bass drawn from slowed bicycle hubs frame Nao Mibu’s intimate Japanese alto; wheel clicks carry rhythm where a kick drum might sit. “Same Corner Twice” brings the record’s brightest interlocking motion, while the title track suspends two chords inside wavering vocal clouds. Across deliveries, shared food and kitchen preparations, overlapping routines replace solitary travel. “Leave the Entrance Clear” closes with one complete vocal take and a mechanism quietly exhausting its momentum.

albums.title: Almost Human
albums.label: Acacia Wire Records
albums.notes: On Almost Human, Cassian Mothusi loosens the arrangements and lets the trio’s shared room become part of the music. Acoustic strings scrape against clean tremolo guitar, lightly fraying amplifiers and drums whose spill remains audible between phrases. After the brighter insistence of Kisses by Telephone, these longer takes question whether sustained attention can become a refusal to let go. “Ordinary Light” begins without ceremony; the drumless “Your Side of the Window” makes absence tangible. At the centre, “Parallax” and “The Distance Between Stars” let close harmonies rub rather than resolve. By “Leave the Room,” even the ensemble has learned to stop waiting.

albums.title: Todavía sangra el pañuelo
albums.label: Discos Aguafuerte
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Las Falsas Magnolias return to the acoustic apparatus with its repairs showing. Recorded together in a modest recital hall, the quartet and guest strings leave chair movement, bow friction and breathing inside the arrangements. “El saco de mi padre” springs from an unaccompanied verse into buoyant pizzicato; “Maravillas en cuotas” makes professional charm sound precariously over-rehearsed. The loosened instrumental middle of “Mientras cambian el telón” marks the turn toward quieter, simpler songs. By “Hasta que salga alguien,” intricate counterpoint has yielded to four uneven voices sharing a refrain. Inés Valdés’s dry, intimate mezzo holds affection and accountability in the same phrase.

albums.title: Breathing Lessons
albums.label: Cichy Pokój
albums.notes: On Breathing Lessons, Kraków’s Tomasz Zawrel opens the door without losing the close-room grain of Calendula Hours. Nylon-string guitar and viola da gamba remain the foundation; bass clarinet, answering strings and overlapping voices make returning to company feel both welcome and difficult. “A Place at the Table” turns accepting supper into gently insistent chamber folk, while the nearly bare “What I Could Carry” exposes the effort beneath that ease. The crooked round of “Leave Room” gives way to the brisk “Across the Market.” Released by Cichy Pokój in 2023, this is recovery heard as negotiation, ending with six voices relinquishing “Enough for Today” one breath at a time.

albums.title: Unfinished Saturdays
albums.label: Weft Register
albums.notes: On their third release, Twillphase let the gaps carry as much weight as the machinery. Exposed nylon-string guitar, deep bass and soft electronic pulses frame songs about communal life lived on incompatible shifts. The close quarters of Piecework and interlocking patterns of Selvedge Weather remain audible, but repetition now makes room for hesitation. “Keys to Every Floor” and “Leave It by the Door” bring cleaning and delivery work into sharp domestic focus; “A Table Still” answers with the record’s most generous chorus. Guest voices gather without surrendering their differences on “Who Can Make Sunday?”, before the unlooped title track closes on breath and moving chairs.

albums.title: Saved Before Sending
albums.label: Small Interval
albums.notes: On their debut album for Small Interval, Seoul duo Hushframe turn unsent messages and household routines into meticulously shaped electropop. Iseul’s close, airy mezzo stays within speaking distance even as Doyun opens the choruses into luminous synth architecture; breath edits, headphone spill, and small mechanical noises remain part of the songs. “Draft One” finds its pulse cautiously, while “Read Receipts” lets syncopated bass carry a brighter surface. At the center, “Kitchen Light” reduces the conversation to fingerpicked guitar and an uncertain vocoder reply. The later rhythmic lift of “Still Your Address” makes the percussion’s gradual disappearance—and the unresolved room-tone ending of “Leave the Window Open”—feel earned.

albums.title: Terminal Weather
albums.label: Windowseat Recordings
albums.notes: YEO:RAE’s debut album for Windowseat Recordings makes a night in transit feel both intimate and immense. Nylon-string thumb noise, shifting furniture, and clipped consonants become the building blocks of luminous electropop, while her warm mezzo stays close enough to hear each breath. “Room Tone, 01:12” establishes the human scale; “Blue Platform” turns it into a dance floor. At the center, “Leave the Line Open” holds a suspended chord through its final refrain, making release feel earned rather than inevitable. As the machinery recedes toward “When You Get In,” the opening guitar figure returns carrying an electronic pulse: separation persists, but so does the connection.

albums.title: The Spare Key
albums.label: Latchlight Records
albums.notes: On her second album, Wellington’s Nell Harrowby gives domestic negotiations the scale of chamber music without losing the room around them. Thumbed guitar and clipped viola set the measured tread of “Who Has a Key”; “Apples, Soap, Bread” lets an ordinary shopping trip swing lightly into daylight. The divided strings and layered bass clarinets of “Before You Come In” reveal a wider palette, interrupted by the almost-spoken “At Two.” Released by Latchlight Records in 2024, The Spare Key builds toward the tangled, urgent “Both Turning,” then finds a less certain peace in “Leave the Landing Light”: piano, low reed and a viola note held past any easy answer.

albums.title: Rooms Still Listening
albums.label: Palier Records
albums.notes: On her first full-length for Palier Records, Montreal’s Sabine Desrochers lets the apartment door stand open. Nylon-string guitar and conversational alto remain close enough to catch a thumb brushing the wrong string, but bass clarinet, viola, cello and upright piano now have independent lives around them. “The Pharmacy Takes Lunch” finds an almost jaunty rhythm in an obsolete errand; “Pedal Down” makes an empty piano resonance feel inhabited. The bowed-string gathering of “Nothing Needs Me at Six” is the record’s quiet summit. Moving beyond the bedside routines of her debut EP, Desrochers writes freedom as something awkward, funny and not immediately welcome.

albums.title: A Way to Answer
albums.label: Small Current
albums.notes: On their third release, Melbourne's Lumen Relay trade the anticipated drop for the sound of people finding time together. Almost untouched guitar opens “Leave the Line Open”; brushed drums, roaming bass and interlocking mallets gradually bring the room into motion. “Meet Me Half Awake” earns its buoyancy through full-phrase harmonies, while “The Part I Left Out” makes silence and room reflections uncomfortably revealing. Mara Venn's husky alto stays close and largely untreated throughout. The communal percussion and patient ascent of “Until We Find It” extend the trio's electronic grammar, before the title track returns to that opening guitar figure with somewhere gentler to land.

albums.title: Lo que sigue en pie
albums.label: Casa de Sal
albums.notes: On their 2024 Casa de Sal release, Faro de Cobre locate arena-scale feeling in the work of staying together. Bronze-string attack, descending bass lines and five precisely joined voices remain, but the drums occupy a human-sized room and Tomás Araya's weathered tenor needs no disguise. The rolling opener “Todavía da luz” gives way to lean, close-harmony rock before “La primera posición” turns toward kitchen-table memory. “Diente de bronce” releases the tension through charango and electric guitar; the title track rebuilds grandeur from a near-whisper. Maintenance becomes affection here: tools returned, hands protected, knowledge passed on, one final chord shared without embellishment.

albums.title: Nacre Ascendant
albums.label: Pale Meridian Recordings
albums.notes: On their 2024 debut for Pale Meridian Recordings, Sapporo’s Isotherm Chapel turn the exposed intimacy of their 2022 performances into symphonic architecture. Piano pedals, cello fingertips, and Mio Takase’s dusky, wordless alto remain close enough to touch as strings and choir accumulate around them. “Snowglass Pendulum” introduces a tender compound-meter sway; “Six Breaths in the Meridian” opens that solitude into fellowship. The brief suspension of “Still Air” makes the abrasive climb toward “Nacre Ascendant” feel earned, its orchestral thunder powerful without flattening the ensemble’s grain. “The Dome Keeps Turning” withdraws without resolution: ascent here means carrying more, not standing above it.

albums.title: An Opera for Moths
albums.label: Falter Editions
albums.notes: On his third album, released by Falter Editions, Vienna’s Oskar Bellwether turns an apartment-bound evening into chamber pop with competing agendas. Pizzicato strings hurry past clipped percussion; oboe and bass clarinet question what his intimate baritone would prefer to leave uncontested. The bustling “The Committee for My Sleeves” and flirtatious “You Must Be the Light” give way to the exposed financial and emotional reckonings of “What the Room Costs.” More rhythmically independent than his earlier ensembles, these arrangements make their counterarguments audible without obscuring the songs. “Leave the Hall Light On” gathers the recurring figures into a luminous peak before “Nothing Further This Evening” dismantles the stage around an ordinary piano.

tracks.title: A Small Triumph on the Stairs

albums.title: Erratic Bloom
albums.label: Skare Editions
albums.notes: On Erratic Bloom, Iver Ruskedal brings the exposed spaces of Ablation Studies back into the reach of a refrain. Steel-string patterns retain their thumbnail scrape even as saturated grains grind around them; palm strikes give the electronics a dry, bodily counterweight. “Borrowed Ground” finds a steady melody over slipping bass, while “The Bright Fracture” turns uneven picking into something almost jubilant. At the center, “Sleeve” and “Under the Tongue” make breath and silence structural. The closing stretch builds toward the abrasive release of “What the Roots Refuse,” then withdraws into “Still Moving”: change registered without the comfort of a conclusion.

albums.title: Unison Ascending
albums.label: Ferric Hymnal
albums.notes: On their 2024 Ferric Hymnal release, Breakwater Atlas bring orchestral ambition back within touching distance. Guitars, chamber strings and mallet-heavy drums share audible air, while Eilidh Kerr's steady contralto gives these songs their human scale. “A Door Left on the Latch” states its melody before the ensemble gathers; “Spans” turns a fixed pulse into an evolving architecture of percussion and counterlines. Choir arrives late and close, not as spectacle. “Raise the Unfinished” reaches the record's fiercest height with brass following the bass, before “Until We Set It Down” finds warmth without smoothing away the final dissonance.

tracks.title: A Door Left on the Latch

albums.title: Silt Prism
albums.label: Marl Array
albums.notes: On Silt Prism, Euan Tern makes subtraction feel like a new instrument. Newly recorded open-tuned guitar meets a reduced archive of wire, waterworks and stone, each sound given a sharply defined edge and room to disappear. Following Contour Bloom’s drifting expanses, these nine songs ask what reconstruction leaves out—and who gets to name what remains. “Separate Marks” opens with startling gaps between breath, string and metal; “Return Channel” turns clipped syllables into restless counterpoint. The unaccompanied intimacy of “By Hand” resets the ear before the warmer closing stretch, where “Room for Water” quietly dismantles its own repeating figure.

albums.title: Kawki
albums.label: Splot Records
albums.notes: On her 2024 Splot Records debut, Warsaw’s Zofia Rdest makes orchestral folk feel as close as a hand resting on a guitar. Kawki traces a day beneath aerials and tram wires, widening from the spare “Na antenach” into the interlocking strings and clipped horn calls of “Prąd nad ulicą.” Her intimate mezzo holds its measured course while the arrangements become increasingly independent around her. “Osobne oddechy” lets bass clarinet and divided strings breathe at different lengths; “Jeszcze jasno” finally leaves a single cello note hanging beneath an unfinished cadence. Chair creaks, grainy bow attacks and imperfect unisons keep this carefully built debut grounded in shared, ordinary space.

albums.title: Ninety
albums.label: Pale Current Records
albums.notes: On Ninety, Orin Pell pares back Flannel's ensemble warmth into a close, dry chamber folk language of thumb-picked guitar, felt-muted piano and patient inner voices. Written during and after his grandmother's ninetieth year, these nine songs allow appetite, irritation and humour to coexist with bodily difficulty. “Not That Blue” finds affection in an exacting preference; “What I Can Do While Sitting Here” gives bass clarinet and viola room to think where words fail. The brushed pulse of “Another One, Then” briefly opens the room before “In the Morning” settles into unison and an audible breath. Care remains a negotiation, not a halo.

tracks.title: What I Can Do While Sitting Here

albums.title: Infrared Adolescence
albums.label: Night Fare Recordings
albums.notes: On their third release, Bergen duo silt//signal let other bodies into the room. Infrared Adolescence expands their guitar-and-grain vocabulary with bowed double bass, brushed drums and three guest voices, while deriving every electronic texture from the sessions themselves. The unguarded opening of “What I Do Now” gives way to the displaced momentum of “My Face Gives Me Away”; later, “Still Wearing My Coat” finds unease in almost motionless harmony. Signe Velde's low, close delivery holds these shifts together. By “Leave the Room Open,” youthful fear hasn't disappeared—it has become something the ensemble can carry together.

albums.title: Yes Forever
albums.label: Fourfold Records
albums.notes: On their 2024 Fourfold Records release, Aurelian Voltage turn affirmation into a daily practice: shoes on, door open, another attempt. The opening sprint restores the punchy piano and economical guitar fire of their earliest records, but the breathing room belongs to their later years. “Room for Two” makes public tenderness an arena-sized hook; “Some Mornings” gives doubt a seat without handing it the wheel. The lightly swung “We Can Work with That” catches four musicians enjoying one another’s timing. After the chosen-family rush of “All My People,” the title track closes on an added-note chord that leaves the welcome open.

albums.title: Satin Electorate
albums.label: Copper Kettle Recordings
albums.notes: On Satin Electorate, Municipal Swans return to their original five-player scale without surrendering the rhythmic poise of Tinsel Referendum. Upright piano, brushed drums and chamber instruments occupy a generous room; Pieter Vervaet’s baritone leaves space for a cello descent or Lotte’s late-arriving harmony to finish the thought. “The Spare Keys” and “Next Year's Secretary” make the transfer of small responsibilities quietly momentous, while “Carry the Tables” briefly breaks into brisk folk-rock. Released by Copper Kettle Recordings, this mature, warmly imperfect set culminates in “Enough Chairs,” where a communal instrumental refrain offers company rather than closure.

albums.title: Undertow Orchard
albums.label: Sounding Line
albums.notes: On her third release, Sólveig Kambdal lets performances breathe: fingerpicked steel strings remain close enough to hear skin catch, while viola, bowed guitar and reed organ open vast spaces behind them. Undertow Orchard carries Elastic Islands’ rhythmic spring into darker, less exposed percussion, trading compact constructions for patient ensemble movement. “Boundary Wire” makes maintenance quietly propulsive; the nearly bare “I Heard the Phone” locates stewardship in a missed human obligation. The title track gathers resolve without certainty, and “Hold the Ground Open” sustains her fullest ensemble intensity yet. Released by Sounding Line in 2024, it closes with “Leave the Cup,” bringing questions of inheritance and retreat back to an ordinary room.

albums.title: Electric Kinship
albums.label: Red Rivet Records
albums.notes: Across two Toronto anniversary concerts, Electric Kinship makes the audience part of Vesper Cavalcade's arrangements, not merely their backdrop. Released by Red Rivet Records in 2024, it opens with the hall alone on “Say My Name Here,” then sends early songs hurtling forward on lean guitars and mobile bass. “The Waiting Room Has Windows” preserves the panoramic piano writing, while a three-song twelve-string sequence exposes every breath and unfinished thought. Julian Vale's grain-edged tenor remains the dramatic center, but “Glitter on the Bailiff” turns argument into collective protection. By the debut EP closer “Room for One More,” the band can step away: the hall knows what to carry.

albums.title: Read Receipts
albums.label: Soft Relay
albums.notes: On their debut album for Soft Relay, Seoul’s Nacreline turn the smallest traces of performance into electronic architecture: guitar scrapes become luminous clouds, piano pedals mark the silence, and Han Seorin’s close, airy mezzo-soprano blooms into tightly fitted harmonies. Read Receipts moves from the exposed fingerpicking of “Before I Send” toward the widescreen hooks of its title track and “Last Bus, First Train.” At the center, “Typing” makes hesitation audible through misaligned vocal takes; later, “Your Morning, My Night” finds lift in incompatible schedules. These songs measure affection in fares, leave requests, and waiting time, ending not with reunion but with room left open.

albums.title: Ljósaskipti
albums.label: Eyrafold
albums.notes: On their second album, Akureyri’s Saltbréf let the orchestra move closer without surrendering the room around it. Nylon-string guitar, upright bass and harmonium anchor arrangements whose divided strings and answering brass make uncertainty feel communal. Dock-chain fragments become a quiet rhythmic engine on “Milli vakta,” while “Sama heimilisfang” finds extraordinary tension in little more than breath, bellows and low strings. The expansive “Hinum megin við ljósin” earns its processional lift through patient accumulation. Released by Eyrafold in 2024, Ljósaskipti deepens the debut’s practical tenderness into questions about partnership, recognition and choosing to stay.

albums.title: Playback Permission
albums.label: Minute Gloss
albums.notes: On their 2024 debut for Minute Gloss, Seoul's Nacreloop turn saved messages into a quietly exacting pop language. Nylon-string fragments interlock with rounded bass and dry percussion, while Han Iseul's intimate tenor opens into falsetto harmonies whose mismatched breaths remain audible. “Send When Awake” finds buoyancy in the etiquette of distance; “Two Percent Battery” reaches the record's rhythmic summit without sacrificing its small-room scale. From the near-stillness of “Read at 03:12” to the exposed recording that closes “You Can Delete This,” Playback Permission grows more expansive, then more vulnerable, treating each borrowed voice as a person rather than a texture.

albums.title: Acreburn
albums.label: Dryline Recordings
albums.notes: On his debut for Dryline Recordings, Saskatoon songwriter Calder Rusk makes drought audible in rasping bass strings, bowed banjo and the uneasy space before a confession. Acreburn moves at walking pace, allowing repair bills, water disputes and unanswered calls to accumulate their own weight. “Static on the AM” establishes its exposed, room-bound sound; “August Ration” brings the first bruising backbeat. A nearly bare “What I Owe” stops the gathering momentum before “Rain Would Be Something” opens into the record’s longest, widest crescendo. Supporting voices arrive without absolution, and “Leave the Line Open” ends with an answer that leaves the hardest question unresolved.

albums.title: Somniform
albums.label: Nacre Circuit
albums.notes: On Madoriel’s debut for Nacre Circuit, sleep leaves an online likeness awake and answering. Somniform makes that estrangement tactile: felt-muted piano, rattling bass strings and audible pedals gradually acquire bass clarinet, viola and electronics shaped from acoustic residue. Rika Minase’s fine-grained mezzo remains the human measure, even when sampled consonants and enormous vocal stacks crowd its edges. “The Gesture Survives” finds tenderness in inherited movement; “Reply Without Me” turns unattended communication into springy, uneven pop. The expansive “Until You Disappear” repeatedly clips its choral refrain short, making the bare piano and unguarded breath of “Nothing to Confirm” feel less like resolution than release.

albums.title: Todavía feroces
albums.label: Fulgor Cooperativa
albums.notes: En Todavía feroces, Palacio Fulgor convierten la experiencia en peso físico: piano de cola con mecanismos audibles, guitarras que raspan y una base que ya no necesita correr para imponerse. Publicado por Fulgor Cooperativa, el disco prolonga su escala de estadio sin maquillar el aliento de Julián Varela ni las fricciones del conjunto. «No nos retiren la mesa» abre sin preámbulos; «La rodilla y el deseo» encuentra sensualidad en los límites del cuerpo. La desnudez de «Alcanzame el vaso» divide el recorrido antes de una reconstrucción coral que desemboca en «Dejá la luz del patio», una despedida de la noche, no de la banda.

albums.title: Dire doucement
albums.label: Disques Menue
albums.notes: On Dire doucement, Les Escaliers de Poche trade the brittle ornament of Le sucre craque for longer takes, darker registers and the uncomfortable space between a request and its answer. Anaïs Venne’s close, husked mezzo anchors arrangements where cello resonance clouds upright piano and bass clarinet supplies quiet weight. “Pas une victoire” introduces full drums without offering a victory lap; “Tu peux me le dire” lets sibling harmonies expose affection and resentment in the same breath. After the sharp acceleration of “Tout en même temps,” the pulse gradually loosens. The closing “On laissera la lumière” leaves its imperfect harmony intact, entrusting the last word to cello.

albums.title: Nightjar Assembly
albums.label: Spindle Index
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Bristol’s sluice/09 bring the room back into focus: steel-string guitar, bowed fiddle and scavenged percussion move together before electronics abruptly alter the listening angle. Nightjar Assembly turns borrowing tools and keeping evening classes alive into songs with real communal lift. The loose welcome of “Bring What You Have” tightens toward the buckled sprint of “A Key for Everyone”; “After the Chairs” exposes the exhaustion underneath. Harmonium and interleaved verses gradually gather the players again, until “Same Time Next Week” lets the machinery fall silent while human hands carry on. It’s their most outward-facing record, without losing the grain of individual gestures.

albums.title: Facet Ceremony
albums.label: Counterseal Records
albums.notes: On her third release, Ivara Sorel brings the machinery of self-invention into plain sight. Sequenced bass presses against prepared piano, scraped strings and brass that still sounds made of breath; her dark alto leaves the effort of each declaration audible. “The Name You Use” builds a groove from clipped piano fragments, while “Sleeve Work” turns dressing into brisk, affectionate labor. At the center, “Without the Gold” lets flugelhorn answer what a former lover cannot. The gathering scale of “Room for Everyone” feels earned rather than ornamental. Released by Counterseal Records, Facet Ceremony closes with “Stay for Breakfast,” trading spectacle for the intimacy of people remaining in a room.

albums.title: Resonant Occupancy
albums.label: Cantilever Recordings
albums.notes: On Resonant Occupancy, Borrowed Viaduct turn the friction of their earlier records into a patient, physical language of care. Mara Bell’s woody alto sits inside steel-string pulse, bowed-bass grain and softly wheezing organ; Eli Sutherland’s tenor still questions rather than simply harmonises. The brisk appointment-run chronicle “Same Car, Thursday” makes persistence sound almost buoyant, while “Rooms We Still Use” opens into six minutes of bass-led negotiation. “Your Turn to Ring” supplies a necessary flash of irritation before the closing songs shed percussion and rebuild. Recorded facing inward, this is warmth with the difficult conversations left in—and a final collective breath where a triumphant chord might have been.

albums.title: Root Permission
albums.label: Furrow Editions
albums.notes: On Root Permission, Neem Circuit loosen the grid without surrendering the pulse. Fingerpicked steel-string, thumb piano and bass share space with trowel knocks, granular flickers and conversations recorded beside working beds. Kavya Rao’s dry, low alto makes questions of tenancy and time feel immediate, never abstract. The spacious opener “Room to Remain” establishes the trio’s breathing rhythm; “Carry the Trays” offers a brisk release before the patient accumulation of “All the Hours We Put In.” Extending Mulch Dance’s physical rhythms into longer ensemble takes, the Bengaluru group let testimony shape the arrangements. “Here Tomorrow” closes with chairs, breath and strings still audibly occupying the room.

tracks.title: All the Hours We Put In

albums.title: Kiss & Retract
albums.label: Witness Room
albums.notes: On her 2024 Witness Room release, Zorvelli makes changing one's mind sound less like defeat than renewed appetite. Harpsichord, springy bass and precisely cushioned electronic kicks brighten arrangements whose inner voices still refuse easy agreement. The title track opens at a sprint; “The Apology Dress” hides a crooked bridge inside an irresistible hook. At the center, “You Were There Too” and “What I Let Stand” turn accusation toward shared responsibility. After the stripped testimony of Oathless, this is an expansive return to counterpoint: “Everyone May Finish” lets competing memories sing together, while “Let Me Say That Again” closes with an intimate, unembarrassed correction.

tracks.title: A Chair for the Other Account

albums.title: Natação Sincronizada
albums.label: Bancada Discos
albums.notes: On their debut album for Bancada Discos, Lisbon's Clube dos Cometas turn rehearsal-room intimacy into a quietly expansive language for first love. The pizzicato bustle of “Ao Teu Passo” and flute-bright “À Porta da Piscina” extend the tactile chamber pop of Treino de Terça, now with more syncopated bass, structural piano and softly dissonant string overdubs. Tomás Seabra's reedy tenor keeps borrowed shirts, spare keys and mismatched schedules at human scale. “Um Lugar ao Lado” exposes the nerves beneath the buoyancy; the title track earns the record's fullest orchestral lift. “Não É Preciso Esperar” closes smaller, finding intimacy in the freedom to move differently.

albums.title: Tlak a dech
albums.label: Oblouk Editions
albums.notes: On their fourth album, Karstové Divadlo move the weight of their music from the crescendo into the shared act of keeping time. Recorded largely as complete takes in a timber-lined municipal hall, Tlak a dech lets dulcimer attacks, bow friction and small hesitations govern its scale. The interlocking phrases of “Po schodech s vodou” generate momentum without overpowering the room; “Než domluvíš” brings that collective attention down to voice and harmonium. Vránová’s dry Czech alto makes geological time feel bodily and immediate. The expansive strings of “Co unesou trámy” offer release before “Poslední úder” slows toward a dulcimer resonance nobody rushes to silence.

albums.title: The Grinning Mechanism
albums.label: Red Baize Records
albums.notes: On The Grinning Mechanism, Benedict Spindle turns a career’s worth of exposed wires into an invitation: come closer, see how it works. Piano, steel-string guitar and exuberant vocal architecture launch “Nothing Up Our Sleeves,” before “The Spare Key” restores the intimacy beneath the apparatus. Miriam Vale’s chamber strings, compact brass and tuned percussion enter like opinionated guests, particularly across the central “Terms of Admission” suite. Digital edits preserve the players’ breathing room rather than policing it. After the disarming “Leave the Landing Light,” “A Room for the Trick” earns its electric grandeur; “Before You Answer” leaves the gathering suspended, listening.

albums.title: Mercy Assembly
albums.label: Parallax Works
albums.notes: On their third album, Aperture Republic bring the communal scale of their orchestral rock into touching distance. Naledi Maseko’s dry, grain-edged alto leads close-bowed strings, warm bass and patient drums, with distortion saved for moments that need its weight. “A Place Beside You” opens in an easy six-beat sway; “The Seats We Mend” finds melody in ordinary repairs. The muted-flugelhorn procession at the centre makes “Load-Bearing” feel all the larger when its amplifiers finally open. Where Domewake enveloped and Testimony Engine pressed forward, Mercy Assembly listens, answers and leaves room. “Leave the Chairs” closes with a small chorus and the sound of people preparing to return.

albums.title: Apricot Betrothal
albums.label: Foldmark Records
albums.notes: On her 2024 Foldmark Records debut, Osaka's Tomoe Kisaragi makes late-life courtship audible in small adjustments: a bassoon begins walking, a viola steps closer, a second voice finds the first. Nylon guitar and handmade box zither retain their grain, while heel blocks and seed pouches give the early songs a puppet-theatre bustle. “If You Have No Other Plans” strips that stage almost bare for a momentous invitation. From the swaying title track onward, cello harmonies lengthen and harp notes receive their full silence. “Leave the Small Light On” completes the journey without fanfare, turning romantic uncertainty into the ordinary privilege of coming home.

tracks.title: If You Have No Other Plans

albums.title: La trampa impar
albums.label: Sello Aljibe
albums.notes: On La trampa impar, Malena Urdavia turns private rituals into a dispute over who gets to set the rules. Released by Sello Aljibe in 2024, her second album sharpens the exposed textures of Si sale seis into taut chamber art pop: bow strikes answer guitar clicks, prepared piano lands like a shut drawer, and chopped bass clarinet drives uneven grooves. “La mesa inclinada” opens with three competing vocal clocks; “Lugar para el muerto” makes silence feel like an occupied chair. The increasingly danceable “Tu parte del azar” brings the accusation into focus before “Sin decir tu nombre” leaves the bargain suspended between two voices.

albums.title: Mending Static
albums.label: Latchwork Recordings
albums.notes: On Mending Static, Kito Mwangala makes repair audible: scarred room recordings remain in place while muted guitar, thumb piano and live hand percussion learn to move around them. Following the exposed fractures of Unsent Receipts, his 2024 Latchwork Recordings release restores momentum without pretending the damage has disappeared. “Find the Same Step” gathers competing pulses into a workable gait; “Your Own Line” lets answering voices pursue independent melodies. Even the fleet instrumental passage in “Shutter Teeth” keeps its loose joints. By “Leave the Door on the Latch,” collective singing becomes practical companionship, each part falling silent separately until only the room remains.

tracks.title: Leave the Door on the Latch

albums.title: Bitumen Lullabies
albums.label: Dry Verge Records
albums.notes: On their 2024 Dry Verge Records debut, Adelaide’s Ultravoam brings the near-beatless drift of its earliest sessions into focus without polishing away the grain. Fingerpicked guitars retain their pick noise beneath pitch-wavering halos; rounded bass and household percussion give sleepless thoughts a walking pace. Mara Venn’s low alto stays close and unforced, especially when independently sung rounds begin to chafe against one another. “Leave the Landing Light” finds a generous hook inside suspended harmony, while “Heat off the Bonnet” supplies the record’s brightest release. From the constricted entrance of “Night Window” to the unaccompanied farewell of “Everyone Still Sleeping,” Bitumen Lullabies makes departure feel both necessary and unfinished.

albums.title: Personal Best
albums.label: Split Lane Recordings
albums.notes: On her 2024 debut for Split Lane Recordings, Glasgow’s Rona Skevick makes retirement audible as a change in rhythm rather than a finish line. Grainy viola, felt-muted guitar and close, lightly husky alto gradually acquire piano, sub-bass and choirs built from her own voice. “Chlorine on Your Cuffs” delivers the first generous harmonic release; “Veterans’ Heat” compresses old competitive reflexes into an abrasive, asymmetrical circuit. The retreat to “Tuesday Without Training” is just as consequential. Across ten songs, applause shifts from reassurance to interference before disappearing altogether, leaving affection expressed in repairs, adjusted routines and time no longer measured against a personal best.

albums.title: Gente Inteira
albums.label: Dobradiça Edições
albums.notes: On Gente Inteira, Tomás Nespereira brings the guitar back within touching distance without surrendering the orchestral breadth of Terreno Baldio. Recorded largely with his core quartet sharing a room, these twelve portraits let bassoon keys, fingernails and shifting pulses remain audible. The buoyant “Pelo Meu Nome” opens onto harder questions of partnership, inheritance and who gets to tell whose story. “A Meias” makes negotiation dance; “Não Levo a Chave” turns refusal into a quietly expansive refrain. Released by Dobradiça Edições, the album closes with “Gente Inteira,” where voice, viola and bassoon find a common melody rather than a triumphant resolution.

albums.title: Pozlátko
albums.label: Silt Ribbon
albums.notes: On her debut album for Silt Ribbon, Brno’s Lenka Vratilová expands the spare guitar-and-voice settings of her 2023 performances without disturbing their intimacy. Nylon strings retain their nail clicks; viola da gamba answers rather than blankets her measured alto. Gilding becomes a question of care, ownership, and concealment, traced through fastenings, names, and institutional paperwork. “Under the Clasp” introduces a quietly walking bass, while “The Accession Number” arrests the gathering motion with an almost spoken reckoning. The widening strings of “Say Her Name Slowly” eventually give way to “What Remains Ours,” whose final open guitar interval refuses an easy settlement.

albums.title: Beautiful Blunders
albums.label: Klaaspind
albums.notes: On their second album, Tallinn’s Käigukuma let the pieces move without knowing where they will land. Pizzicato strings and granular synths remain sharply etched, but brushed drums, bass clarinet and cello introduce a welcome instability. Liise Vaher’s silvery soprano moves from the exposed opening of “What I Can Carry” to the conversational vulnerability of “No Good Move,” where viola becomes her only partner. “Borrowed Tempo” turns uneven phrasing into supple dance music; “Room for Everyone” opens the record’s largest refrain into a breathing, antiphonal chorus. Released by Klaaspind, Beautiful Blunders exchanges Touchmove’s immaculate defenses for something warmer: precision that makes space for another person.

albums.title: Undertow Arithmetic
albums.label: Tidal Relay
albums.notes: On Undertow Arithmetic, Bristol’s kitevault lets the room into the machinery. Hammered dulcimer still splinters into hooks and percussion, but loose drum takes, amplifier hiss and audible breathing complicate the precision of Trophywater. “Walking Home Dry” delays its kick until the first chorus has passed; “No Personal Best” finally opens the floodgates. At the centre, “Shared Room” and “Grain of the Door” strip away the pumping architecture to expose Ellis Mercer’s grain-edged tenor. The closing stretch rebuilds without restoring the old armour: “All Our Names” turns achievement into fellowship, and “Leave the Light Between Us” lets its choir resolve into individual people.

albums.title: Correspondencia sin destinatario
albums.label: Hebra Discos
albums.notes: En su segundo lanzamiento, Lucía Bermejal ensancha el cuarto íntimo de Compás ausente sin borrar el roce de las cuerdas ni el peso del bombo. Correspondencia sin destinatario, editado por Hebra Discos en 2024, convierte diez conversaciones con un maestro ausente en una emancipación musical: la orquesta aprende a disentir. «La digitación» tensa charango y percusión sobre una chacarera quebrada; «Polvo de ensayo» detiene el pulso casi hasta el susurro. El arco alcanza su mayor densidad en «Lo que no corregiste», antes del despojamiento de «A solas con tu letra». En «Sin remite», los instrumentos siguen hablando cuando ella ya ha terminado.

albums.title: Hands Without Heirs
albums.label: Šiv Records
albums.notes: On her second album, Vitrajune lets the miniature theatre of Never Whistle Here breathe into larger rooms. Felt-piano creaks remain close, but electronic bass reaches deeper and brass answers from across an audible distance. “Leave the Chair” establishes the patient pulse; “Gold Size” finds warmth in suspended harmony and a sign painter’s tools. At the centre, “Through the Eye” splinters solitary singing into a granular ensemble before “Not for Display” delivers the record’s fiercest bodily release. These songs attend to skilled hands without turning their owners into relics. The title track’s expansive refrain finally falls away to the unprocessed sound of breathing.

albums.title: Foxglove Tribunal
albums.label: Spindlebank
albums.notes: On their 2024 Spindlebank release, Bracken Dial turn a garden hearing into chamber folk of extraordinary patience and bite. The acoustic intimacy of After Forty Winters remains, but the ensemble again lets independent lines contest the singer's account. “The Gardener Calls It Weather” opens nimbly; “Articles of the Border” tightens the argument through interlocking reeds, strings and small percussion. The expansive “The Bed Divided” makes instrumental counterpoint carry the dispute before two spare testimonies restore human scale. Throughout, Riddell's dry baritone refuses melodrama. “Until the Garden Answers” leaves the final deliberation to instruments whose beautifully articulated disagreement offers no comfortable verdict.

albums.title: Mouthful of Ferns
albums.label: Pale Basin Records
albums.notes: On her second album, Kyoto’s Sayo Nerihata gives her ambient pop a firmer bodily pulse: fingernails catch nylon strings, organ keys click, and breaths lead melodies into rooms still damp with resonance. Mouthful of Ferns retains Chlorine Halo’s suspended harmonies but lets verses speak more plainly and refrains return with new confidence. “Water Before Tea” turns domestic care into a gently insistent hook; “Room for One More” opens into buoyant, imperfectly synchronized ensemble singing. Between them, the spare “Stem” makes every fretting-hand movement count. Released by Pale Basin Records, this is intimate music learning how to extend an invitation.

tracks.title: Say It While the Rice Is Warm

albums.title: Ce que les légendes taisent
albums.label: Petite Mesure
albums.notes: On her third release, Éloïse Carreau turns annotated family photographs into questions that arrangement alone cannot resolve. Her dry, articulate guitar remains close enough to hear the fingers, while harp, low clarinet, strings and pump organ deepen the surrounding space. The nimble pizzicato of “Deux noms pour elle” gives way to the displaced meters and withheld cadences of “La Date corrigée” and “Qui manque.” After the instrumental “Papier cristal,” simpler melodies become a way of sharing uncertainty rather than conquering it. Released by Petite Mesure, this is Carreau’s most expansive chamber-folk record, ending with the unfinished sentence and solitary viola of “Et si tu retrouves.”

tracks.title: Au dos, peut-être
tracks.lyrics:
[Intro]
Elle tient la photo par le bord.

[Verse]
Au dos, « Jeanne », puis un trait fin,
le point d’interrogation demeure.
La mine a creusé dans le grain
un petit pli sous la dernière lettre.
Tu dis : « C’est sûrement sa sœur. »
Je rapproche la lampe pour voir.

[Interlude]

[Verse]
Le coin s’est pris dans la rainure
quand tu l’as poussée jusqu’à moi.
On voit trois tasses, une voiture,
un bras dont la manche est coupée.
Tu reconnais la cour, le toit ;
pour elle, tu n’as rien ajouté.

[Interlude]

[Verse]
J’écris « peut-être » sur la pochette,
pas sur le dos, près du prénom.
Tu ramasses les miettes ; j’attends
que ta main quitte enfin la table.
Puis nous rangeons, pour le moment,
celle dont nous gardons le nom.

[Outro]
Je tiens la photo par le bord.

albums.title: Common Receiver
albums.label: Soft Circuit Records
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Relayweather turn outward without losing the close-mic intimacy that made their earlier records compelling. Common Receiver lets you hear pleasure being assembled: chair creaks become rhythm, guitar brushes become light, and imperfect ensemble entrances supply the lift once carried by synth stacks. “Make Room” establishes that tactile welcome; “Somebody Waves Back” and “Stay for the Next One” deliver radiant dance-floor choruses with answering voices still woven through the drops. After Public Tenderness’s exposed scrutiny, this 2025 Soft Circuit Records album finds warmth in practical care, shared rooms and the patient, three-voice gathering of its title-track finale.

albums.title: A Different Kind of North
albums.label: Mellomrom Records
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Svalevev turn the restlessness of departure into the collective work of staying. Recorded with the trio playing together, A Different Kind of North lets breathing tempos tug against discreet synthesis and sampled acoustic shadows. “Windows Open Inland” offers an unusually buoyant welcome; “The New Waterline” and “What the Hinges Know” make tangled metres feel conversational. Across low-string guitar pulses, suspended upper figures and percussion made from small resonant objects, Ingrid Velde’s intimate alto finds dignity in repairs and revised routines. The swift “Before the Ferry” gives way to an increasingly spare final stretch, ending with the hard-won harmonic arrival of “Leave a Light Here.”

albums.title: Polen de cobre
albums.label: Sello Greda
albums.notes: En Polen de cobre, Inés Talavera convierte la orquesta de cámara en una geografía de consecuencias: el polvo atraviesa cercos y las deudas cambian de manos. Publicado por Sello Greda en 2025, su segundo álbum invierte el crecimiento orgánico de Acequia mineral: aquí las estructuras instrumentales preceden a la voz. El charango mecanizado de «Fuera del cerco» tropieza con un ensemble de ataques ásperos; «Turno de viento» hace caminar sus compases alternos sin descanso. En el centro, «La pieza del fondo» reduce la escala a respiración y madera. Tras el empuje instrumental de «Cota de dispersión», «Lo que queda a nombre nuestro» termina sin absolución, apenas voz y una nota pulsada.

tracks.title: Lo que queda a nombre nuestro

albums.title: Soft Tissue
albums.label: Mica Bloom
albums.notes: On her debut for Mica Bloom, Seoul’s Yune Sori stretches songs built for nylon-string guitar into chamber arrangements threaded with granular electronics. Her intimate, husky mezzo remains the point of contact: consonants catch against clipped bass, while vowels drift into precarious harmony. “Skin Login” makes recognition feel tentative and tactile; “Saliva Index” turns bodily boundaries into the record’s sharpest rhythmic exchange. At its center, percussion falls away, leaving bows, breath and the uneasy comfort of a familiar recording. “Unsent Mouth” patiently recovers language from a fractured choir, before “Animal Permission” releases the machinery altogether. Soft Tissue finds solace in what a recording preserves—and honesty in what it cannot return.

albums.title: Suture Confetti
albums.label: Papillary Records
albums.notes: On Suture Confetti, Odile Marchand-Lowe turns the intimate chamber language of Aseptic Bloom and Capillary Ballet toward the dance floor without sanding away its awkward edges. Rounded synth bass, dry percussion, and bright flute figures carry songs about pleasure, permission, and the uneven work of recovery. “Good Scissors” opens in midair; “Permission Slip” makes counterpoint feel like a bodily reflex. At the center, “The Spare Key” lets detuned piano and viola expose the anxiety beneath the newfound confidence. Released by Papillary Records in 2025, the album ends not with grandeur but with company: shared rhythms, overlapping voices, and a laugh nobody edits out.

albums.title: Violet Fermata
albums.label: Pärl Editions
albums.notes: On Violet Fermata, Liisi Orvek turns inherited testimony into intimate, sometimes resistant replies. Her third release brings bass clarinet, cello, divided violas and a solitary horn into close acoustic focus, leaving bow friction and shared-room spill intact. The low cello tread of “Sinu lause lõpus” opens a sequence that gathers motion without surrendering its restraint; “Ära vasta veel” lands in clipped ensemble accents rather than orchestral uplift. Between exposed guitar songs and dark unisons, “Oma samm” finally lets the body move. “Kannikesed laual” closes with Orvek’s voice falling silent before the strings, leaving affection unresolved but unmistakably present.

albums.title: Pupil Bloom
albums.label: Lichen Index
albums.notes: On their third album, Bergen trio Myrglass lets warmth into the machinery. Steel-string figures still snag against clipped kicks and displaced room noise, but round electric bass and saturated harmonium now give these fractured songs somewhere to land. “Let Me In Slowly” opens with a voice alone; “Your Side of the Table” turns the invitation into their sharpest pop chorus yet. At the center, “Held Breath” makes an unfinished sentence feel enormous. Pupil Bloom brings affection into plain speech without making it easy: its brightest grooves keep losing their footing, until “Stay Until Morning” leaves only a restrained tenor and untreated guitar.

albums.title: Pollen Alphabet
albums.label: Petiole Recordings
albums.notes: On her third release, Wellington's Elspeth Rooke turns inherited family language toward its next listeners. Pollen Alphabet brightens her close-recorded chamber pop with wiry harpsichord, springing bass and handclaps, while keeping woodwind breath and guitar grain within touching distance. The nimble 'Leave the Ending Open' offers family sayings without their sting; 'No Quotation Marks' finds tenderness in refusing disclosure. Between them, instrumental miniature 'Comma, Window' makes silence feel purposeful. The buoyant title track imagines words travelling beyond their owners, before 'A Saucer of Rain' sheds its ensemble and leaves a small instruction for the future. Released in 2025 on Petiole Recordings.

albums.title: Apricot Psalms
albums.label: Mica Bloom
albums.notes: On Apricot Psalms, Avelune opens the room without smoothing its edges. Prepared upright piano, plucked cello and bass clarinet share audible air; bow scrape and pedal noise give these songs the friction of people working together. Following Velvet Metabolism's elastic electronics, synthesized choirs now resolve into recognizable human company. “Everybody Puts In” turns handclapped brightness into a sharply itemized argument about money, while “Not a Prayer” strips caregiving down to an almost solitary admission. The restless “The Spare Key Changes Hands” makes trust a rhythmic negotiation. By “Enough for Whoever Comes,” the gathering feels real precisely because nothing is neatly settled.

albums.title: Bestiário de Seda
albums.label: Semente Oblíqua
albums.notes: On her fourth release, Coimbra’s Inês Valdouro puts the embroidered creatures of festive clothing to work as witnesses, tricksters and travelling companions. Bestiário de Seda restores the bodily momentum held in reserve on Altitude de Agosto: nylon-string bass figures meet woody pizzicato, brushed frame drum and a sextet whose viola lines are as telling as its violin melodies. “Andorinha do Turno da Manhã” finds lift in the daily commute; “Raposa no Avesso” turns concealed wages into crooked-meter intrigue. Throughout, Valdouro’s dark, silver-edged mezzo draws closer under pressure. The hushed “Ombros de Domingo” clears the air before the final dances and the patiently unwinding cello coda of “Enquanto Houver Linha.”

tracks.title: A Cigarra Não Conta os Dias
O Nome que Ficou na Bainha

albums.title: Latency Psalms
albums.label: Tender Circuit
albums.notes: On their debut for Tender Circuit, Seoul duo Serein Index make waiting sound tactile: nylon strings scrape, felted piano hammers settle, and clipped syllables drift beyond the edges of Hae-in’s close, intelligible alto. Latency Psalms expands patiently from the exposed promise of “When You See This” into chest-warm bass and softly articulated hooks. “I’ll Keep the Evening” supplies its clearest declaration over a beautifully unsteady kick; “Same Figure, Different Room” bends a familiar piano phrase toward a less certain answer. Across nine songs, Korean and English register changing degrees of intimacy, while the electronics increasingly interrupt what they once sheltered. “Before You Answer” finally leaves the machinery behind, ending with breath.

albums.title: Hush Protocol
albums.label: Small Current
albums.notes: On Hush Protocol, elayra.exe makes subtraction feel structural. Following Peachbuffer’s candy-colored edits and Peripheral Sunshine’s panoramic drift, the Singapore producer leaves guitar gestures intact, drums dry and silence conspicuous. Elian Teo’s close tenor carries melodies that open outward without demanding bigger drops. “Two Drinks” and “Keep the Receipt” recover a careful dance pulse; “Separate Shelves” finds its tension in the space between domestic objects. The late bloom of “Room for the Weather” earns the record’s single expansive release before “Without Saving” closes on an unresolved guitar figure. Finger squeaks, uneven doubles and unguarded room sound become the architecture, not decoration.

albums.title: Fricción lenta
albums.label: Sello Ladera
albums.notes: On their fourth release, Valparaíso’s Isóbara let collective timing become the composition. Altered-tuning guitars rub against bowed charango and drifting oscillators; frame drums give these patient performances a bodily pull. “Hasta que ceda” waits two full minutes before admitting voice, while “La puerta roza” finds a compact melodic edge in an uneven meter. The extended instrumental “Dos superficies” makes tuning itself expressive. At the spare center, “Ya no sé por qué” asks what keeps a promise alive after certainty recedes. From there, density gathers without acceleration, until “A una” leaves its count-in and wavering final unison exposed: endurance heard as something people practice together.

albums.title: Suzanne rit encore
albums.label: Éditions Coudrier
albums.notes: On her third release, Montréal’s Céleste Vaudrel makes family memory feel less like an archive than a roomful of overlapping conversations. Nylon-string guitar, felted piano and bass clarinet remain the hearth; a twelve-player ensemble brings air, friction and buoyancy without crowding her close, softly grained mezzo. The mid-gesture opening of “Tu connais la suite” sets stories circulating before anyone can establish ownership. At the center, “Les deux versions” and “Ce qu’elle n’a pas dit” let incompatible melodies coexist. Later, “Presque une valse” finds a tentative communal swing. The title track leaves the musicians quietly carrying on after Vaudrel stops: affectionate, unresolved, alive.

albums.title: Unbraiding
albums.label: Rushbed Records
albums.notes: Where Harestep found tension in close quarters, Unbraiding lets the room become part of the argument. Recorded in a converted agricultural building, these ten songs place low-tuned guitar, dark reeds, bowed strings and six answering singers at audible distances. “Leave the Gate” gathers a pulse from isolated attacks; “Contour Lines” turns competing metres into purposeful momentum. At the centre, “The Knot Between Us” dismantles its melody through patient instrumental exchanges before “What We Agreed” brings Keld’s tenor almost unbearably close. The closing “Tools Down” offers no grand resolution: the ensemble recedes, leaving breath, outdoor air and the practical clatter of work ending.

albums.title: Raucous Mercy
albums.label: Cairn Signal
albums.notes: Drawn from complete performances across two consecutive Dunedin theatre shows, Raucous Mercy lets The Quarry Hours’ communal force retain its individual frictions. The early favorite “Splitlip” starts at full stride; “Ochre Parade” opens its processional sway into brass-backed, straight-time release. Between those broad choruses, Tender Defiance material bites with dry drums and muted electric guitar. A four-song acoustic centre brings “Stone Still Warm” and the nearly unaccompanied “No One Carries Nothing” within breathing distance. The previously unrecorded “Enough Hands” turns assistance into action before “Keep a Place” hands its refrain to the room. No replacement vocals, no tidying away the return.

albums.title: Ladle
albums.label: Copper Kettle Recordings
albums.notes: On her 2025 Copper Kettle Recordings debut, Cape Town’s Nandi Veyalo makes the work of care audible in thumbed bass strings, hesitant breaths and the space between replies. Ladle begins at bedside scale: “Washcloth” scarcely needs more than voice and guitar, while “Two Spoons” introduces a turning waltz and an answering cello. The arrangements widen toward “Orange Plastic Chair,” where interwoven cellos and a three-part flugelhorn passage frame an unsentimental waiting-room account. Veyalo’s warm, grain-edged mezzo keeps every admission conversational. By “You Can Sleep,” that breadth has receded, leaving reassurance without certainty and a room that continues after the guitar stops.

albums.title: Stay Until Stereo
albums.label: Nightjar Circuit
albums.notes: On Stay Until Stereo, morrow// FM make staying put sound expansive. Their fourth release reconciles Soft Reset’s exposed guitar-and-laptop intimacy with Overdrive Hearts’ physical lift and Almost Awake’s unresolved tenderness. Rounded bass and hand-played subdivisions give these songs room to breathe; Eli Venn’s husked tenor remains close enough to catch each hesitation. “Passenger Side” finds honesty in shared silence, while the spare “The Spare Key” refuses an easy reconciliation. By “Room for Everyone,” acoustic fragments have become bright, communal propulsion. The closing title track brings the opening guitar figure home, letting live voices—not bigger synthesizers—deliver the record’s earned release.

albums.title: Milkglass Vigil
albums.label: Quiet Basin Recordings
albums.notes: On Hushmere's debut, Milkglass Vigil, overnight care is heard in small adjustments: a glass moved closer, bedding turned, an answer offered again. Released by Quiet Basin Recordings in 2025, the Wellington artist's album begins with dry steel-string picking and a tenor close enough to catch every consonant. Harmonium breath gradually fills the room; brushed tom lends “An Easier Reach” a bodily sway before “Weather Through the Wall” loosens the pulse into radio static and sustain. The stereo bloom of “Pale at the Curtains” admits daylight without promising recovery. “Cup on Wood” finally returns everything to human scale: voice, touch, and a chord left ringing.

albums.title: Almost Audible
albums.label: Stillhet Utgivelser
albums.notes: On Almost Audible, Eira Solhavn lets the sentence arrive before its echo. Following the submerged electronics of Afterimage Studies, her third release brings an unprocessed alto into close focus, surrounded by plucked viola, felt piano and bass lines with newly assured movement. “Etter første setning” opens without accompaniment; “Gå ved siden av” finds unexpected ease in a lightly swung walking pulse. At the center, “Det jeg ikke sa” suspends that momentum, making the answering strings of the following songs feel earned. The room-resonant ensemble on “Plass til alle” offers the record’s widest embrace before “Nå har du hørt det” returns to one voice, one piano and nothing left unfinished.

albums.title: Eight Hours East
albums.label: Moth Dial
albums.notes: On their first full-length for Moth Dial, Taipei trio petalcodec turn the exchanged sketches of Oolong Frequencies into songs with firmer choruses and roomier horizons. Nylon strings, rounded sub-bass and desk-tap percussion stay tactile, while worn backing harmonies drift toward the stereo margins. “Your Morning, My Evening” makes incompatible schedules briefly singable; “Leave the Kettle” interrupts the gathering momentum with harmonium and consequential silence. The buoyant “Green Light All the Way” earns its brightness through interlocking parts rather than gloss. By “We Can Talk Now,” the record’s small acts of care have accumulated into an unhurried, imperfect connection.

tracks.title: The Long Way to the Station

albums.title: Apogeo
albums.label: Cúpula Discos
albums.notes: On Apogeo, Amalia Zorzán lets distance remain difficult. Following Perigeo’s small-room intimacy and Sizigia’s interlocking crescendos, her 2025 Cúpula Discos release places a remarkably close voice against strings heard farther back, preserving breath, guitar buzz and long decays. Guitarless opener “Dejar la luz” establishes the exposed language; “Hasta que barran” briefly turns it into an insistent chacarera. The caregiving songs “Cada ocho horas” and “El agua tibia” form the record’s tender centre. Across the closing triptych, orchestral weight grows without haste, until “Si llamás” returns to bare guitar and a promise left harmonically unresolved.

albums.title: Vegetative Multiplication
albums.label: Propagation Records
albums.notes: On her third release, Adjoa Kessiri pares back Grafting Season’s luxuriant ensemble to examine the cost of being perpetually useful. Isolated nylon-string notes, abbreviated bow strokes and bass clarinet breath meet electronics whose cycles rarely settle together. Repetition exposes wear: syllables disappear, entrances drift, offers of care become obligations. “One for Every Room” turns vocal multiplication into a quietly alarming inventory; “Again Is Not Enough” drives that pressure to its abrasive limit. The miniature “Small Pot” restores touch and breathing space. By “Enough, in Several Voices,” longer melodies return, but the separately sustained voices retain their differences—a provisional community rather than a perfected self.

albums.title: Koe dake
albums.label: Komorebi Editions
albums.notes: On their third release, Kyoto duo kasane/84 make absence audible without letting atmosphere obscure the song. Koe dake brings Emi Kuroda’s low-tuned nylon strings and intimate mezzo into a dry room, leaving Sota Nishimura’s processing to surface like an uncertain recollection. “Mada Koko ni” waits until its final half-minute to fracture; “Kigi no Aizu” turns mismatched loops and wooden taps into watchful motion. The spacious “Anata no Seki” earns the record’s only broad crest, with breath chords, bass clarinet and bowed strings arriving separately. From there, the arrangements recede until “Koe dake” leaves only a voice, a room and an unfinished breath.

albums.title: La Pesanteur des choses
albums.label: Disques Contrepoids
albums.notes: Après les inventaires intimes de Les Poignets vides, Mireille Dorsenne élargit la pièce sans en dissimuler les coutures. Clavecin, cordes et clarinette basse entourent une voix dont chaque consonne semble peser un objet. « Ce qui reste à porter » ouvre lentement l’espace ; « Les Créanciers » y installe un pas plus ferme. Au centre, le dialogue presque parlé de « Tu prends quoi ? » ramène les comptes à hauteur de famille. L’ampleur de « Là où passe le fil » ne promet aucune délivrance : elle rend simplement visible le travail collectif. Jusqu’au dernier lever d’archet, ce deuxième album fait de la précision une manière de prendre soin.

albums.title: Tendon Studies
albums.label: Pihka Editions
albums.notes: On her debut album for Pihka Editions, Tampere’s Aino Kuurasto gives the spare songs of her 2023 performances a quietly contrapuntal frame. Felt-muted kantele, rasping wooden preparations and fingertip-worn guitar keep time at bodily scale; the quartet occupies a room beyond her close, warm alto. Tendon Studies follows one ordinary day after competition, finding its stakes in sleeves, distances and accepting help. The lopsided, entirely plucked momentum of “Sleeve First” is its rhythmic fulcrum; “Enough for Two” earns an orchestral release without drums. By “Within Reach,” recovery sounds less like a destination than tomorrow’s clothes laid out tonight.

albums.title: Dessert for Estranged Relations
albums.label: Sideboard Recordings
albums.notes: On their seventh release, The Lacquer Picnic return to the family table with less interest in winning the conversation than keeping a place open. Recorded largely live, these songs preserve guitar-finger noise, separate breaths and the grain of older harmonies; woodwinds enter sparingly, each with something consequential to say. The buoyant, irregular phrases of “Everybody Brings Something” give way to the exposed grief of “One More Setting.” From there, the record patiently gathers its strength. The continuous closing pair, “Room at the End” and “Until the Cups Are Empty,” turns bassoon, rising strings and competing recollections toward a shared, unadorned melody.
